      Section 8 · Mind-map branch 05, model optimisation

      Prompting, RAG and fine-tuning

      About 25 minutes · Builds on Section 7

      • The three ways to make an LLM fit your task
      • How to write a good prompt: zero-shot, few-shot, chain of thought, system prompts
      • What RAG adds, in one picture
      • Full fine-tuning vs LoRA, and catastrophic forgetting
      • A decision flowchart for choosing, and how to combine all three
      In one line

      You can improve an LLM's answers in three ways: write better instructions (prompt engineering), hand it the right facts at question time (RAG), or retrain its weights on your examples (fine-tuning), and the cheapest one that works is usually the right one.

      8.1The problem these methods solve

      A general model out of the box has three gaps: it doesn't know your private data (your policies, products, customers), it doesn't know anything after its training cut-off, and it doesn't naturally follow your style and format.

      IBM's example: "Who is Martin Keen?"
      • Plain model: may confuse him with the founder of the Keen shoe company, or give an outdated answer.
      • Better prompt: "Who is Martin Keen, the Master Inventor at IBM?" points the model's attention to the right facts it already knows.
      • RAG: the system looks up his current biography on the company wiki and gives it to the model with the question, so the answer is current and can cite its source.
      • Fine-tuning: train the model on transcripts of his videos, and it learns to answer in his style without needing to look anything up.

      8.2The three methods side by side

      Prompt engineering

      Changes: only the input text.
      Adds new knowledge? No, it uses what the model already knows.
      Cost: almost nothing; instant to try.

      RAG

      Changes: the input, by adding retrieved documents.
      Adds new knowledge? Yes, fresh and private facts, at question time.
      Cost: a search pipeline and vector database; slightly slower answers.

      Fine-tuning

      Changes: the model's weights.
      Adds new knowledge? Mostly teaches behaviour, style and format; facts get frozen in.
      Cost: GPUs, training data, and retraining when things change.

      8.3Prompt engineering

      A prompt is everything you send the model. Good prompts read like a clear brief to a capable new colleague. Most strong prompts contain these parts:

      PartExample
      Role"You are a support assistant for an online electronics shop."
      Task"Classify the customer message into one category."
      Context"Categories: Delivery, Refund, Technical, Other. Refunds are allowed within 30 days."
      ExamplesTwo or three sample messages with the right category.
      Output format"Reply with only the category name."
      Constraints"If unsure, answer Other. Never invent order numbers."

      The main techniques

      Zero-shot

      Just ask, with no examples. Fine for simple, common tasks.

      Few-shot

      Include a few input → output examples so the model copies the pattern and format.

      Chain of thought

      Ask it to reason step by step before answering. Helps with maths, logic and multi-step problems.

      System prompt

      Standing instructions (role, rules, tone) that apply to the whole conversation. Every chatbot and agent has one.

      Weak prompt

      "Summarise this."

      Strong prompt

      "Summarise this customer complaint for a support manager in 3 bullet points: the problem, what the customer wants, and how urgent it is (low / medium / high). Use only facts from the text."

      Python · a few-shot prompt as a string
      prompt = """Classify each customer message as Delivery, Refund, Technical or Other.
Reply with the category only.

Message: My parcel says delivered but I never got it.
Category: Delivery

Message: The speaker turns off after five minutes.
Category: Technical

Message: I returned the shoes last week, where is my money?
Category:"""
# Sent to an LLM at low temperature, the expected reply is: Refund
      Think of it like

      Giving directions to a taxi driver who knows the city well. You can't teach them new roads by talking, but a clear destination, a landmark and "take the fastest route" gets you somewhere much better than "drive me somewhere nice".

      8.4RAG in one picture

      Retrieval-augmented generation adds a search step before the model answers. Section 12 covers how the search works (embeddings and vector databases); here is the idea.

      8.5Fine-tuning

      Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on your own examples: pairs of inputs and the outputs you want. It uses the same loss-and-backpropagation process as Section 6, so the model's weights change.

      Training data · a few lines of a typical JSONL file
      {"prompt": "Where is order 4471?", "completion": "It left today; 2–3 days to you. 📦"}
{"prompt": "Can I change my address?", "completion": "Sure! Send it and we'll update it."}
{"prompt": "The app keeps crashing.", "completion": "Sorry! Please update the app first."}

      JSONL means one complete JSON example per line, so the lines can't be wrapped. Real examples are usually longer than these.

      Hundreds or thousands of such examples teach the model your tone, format and typical moves. Two ways to do it:

      Full fine-tuning

      Updates all the weights. Most powerful, but needs big GPUs, creates a whole new model to store and host, and risks catastrophic forgetting.

      Parameter-efficient (PEFT, e.g. LoRA)

      Freezes the original weights and trains a small add-on (often under 1% of the size). Much cheaper; one base model can serve many small add-ons.

      Think of it like (IBM's analogy)

      A cold draught under the door. Full fine-tuning is knocking down walls and rebuilding the house to fix it, then building a new garage for the tools. PEFT is putting a draught stopper under the door: the house stays the same, the problem is fixed.

      Catastrophic forgetting

      When a model is heavily fine-tuned on a narrow dataset, it can lose general abilities it had before. A model tuned only on legal contracts might get worse at ordinary conversation or maths. RAG avoids this because it never changes the weights.

      8.6Comparison matrix

      Prompt engineeringRAGFine-tuning
      Main purposeGuide focus and formatGive fresh or private factsTeach behaviour, style, specialised skills
      Model weightsUnchangedUnchangedChanged
      New knowledgeNoneYes, live from your documentsFrozen at training time
      Speed of answersFastSlower (search step)Fast
      What you needNothing extraEmbedding model and vector databaseTraining data and GPUs
      Main riskBrittle prompts, limited reachRetrieving the wrong passagesCost, forgetting, going stale

      8.7Which one should I use?

      Real world
      • Hospital assistant: patient records change every hour, so RAG pulls the latest records securely at question time. Fine-tuning would be stale the next day.
      • Customer support: fine-tune (or LoRA) for the brand's friendly tone, plus RAG for live order status.
      • Law firm (all three): RAG retrieves recent case law; fine-tuning teaches the firm's drafting style; a prompt template formats the output as a court filing.
      • Internal HR bot: often just a good prompt plus RAG over the policy handbook.
      Common mistakes
      • Fine-tuning to teach facts that change. Use RAG for knowledge; fine-tune for behaviour.
      • Skipping prompt work. A clear prompt with examples often solves the problem for free.
      • Building RAG on messy documents. If retrieval finds the wrong passage, the model confidently answers from it.
      • Judging changes by "it looks better". Keep a small test set and measure before and after.

      8.8Key terms

      TermMeaning
      Prompt engineeringDesigning the input so the model does what you want.
      Zero-shot / few-shotAsking without examples / with a few examples.
      Chain of thoughtAsking the model to reason step by step.
      System promptStanding instructions for the whole conversation.
      RAGRetrieving relevant documents and adding them to the prompt.
      Fine-tuningFurther training that changes the model's weights.
      PEFT / LoRAFine-tuning a small add-on while the base model stays frozen.
      Catastrophic forgettingLosing general skills after narrow fine-tuning.

      8.9Key takeaways

      • Prompting changes the question, RAG changes what the model reads, fine-tuning changes the model.
      • Start with the prompt. It is free and fast to iterate.
      • Use RAG for facts that are private, recent or changing; it also gives sources.
      • Use fine-tuning (LoRA first) for consistent style, format or specialised behaviour.
      • Real systems often combine all three.

      8.10Quick check

      A hospital assistant must answer from patient records that update all day. Which method?

      RAG. The data changes constantly and is private; RAG fetches the latest records at question time, gives sources, and never bakes patient data into the model's weights.

      What is catastrophic forgetting, and why doesn't RAG have it?

      A model losing general abilities after heavy fine-tuning on narrow data. RAG leaves the weights untouched, so nothing is overwritten; new knowledge arrives only in the prompt.

      Your bot answers correctly but in the wrong tone and format every time, and you have 2,000 examples of ideal replies. What do you try?

      First tighten the prompt with a few examples. If that is not enough, fine-tune with a parameter-efficient method such as LoRA using the 2,000 examples.

      Put the three methods in order from cheapest to most expensive to try.

      Prompt engineering, then RAG, then fine-tuning.

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering: Optimizing AI Models"; "What Makes Large Language Models Expensive?" (PEFT analogy)
      • Reference guide: AI Fundamentals-2, Modules 5 and 6
      ← Generative AI and LLMsNext: Natural language processing →
      Section 9 · Mind-map branch 06

      Natural language processing

      About 20 minutes · Builds on Sections 5 and 7

      • What NLP, NLU and NLG are, and how they connect
      • Why human language is hard for computers
      • The classic pipeline: tokenization, POS tagging, stemming or lemmatization, NER
      • Common NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis and summarisation
      • How a chatbot turns a message into an action and a reply
      In one line

      Natural language processing is the part of AI that lets computers understand, interpret and produce human language, acting as the bridge between messy human text or speech and the structured data that software can act on.

      9.1The bridge between people and data

      Software works with structured data: fields, values, commands. People speak in unstructured sentences. NLP translates in both directions. Its two halves have their own names:

      • NLU (natural language understanding): text → meaning. Reading comprehension for machines.
      • NLG (natural language generation): data → text. Writing for machines.

      9.2Why language is hard

      The same word can mean different things depending on its neighbours, and people rely on context constantly:

      "current"

      "Alice swam against the current" → flowing water (a noun).
      "The current version is in the cloud" → latest (an adjective).

      "make"

      "I will make dinner" → a verb.
      "What make is your laptop?" → a noun meaning brand.

      Idioms

      "It's raining cats and dogs" is about weather, not animals. Word-by-word processing gets this badly wrong.

      9.3The classic NLP pipeline

      Before LLMs, NLP systems were built as a chain of tools, each adding a layer of structure. These tools are still used in search engines, data cleaning and high-volume systems where an LLM would be too slow or costly.

      StepWhat it doesExample
      TokenizationSplits text into units (tokens)"I'm running late" → I · 'm · running · late
      POS taggingLabels each word's grammatical role from context"make dinner" → verb; "what make" → noun
      StemmingChops off word endings with simple rules; fast but cruderunning → run; studies → studi; ran → ran (misses it)
      LemmatizationFinds the real dictionary root using vocabulary and grammarran → run; studies → study; better → good
      NERFinds and labels named things"Ralph flew to Arizona on Monday" → Ralph = Person, Arizona = Place, Monday = Date
      Python · stemming vs lemmatization with NLTK
      from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer, WordNetLemmatizer
# first time only: import nltk; nltk.download("wordnet")

stem = PorterStemmer()
lemma = WordNetLemmatizer()

words = [("running", "v"), ("ran", "v"), ("studies", "n"),
         ("better", "a"), ("university", "n"), ("universal", "a")]
for w, pos in words:                      # pos: v = verb, n = noun, a = adjective
    print(f"{w:<11} stem: {stem.stem(w):<8} lemma: {lemma.lemmatize(w, pos)}")
      running stem: run lemma: run ran stem: ran lemma: run studies stem: studi lemma: study better stem: better lemma: good university stem: univers lemma: university universal stem: univers lemma: universal

      Notice the stemmer's two failures: it can't handle the irregular "ran", and it squashes "university" and "universal" into the same stem even though they mean different things. The lemmatizer gets all of them right because it uses a dictionary, but it is slower and needs to know each word's part of speech.

      9.4Common NLP tasks

      Sentiment analysis

      Is this review or email positive, negative or neutral? Used to flag angry customers.

      Text classification

      Sort text into categories: route a ticket to Billing or Technical.

      Entity extraction

      Pull names, amounts, dates and IDs out of documents such as invoices.

      Summarisation

      Condense a long report or meeting transcript.

      Question answering

      Answer questions from a document or knowledge base.

      Translation

      Convert between languages (Section 10).

      9.5How NLG writes a sentence

      Generating good text from data happens in three stages, whether a template system or an LLM does it:

      1. Text planning: decide what to say and in what order ("roses in stock, then offer to order").
      2. Sentence planning: choose sentence structure, word choice and where sentences break.
      3. Realisation: apply grammar so the final text is correct (the past tense of "run" is "ran", not "runned").

      9.6Inside a chatbot

      Think of it like

      A good waiter. They listen to your order in your own words (NLU), write it on a ticket in kitchen shorthand (structured data), the kitchen cooks it (backend), and they come back and tell you in friendly words that it's ready (NLG).

      Classic pipeline vs LLM

      A modern LLM does tokenization, tagging, entity recognition, understanding and generation implicitly inside one model, so many new chatbots simply prompt an LLM. The classic tools still matter for speed, cost and control: running sentiment on a million reviews with a small classifier costs a tiny fraction of sending them all to an LLM.

      Real world
      • Banking chatbots verify you, fetch your balance from the core banking system and reply, without a human teller (IBM's "Birdie" example).
      • Email: Smart Reply suggestions and spam filtering are NLP.
      • Support desks run sentiment analysis so angry or urgent emails jump the queue.
      • Voice assistants turn speech into text, then NLU decides the command ("set an alarm for 6").
      • Finance and legal teams extract parties, dates and amounts from contracts automatically.
      Common mistakes
      • Thinking NLP and LLM mean the same thing. LLMs are one (very powerful) way to do NLP.
      • Using stemming where meaning matters; it merges words like "university" and "universal".
      • Ignoring languages other than English. Tokenizers and models often work less well on Hindi, Tamil or mixed "Hinglish" text; test with real user messages.
      • Letting a chatbot invent facts. Facts such as stock levels or balances should come from the backend, not from the language model.

      9.7Key terms

      TermMeaning
      NLPThe field of AI for understanding and generating human language.
      NLU / NLGTurning text into structured meaning / turning data into text.
      TokenizationSplitting text into tokens.
      StemmingCrude rule-based removal of word endings.
      LemmatizationDictionary-based reduction to the root word.
      POS taggingLabelling each word's grammatical role.
      NERFinding names of people, places, organisations, dates.
      Intent / entityWhat the user wants / the details in their request.
      Sentiment analysisDetecting positive, negative or neutral tone.

      9.8Key takeaways

      • NLP bridges unstructured language and structured data: NLU reads, NLG writes.
      • Language is ambiguous; context decides meaning.
      • The classic pipeline is tokenization → POS tagging → stemming or lemmatization → NER. POS tagging comes before lemmatization because a lemmatizer needs each word's part of speech.
      • Lemmatization is more accurate than stemming; stemming is faster.
      • Chatbots find the intent and entities, call a backend for facts, then generate a reply.

      9.9Quick check

      What is the difference between stemming and lemmatization? Give an example where stemming fails.

      Stemming chops word endings with simple rules; lemmatization uses a dictionary and grammar to find the true root. Stemming turns "ran" into "ran" (it misses the irregular form) and merges "university" and "universal" into "univers"; lemmatization gives "run", "university" and "universal".

      In "Book a flight to Delhi for Friday", what is the intent and what are the entities?

      Intent: book_flight. Entities: destination = Delhi, date = Friday.

      Name the three stages of NLG.

      Text planning (what to say), sentence planning (how to structure it) and realisation (correct grammar and word forms).

      Why should a chatbot get the stock level from a database rather than from the LLM?

      The LLM does not know your live inventory and may invent a number. Facts must come from the system of record; the LLM only phrases the reply.

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "NLP vs NLU vs NLG"; "What is NLP (Natural Language Processing)?"; "What is a Chatbot?"
      • Reference guide: AI Fundamentals-2, Module 4
      ← Prompting, RAG and fine-tuningNext: Machine translation →
      Section 10 · Mind-map branch 07

      Machine translation

      About 12 minutes · Builds on Sections 6 and 9

      • Why translation is a big business problem
      • The four generations: rule-based, statistical, neural, LLM
      • How encoder–decoder models and attention translate a sentence
      • How to use an LLM for translation safely
      In one line

      Machine translation is software that converts text or speech from one language to another; modern systems read the whole sentence, capture its meaning, and then write it in the target language, instead of swapping words one by one.

      10.1Why it matters

      Most people online are not native English speakers. IBM's figures: over 75% of internet users are non-native English speakers, more than 65% prefer content in their own language, and over 70% expect customer support in it. In India alone the Constitution recognises 22 scheduled languages, so a product that only speaks English leaves most potential customers behind.

      10.2Four generations of machine translation

      ApproachHow it worksStrengthWeakness
      Rule-based (RBMT)Linguists write grammar rules and bilingual dictionariesPredictableHuge effort; stiff, literal output
      Statistical (SMT)Learns which phrases usually translate to which, from millions of human translationsLearns from dataTranslates in chunks; poor grammar over long sentences
      Neural (NMT)A neural network reads the whole sentence and generates the translationFluent, handles contextNeeds lots of parallel text; weaker on rare languages
      LLM-basedA large Transformer model translates as one of many language skillsHandles tone, idioms, instructions, glossariesCan hallucinate or drop content; costlier per word
      A famous cautionary tale

      A well-known (possibly embellished) story tells of an early system translating "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak" into Russian and back, producing "The vodka is good, but the meat is rotten." Whether or not it happened exactly, it shows the problem with word-by-word translation: "spirit" and "flesh" were swapped for the wrong senses. Modern systems model the meaning of the whole sentence to avoid this.

      10.3How neural translation works: encoder, decoder and attention

      Attention matters most when languages order words differently. English puts the verb in the middle; Hindi usually puts it at the end:

      Think of it like

      A pocket dictionary versus a professional interpreter. With the dictionary you translate word by word and get nonsense for idioms. The interpreter listens to the whole sentence first (encoder), keeps glancing back at the key words while speaking (attention), and then says it naturally in the other language (decoder).

      10.4When is machine translation safe to use?

      10.5Worked example: an LLM translation prompt

      LLMs translate well when you give them the context a human translator would ask for: audience, tone, and terms that must not change.

      Prompt · translation with a glossary
      Translate the customer message below from English to Hindi.

Audience: everyday shoppers on a mobile app.
Tone: friendly and simple; use everyday Hindi, not formal Sanskrit-heavy words.
Keep these terms in English exactly as written: "Cash on Delivery", "OTP", "QuickCart".
Do not add or remove information. If something is ambiguous, keep it ambiguous.

Message:
"Your QuickCart order is on its way. Share the OTP with the delivery partner
only when you receive the parcel. Cash on Delivery orders must be paid in full."

      Translation quality is measured with automatic scores (such as BLEU, which compares output with human reference translations) and, for anything important, with native speakers rating fluency and accuracy.

      Real world
      • Shopping apps show product listings and support chats in regional languages.
      • Camera translation in phone apps reads a menu or sign and overlays the translation.
      • Live captions combine speech recognition with translation for video calls and lectures.
      • Global companies translate documentation and help centres automatically, with human review for key pages.
      • Government services translate forms and notices so citizens can read them in their own language.
      Common mistakes
      • Publishing machine-translated legal or medical text without expert review.
      • Letting brand names, product codes or legal terms get translated. Use a glossary.
      • Assuming every language works equally well. Languages with less training data ("low-resource" languages) get noticeably worse results.
      • Checking translations only by translating back to English. Back-translation can hide errors; ask a native speaker.

      10.6Key terms

      TermMeaning
      RBMT / SMT / NMTRule-based / statistical / neural machine translation.
      Parallel corpusLarge collections of the same texts in two languages, used for training.
      Sequence-to-sequenceA model that maps an input sequence to an output sequence (encoder + decoder).
      AttentionLets the decoder focus on the most relevant source words for each output word.
      BLEUAn automatic score comparing machine output with human translations.
      Low-resource languageA language with little digital training text.

      10.7Key takeaways

      • Translation evolved from hand-written rules, to statistics, to neural networks, to LLMs.
      • Encoder–decoder models read the whole sentence, then write; attention links each output word to the right input words.
      • LLMs add control: tone, audience and glossaries can be set in the prompt.
      • Human review is essential for legal, medical and brand-critical text.

      10.8Quick check

      Why does word-by-word translation fail on idioms?

      An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words. Only a system that models the meaning of the whole phrase or sentence can find the equivalent expression.

      What job does attention do in a translation model?

      For each word the decoder writes, attention weights the source words by relevance, so the model looks at the right input word even when the two languages order words differently.

      Your company wants to translate its medicine dosage leaflets. What process do you propose?

      Machine translation for a first draft, then review and sign-off by a qualified medical translator. Errors could harm patients, so automatic output alone is not acceptable.

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "AI and Large Language Models Boost Language Translation"; "NLP vs NLU vs NLG"
      • Reference guide: AI Fundamentals-2, Module 4
      ← Natural language processingNext: Computer vision and speech →
      Section 11 · New mind-map branch (added in the coverage review)

      Computer vision and speech

      About 18 minutes · Builds on Section 6

      • The four core vision tasks: classification, detection, segmentation, OCR
      • How a vision system goes from camera to decision
      • How speech recognition and text-to-speech work
      • How a voice assistant chains speech and language AI
      • How vision and speech quality are measured (IoU, word error rate)
      In one line

      Computer vision lets machines understand images and video, and speech AI lets them turn spoken audio into text and text back into natural speech; together they give AI systems "eyes and ears".

      This branch was not in the original mind map. It was added because perception (seeing and hearing) is one of the core abilities of AI and appears in many of the use cases in Section 19.

      11.1Four things a vision model can tell you

      TaskOutputExample
      Image classificationOne label for the whole image"Defective" or "OK" for a photo of a part
      Object detectionA box, label and confidence for each objectCounting cars at a junction; spotting a helmet on a worker
      SegmentationThe exact outline (every pixel) of each objectOutlining a tumour on a scan; road vs pavement for self-driving
      OCRThe text in an imageReading invoices, ID cards, number plates

      Vision models are usually CNNs (Section 6) or newer vision transformers, and almost always start from a model pre-trained on millions of images. Many modern LLMs are multimodal and can also describe or answer questions about an image.

      11.2From camera to decision

      Think of it like

      A trainee quality inspector who has studied thousands of photos of good and bad parts. They are fast and never tired, but when they are unsure they call a senior inspector. The confidence threshold is the rule for when to call.

      11.3Speech: listening and talking

      Speech recognition (ASR)

      Audio → text. The sound wave is turned into a picture of frequencies over time (a spectrogram), and a neural network turns that into words. Used for voice typing, captions and call transcripts.

      Text-to-speech (TTS)

      Text → audio. Modern neural TTS produces natural voices with pauses and emphasis. Used by assistants, navigation and screen readers.

      11.4Measuring quality

      IoU (intersection over union)

      For detection: how much the predicted box overlaps the true box. 1.0 is a perfect match; above 0.5 is usually counted as a correct detection.

      WER (word error rate)

      For speech: (substituted + deleted + inserted words) ÷ words in the correct transcript. If a 10-word sentence has 1 wrong word and 1 missing word, WER = 2 ÷ 10 = 20%.

      Python · IoU of two boxes
      def iou(a, b):
    """Boxes are (x1, y1, x2, y2): top-left and bottom-right corners."""
    x1, y1 = max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1])
    x2, y2 = min(a[2], b[2]), min(a[3], b[3])
    inter = max(0, x2 - x1) * max(0, y2 - y1)          # overlapping area
    area = lambda r: (r[2] - r[0]) * (r[3] - r[1])
    return inter / (area(a) + area(b) - inter)

print(round(iou((10, 10, 60, 60), (30, 30, 80, 80)), 2))   # poor overlap
print(round(iou((10, 10, 60, 60), (12, 12, 62, 62)), 2))   # good overlap
      0.22 0.85
      Python · transcribing audio with an open-source model (needs a download)
      # pip install openai-whisper   (also needs ffmpeg)
import whisper

model = whisper.load_model("small")             # a mid-sized speech model
result = model.transcribe("support_call.mp3")   # language is detected automatically
print(result["text"])
      Real world
      • Manufacturing: cameras check welds, labels and surface defects on every item, not just a sample.
      • Healthcare: models highlight suspicious areas on X-rays and mammograms for radiologists.
      • Banking and telecom onboarding: OCR reads ID documents, and face matching checks the selfie against the ID photo.
      • Traffic: number-plate recognition for tolls and parking.
      • Retail: shelf cameras spot empty or misplaced products.
      • Call centres: every call is transcribed, then summarised and scored for sentiment.
      • Accessibility: live captions for deaf users; screen readers and image descriptions for blind users.
      Common mistakes
      • Training on clean, well-lit photos and deploying in a dusty, dim factory. Collect training images from the real cameras.
      • Testing speech recognition only on one accent. Test with the accents, languages and background noise your users really have.
      • Using face recognition without consent and a legal basis. Faces and voices are sensitive personal data.
      • Trusting OCR on handwriting or blurry scans without a confidence check and a human fallback.

      11.5Key terms

      TermMeaning
      Computer visionAI that understands images and video.
      Classification / detection / segmentationOne label / boxes around objects / exact pixel outlines.
      OCRReading text from images.
      Vision transformerA Transformer model applied to image patches.
      ASR / TTSSpeech to text / text to speech.
      SpectrogramA picture of sound frequencies over time.
      IoUOverlap score between predicted and true boxes.
      WERShare of words a transcript gets wrong.

      11.6Key takeaways

      • Vision tasks go from coarse to fine: classification, detection, segmentation; OCR reads text.
      • A vision model gives predictions and confidence; business rules and people decide the action.
      • Speech AI has two directions: ASR (listen) and TTS (speak).
      • Voice assistants chain ASR, NLU, action, NLG and TTS, so early errors spread.
      • Train and test on real-world conditions, and treat faces and voices as sensitive data.

      11.7Quick check

      You need to count the people in each frame of a shop's camera feed. Which vision task?

      Object detection: it finds and boxes each person, so you can count the boxes.

      A transcript of a 20-word sentence has 2 wrong words and 1 extra word. What is the WER?

      (2 substitutions + 1 insertion) ÷ 20 = 3 ÷ 20 = 15%.

      Why is a confidence threshold with a human fallback useful in visual inspection?

      The model is reliable when it is very sure but makes mistakes in unclear cases. Sending the uncertain middle band to a person catches those mistakes without slowing down the clear cases.

      Sources and further watching

      • Added topic: standard introductory computer vision and speech concepts. Related IBM Technology videos: "Ten Everyday Machine Learning Use Cases" (voice assistants, phone photography, healthcare imaging)
      • Reference guide: AI Fundamentals-2, Module 3 (use cases)
      ← Machine translationNext: Embeddings, vector databases and RAG →
      Section 12 · Mind-map branch 08

      Embeddings, vector databases, RAG and CAG

      About 30 minutes · Builds on Sections 7 and 8

      • What an embedding is and how "meaning" becomes numbers
      • What a vector database does
      • The full RAG pipeline: ingestion, chunking, retrieval, reranking, generation
      • Long context vs RAG vs CAG, and the "lost in the middle" effect
      • Context engineering: deciding what the model gets to read
      In one line

      RAG gives an LLM the right facts at the moment it answers: your documents are turned into embeddings (lists of numbers that capture meaning) and stored in a vector database, and for each question the closest passages are found and placed in the prompt.

      12.1Embeddings: meaning as numbers

      An embedding model turns a piece of text (or an image) into a vector: a long list of numbers, often 384 to 3,072 of them. It is trained so that texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions, even if they share no words. "How do I get my money back?" and "refund process" end up close together.

      Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity: 1 means pointing the same way (same meaning), near 0 means unrelated.

      Python · cosine similarity with toy 3-number embeddings
      import numpy as np

v = {"dog":     np.array([0.90, 0.80, 0.10]),
     "puppy":   np.array([0.85, 0.75, 0.20]),
     "invoice": np.array([0.10, 0.20, 0.95])}

cos = lambda a, b: a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
print("dog vs puppy:  ", round(cos(v["dog"], v["puppy"]), 3))
print("dog vs invoice:", round(cos(v["dog"], v["invoice"]), 3))
      dog vs puppy: 0.996 dog vs invoice: 0.293

      12.2Vector databases

      A vector database stores each chunk of text with its embedding and some metadata (source file, page, date, who may see it), and can find the nearest vectors to a query among millions in milliseconds, using approximate nearest-neighbour indexes. Examples include pgvector (inside PostgreSQL), Milvus, Pinecone, Weaviate and Chroma; FAISS is a popular library for the same job.

      Think of it like

      A librarian who has read every book and shelved them by topic rather than by title. Ask about "getting money back" and they walk straight to the shelf about refunds, even though your words don't appear in any title.

      12.3The full RAG pipeline

      RAG has two phases. Ingestion runs ahead of time (and again whenever documents change). Retrieval and generation run for every question.

      StepWhy it mattersPractical tip
      ConversionGarbage in, garbage out. PDFs hide tables, columns and headers that naive extraction scrambles.Use a layout-aware converter (IBM's Docling is one) that outputs Markdown with tables intact.
      ChunkingChunks too big dilute the match; too small lose context.Start around 200–500 words with some overlap; split on headings where possible.
      MetadataLets you filter by date, product or permission.Never let a user retrieve chunks from documents they are not allowed to see.
      Hybrid searchVectors catch meaning; keyword search catches exact codes and names ("error E-4012").Combine both, then merge the results.
      RerankingA second, more careful model re-scores the top candidates.Retrieve ~20, rerank, keep the best 3–5.
      PromptTells the model to answer only from the passages.Ask for citations and for "I don't know" when the passages don't answer it.

      12.4Worked example: retrieval going right and wrong

      This runnable sketch uses TF-IDF, a keyword-based method, in place of a real embedding model so it runs with only scikit-learn installed.

      Python · retrieve the best chunks for a question
      from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

chunks = [
    "Refunds are issued within 7 working days after the returned item reaches our warehouse.",
    "Standard delivery takes 3 to 5 days. Express delivery arrives the next day in metro cities.",
    "Items can be returned within 30 days if they are unused and in the original packaging.",
    "We accept UPI, credit cards, debit cards and cash on delivery.",
]
question = "How many days until I get my refund after returning an item?"

vec = TfidfVectorizer().fit(chunks + [question])
scores = cosine_similarity(vec.transform([question]), vec.transform(chunks))[0]
for i in scores.argsort()[::-1][:2]:          # top 2 chunks
    print(round(scores[i], 2), chunks[i])
      0.16 Refunds are issued within 7 working days after the returned item reaches our warehouse. 0.03 Standard delivery takes 3 to 5 days. Express delivery arrives the next day in metro cities.

      The top hit is right. Second place is actually a tie: the delivery chunk and the returns chunk both score 0.028, because each shares only the word "days" with the question. Keyword matching can't see that "returning" and "returned", or "item" and "items", mean the same thing, so the returns chunk gets no extra credit. The tie is broken by the sort order alone, and the delivery chunk wins second place by luck. This is exactly why real systems use embeddings (which match meaning), hybrid search and reranking. Once retrieval works (here, the refund and returns chunks a better retriever would pick), the chunks go into a prompt like this:

      Prompt template · the "augment" step
      Answer the customer's question using ONLY the policy extracts below.
Quote the extract number you used, like [1]. If the extracts do not
contain the answer, say "I'm not sure, let me connect you to an agent."

[1] Refunds are issued within 7 working days after the returned item reaches our warehouse.
[2] Items can be returned within 30 days if they are unused and in the original packaging.

Question: How many days until I get my refund after returning an item?

      12.5Long context, RAG or CAG?

      Models now accept hundreds of thousands of tokens, so why not paste everything in? There are three ways to give a model knowledge, each with trade-offs:

      Long context

      Paste whole documents into the prompt. Simplest, but every question pays for all those tokens, answers get slower, and facts buried in the middle are often missed (the lost in the middle effect).

      RAG

      Retrieve only the relevant chunks. Scales to millions of documents and handles constantly changing data, but needs a retrieval pipeline that can miss things.

      CAG (cache-augmented generation)

      For a small, stable document set: process it once, save the model's internal working memory for it (the KV cache), and reuse that for every question. Very fast and cheap per question; must be rebuilt whenever the documents change.

      Prompt caching: CAG you already have

      Many LLM APIs offer prompt caching: if many requests start with the same long text (a policy handbook, a big system prompt), the provider caches it and charges much less for it on repeat requests. In IBM's HR-policy example, caching the stable policy set made answers roughly 10–40× faster and cut token costs by around 90% compared with resending everything.

      Context engineering

      Whatever the method, the model only knows what lands in its context window. Context engineering is the practice of deciding exactly what goes in: which instructions, which retrieved passages, which conversation history, which tool results, in what order, within the token budget. Many "the model is dumb" problems are really "the model was given the wrong context" problems.

      Think of it like (IBM's hardware-store analogy)

      RAG is the reference manuals aisle: it gives precise, grounded facts. Agent toolkits (Section 15) are the tools aisle: saws and drills that take action. Many real systems need both aisles.

      Real world
      • Employee help desks: RAG over HR, IT and finance policies, with answers linking to the source page.
      • Customer support: RAG over product manuals and past resolved tickets.
      • Legal and compliance: retrieve the exact clause or regulation and quote it.
      • Private, on-premises RAG: banks and hospitals run open-weight models and vector databases on their own servers so data never leaves the building.
      • Multimodal RAG: searching diagrams, scanned forms and images as well as text, using image embeddings.
      Common mistakes
      • Dumping raw PDFs into the vector store. Bad parsing of tables and columns is the most common cause of bad answers.
      • Ignoring permissions: a junior employee's question retrieving a confidential salary document.
      • Forgetting to re-index when documents change, so answers quote last year's policy.
      • Only checking the final answer. Check retrieval separately: did the right chunk come back at all?
      • Believing a big context window makes RAG unnecessary. Cost, speed and "lost in the middle" still apply.

      12.6Key terms

      TermMeaning
      EmbeddingA vector of numbers representing the meaning of text or an image.
      Embedding modelThe neural network that produces embeddings.
      Vector databaseStorage built for finding the nearest vectors quickly.
      Cosine similarityA closeness score between two vectors (1 = same direction).
      ChunkingSplitting documents into passages before embedding.
      Top-KThe K most similar chunks returned by a search.
      Hybrid searchCombining vector (meaning) search with keyword search.
      RerankerA model that re-scores retrieved chunks for relevance.
      Lost in the middleLLMs recall the start and end of long contexts better than the middle.
      KV cache / CAGSaved internal attention data / reusing it for fast answers on fixed knowledge.
      Context engineeringChoosing and arranging everything the model reads.

      12.7Key takeaways

      • Embeddings turn meaning into vectors; similar meanings are close together.
      • RAG = ingest (convert, chunk, embed, store) + answer (embed question, search, rerank, prompt, generate).
      • Retrieval quality decides answer quality: clean parsing, good chunks, hybrid search, reranking.
      • Use RAG for large or changing knowledge, caching (CAG) for small stable knowledge, and long context sparingly.
      • Always respect document permissions and keep the index up to date.

      12.8Quick check

      Why can embedding search find "refund process" for the question "how do I get my money back?"

      Because embeddings represent meaning, not exact words. Both phrases have similar meaning, so their vectors are close, even with no words in common.

      Why not just paste a 2-million-token document set into every prompt?

      High cost per question, slow answers, and the "lost in the middle" effect, where the model misses facts buried in the middle of a very long context.

      When is CAG a better fit than RAG?

      When the knowledge base is small enough to fit in the context window and rarely changes (for example an HR policy handbook), so the pre-computed cache stays valid and every question is fast and cheap.

      Users search for the error code "E-4012" and RAG returns unrelated passages. What would you add?

      Hybrid search: add keyword search alongside vector search, because exact codes and names are matched better by keywords than by meaning.

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "CAG vs Long Context: How AI Models Use and Remember Information"; "RAG vs Agentic AI: How LLMs Connect Data for Smarter AI"; "What is Multimodal RAG?"; "ADK vs RAG: How to Choose the Right AI Stack"
      • Reference guides: AI Fundamental-1, Module 3; AI Fundamentals-2, Module 6

      Section 13 · Mind-map branch 09

      AI agents and memory

      About 30 minutes · Builds on Sections 7, 8 and 12

      • The difference between an LLM and an AI agent
      • The agentic harness: tools, memory and the loop
      • How tool use (function calling) works, with code
      • The ReAct pattern, workflows vs agents, agents vs business rules
      • The four memory types of the CoALA framework
      • Multi-agent systems and verification
      In one line

      An AI agent is an AI model wrapped in software that lets it pursue a goal on its own: it plans, uses tools to act, looks at the results, and repeats until the job is done, while remembering what it needs along the way.

      13.1From a brain in a jar to an agent

      An LLM on its own is a "brain in a jar": it can reason and write, but it cannot run code, open files, browse the web, or remember yesterday's conversation. What turns it into an agent is the agentic harness around it, the software that gives the brain hands, eyes and a notebook.

      LLM: "What does error 500 mean?"

      Returns a textbook explanation of an internal server error. Then it's your problem.

      Agent: "Fix the error 500 on checkout"

      Reads the logs, runs a diagnostic script, finds a broken database connection setting, proposes a patch, runs the tests, and reports back for approval.

      13.2The agentic loop

      Tool use (function calling)

      The model cannot run anything itself. Instead, the developer describes the available tools (a name, a description and the inputs), and the model replies with a structured request such as "call get_order_status with order_id = 4471". The harness runs the real function and sends the result back.

      Python · a minimal agent loop with tool use (needs an API key)
      import anthropic, json
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def get_order_status(order_id):                      # your real business code
    return {"order_id": order_id, "due": "2026-10-12", "status": "in transit"}

tools = [{
    "name": "get_order_status",
    "description": "Look up delivery status and due date for an order.",
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["order_id"]},
}]
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Is order 4471 late? Today is 14 Oct 2026."}]

for step in range(5):                                # always cap the loop
    reply = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=2000,
                                   tools=tools, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})
    if reply.stop_reason != "tool_use":              # model gave a final answer
        print(next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"))
        break
    results = []
    for block in reply.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":                 # model asked for a tool
            output = get_order_status(**block.input)
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": json.dumps(output)})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

      The ReAct pattern

      ReAct (reason + act) is the standard name for this loop: the model alternates between a short thought, an action, and reading the observation.

      Thought: I need the order's due date and status. Action: get_order_status(order_id="4471") Observation: due 2026-10-12, status in transit Thought: Today is 14 Oct, so it is 2 days late. Policy allows a coupon after 2 days. Action: issue_coupon(order_id="4471", value=100) Observation: coupon SAVE100 created Answer: Your order is 2 days late, sorry! Here is a ₹100 coupon: SAVE100.
      Think of it like

      A new employee with a laptop and a manager's checklist. You give them a goal ("sort out this customer's late order"), they decide the steps, use the company systems (tools), check the results, and come back when done or when they need approval for something big.

      13.3When to use an agent (and when not)

      Workflow

      Fixed steps written by a developer: always retrieve, then summarise, then email. Predictable, cheap, easy to test.

      Agent

      The model decides the steps at run time. Flexible for open-ended tasks, but less predictable and more expensive.

      Business rules

      IF order_age < 30 days AND not final_sale THEN approve refund. Instant, free, auditable, perfect for clear regulated decisions.

      13.4Memory: the four types (CoALA)

      Memory separates a forgetful chatbot from an agent that improves over time. The CoALA framework (Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents, from Princeton researchers) borrows four memory types from human psychology:

      MemoryHuman versionIn an agentExample
      WorkingWhat you're holding in mind right nowThe context window (like RAM): fast, temporary, cleared after the sessionThe current conversation and tool results
      SemanticFacts you knowKnowledge files, vector indexes, knowledge graphsagents.md with project conventions; RAG over the wiki
      ProceduralSkills you know how to doAgent skills: instruction files and scripts for specific tasksA "triage-incident" skill with steps to follow
      EpisodicExperiences you rememberDistilled notes from past sessions, what worked and what failed"Last week this error came from the middleware config"
      Progressive disclosure and forgetting

      An agent may have hundreds of skills, far too many to load at once. With progressive disclosure it keeps only a short index (name and one-line description, around 100 tokens each) in working memory and loads a skill's full instructions only when a task needs it. Equally important is forgetting: episodic memory that is never pruned fills the context with stale, misleading notes.

      13.5Multi-agent systems

      A single LLM has hallucinated confidence: it sounds equally sure when right and when wrong, because it has no built-in uncertainty meter. For high-stakes work, multi-agent systems borrow an idea from human institutions: no single person signs off alone.

      The Apollo 11 story

      During the 1969 Moon landing, the guidance computer raised unfamiliar "1201" and "1202" alarms. Instead of one person guessing, specialist controllers each checked their own data. Engineer Jack Garman recognised the alarms as the computer shedding low-priority work under overload, not a fatal fault, and Flight Director Gene Kranz's team called "GO". The landing continued safely. Specialisation plus cross-checking beat a single confident guess.

      Real world
      • Coding agents (Claude Code, Copilot agent mode, Cursor) read a repository, edit files, run tests and open pull requests.
      • IT operations: an agent receives an alert, queries logs and dashboards, runs diagnostics, and drafts an incident report for the on-call engineer.
      • Customer service: an agent checks the order, the policy and the photos, then issues a refund within its limit or hands over to a person.
      • Research assistants search the web, read sources and write a cited report.
      Common mistakes
      • Giving the agent more permissions than the task needs (for example, delete access to production).
      • No step limit or budget, so a confused agent loops forever and runs up a bill.
      • Using an agent where a fixed workflow or a rule would do; you pay in cost and unpredictability.
      • Letting agents take irreversible actions (payments, deletions, emails to customers) without human approval.
      • Trusting the agent's "done" without checking evidence such as test results.

      13.6Key terms

      TermMeaning
      AI agentA model plus harness that plans and acts with tools towards a goal.
      Agentic harnessThe runtime giving the model tools, memory and a loop.
      Tool use / function callingThe model requests a function call; the harness runs it and returns the result.
      ReActReason + act: alternating thoughts, actions and observations.
      agents.md / CLAUDE.mdInstruction files in a project that tell an agent the rules and commands.
      Context compactionSummarising old steps to stay within the context window.
      Working / semantic / procedural / episodic memoryCurrent context / facts / skills / past experiences.
      Progressive disclosureLoading full instructions only when needed.
      Multi-agent systemSeveral specialised agents coordinated by an orchestrator.
      Human-in-the-loopA person approves or corrects key steps.

      13.7Key takeaways

      • Model + harness = agent. The harness supplies tools, memory and the loop.
      • Agents loop: plan, act, observe, verify, until the goal is met or a limit is reached.
      • Function calling: the model asks, your code decides and executes.
      • Use rules for clear cases, workflows for fixed processes, agents for messy open-ended ones.
      • Memory comes in four types: working, semantic, procedural, episodic.
      • For high stakes, add verifiers, adversaries and human approval.

      13.8Quick check

      Two products use the same LLM, but one is far better at coding tasks. Why?

      The harness: the tools it exposes, how it searches files, how it manages and compacts context, and whether it verifies its work (runs tests, checks results).

      In function calling, who actually runs the function?

      Your code (the harness). The model only returns a structured request naming the tool and its inputs; the harness validates it, runs it and sends back the result.

      Which memory type is a "deploy-to-staging" skill file, and which is "last time the deploy failed because of a missing env variable"?

      The skill file is procedural memory. The lesson from last time is episodic memory.

      What does an adversary agent do in a multi-agent system?

      It deliberately tries to break the proposed solution: find edge cases, logical flaws, security holes or prompt-injection risks before anything is executed.

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "5 AI Agent Terms You Need to Know"; "AI Model vs Agentic Harness: What Actually Drives AI"; "AI Agents vs Business Rules: Which Should Make Decisions?"
      • IBM Technology: "The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent Needs"; "Skills vs MCP vs RAG vs Memory"; "Multi AI Agent Systems: When One AI Brain Isn't Enough"

      Section 14 · Mind-map branch 10

      APIs, MCP and A2A

      About 25 minutes · Builds on Section 13

      • What an API is, and REST in five minutes
      • The integration problem that MCP solves
      • MCP hosts, clients, servers, and the three primitives
      • How an agent discovers and calls tools at run time
      • A2A for agent-to-agent teamwork, and where gRPC fits
      In one line

      Protocols are agreed rules for how software talks: APIs let programs call each other, MCP gives AI agents one standard way to plug into tools and data, and A2A lets independent agents find each other and hand over work.

      14.1APIs: how programs talk

      An API (application programming interface) is a published set of requests a system accepts and the responses it gives back. Most web APIs follow the REST style: each thing is a URL (a "resource"), and HTTP methods say what to do with it.

      MethodMeaningExample
      GETReadGET /orders/4471 → the order's details
      POSTCreatePOST /orders with the cart → a new order
      PUT / PATCHUpdatePATCH /orders/4471 with a new address
      DELETERemoveDELETE /orders/4471 → cancel the order
      Think of it like

      A restaurant menu. You don't walk into the kitchen; you order from a fixed list in an agreed format, and the kitchen sends back the dish. The menu is the API.

      14.2The problem MCP solves

      Every API is different: its own URLs, parameters, login method and error format. Connecting an AI app to five systems meant writing five custom adapters, and every other AI app had to write the same five again. With M apps and N tools that is M × N integrations.

      Before: custom adapters

      Agent → adapter for GitHub API
      Agent → adapter for database
      Agent → adapter for Slack
      …each written and maintained by hand; tools fixed in code.

      With MCP: one standard plug

      Agent → MCP client → GitHub MCP server, database MCP server, Slack MCP server.
      Each server is written once, and every MCP-compatible app can use it.

      The Model Context Protocol (MCP) was released by Anthropic as an open standard in November 2024 and is now governed under the Linux Foundation. It is often described as USB-C for AI: one port shape for any device.

      14.3How MCP is built

      Tools

      Functions the model can run to act: create_issue, run_sql_query, send_message.

      Resources

      Read-only data the app can fetch for context: a file, a log, a database record.

      Prompts

      Ready-made prompt templates the server offers for common tasks.

      Dynamic discovery

      The key difference from a plain API: the agent asks the server at run time what it can do. Each tool comes with a natural-language description, so the model understands when and why to use it.

      JSON-RPC · what a tool call looks like on the wire
      {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/call",
 "params": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune"}}}

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7,
 "result": {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "31°C, clear skies"}]}}
      Python · a small MCP server with the official SDK (version 2)
      # pip install mcp      (in SDK 1.x this class was FastMCP, from mcp.server.fastmcp)
from mcp.server import MCPServer

mcp = MCPServer("orders")

@mcp.tool()
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the delivery status and due date of a customer order."""
    # In real code, call your orders database or REST API here.
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "in transit", "due": "2026-10-12"}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()          # stdio by default: a desktop app or IDE can launch it

      The function's name, type hints and docstring become the tool's schema and description automatically. That description is what the model reads, so write it as carefully as a prompt.

      REST APIMCP
      Built forAny software talking to any softwareAI apps and agents using tools and data
      InterfaceDifferent for every APISame shape for every server
      DiscoveryRead the docs, write code in advanceAsk the server at run time (tools/list)
      DescriptionsFor human developersFor the model, in natural language
      RelationshipThe underlying serviceUsually a wrapper around REST APIs, not a replacement

      14.4A2A: agents talking to agents

      MCP connects an agent down to its tools. The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, started by Google and also hosted by the Linux Foundation, connects agents sideways to other agents, even ones built by other companies on other frameworks. Each agent publishes an Agent Card: a JSON file describing what it can do, where to reach it and how to log in.

      JSON · a simplified Agent Card
      {
  "name": "Supplier Ordering Agent",
  "description": "Takes purchase requests for packaging materials and tracks delivery.",
  "url": "https://agents.example-supplier.com/a2a",
  "skills": [
    {"id": "place_order", "description": "Place a purchase order for listed SKUs"},
    {"id": "track_order", "description": "Report fulfilment status of an order"}
  ],
  "capabilities": {"streaming": true},
  "authentication": {"schemes": ["oauth2"]}
}
      Think of it like

      MCP is the toolbelt an employee wears: drill, tape, scanner. A2A is the business phone line between companies: you call the supplier's desk, explain what you need, and they keep you updated. You never see inside their warehouse.

      14.5Where gRPC fits

      gRPC is a fast, binary protocol (Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2) widely used between microservices. It is excellent for speed but carries no natural-language descriptions, so a model can't tell when or why to use a method. Agents reach gRPC services through an adapter layer, often an MCP server that wraps them.

      Real world
      • Developer tools: coding assistants connect to GitHub, Jira and databases through MCP servers.
      • Company CRM: write one MCP server for an in-house CRM, and it works in Claude Desktop, VS Code and your own Python agents.
      • Desktop apps: MCP servers for Google Drive, Slack or a local file system give a chat assistant controlled access to your work.
      • Procurement: buyer and supplier agents at different companies negotiate and track orders over A2A.
      Common mistakes
      • Installing unvetted third-party MCP servers. A server runs code with your access; treat it like any dependency.
      • Forgetting that tool results are untrusted input. A web page or email returned by a tool can contain hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection, Section 18).
      • Exposing dozens of tools with vague descriptions. The model picks the wrong one; keep tool sets small and clearly described.
      • Thinking MCP replaces APIs. It usually sits on top of them.

      14.6Key terms

      TermMeaning
      API / RESTA published interface between programs / a style using URLs and HTTP methods.
      MCPModel Context Protocol: one standard way for AI apps to use tools and data.
      MCP host / client / serverThe AI app / its connector to one server / the wrapper around a tool or data source.
      Tools, resources, promptsThe three things an MCP server can offer.
      JSON-RPC 2.0The simple text message format MCP and A2A use.
      stdio / HTTP streamingTransport for local servers / remote servers.
      A2A / Agent CardAgent-to-agent protocol / an agent's public description of its skills.
      gRPCA fast binary protocol between services.

      14.7Key takeaways

      • APIs let programs talk; REST uses URLs plus GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, DELETE.
      • MCP turns M × N custom integrations into one standard: build a server once, use it everywhere.
      • MCP servers offer tools, resources and prompts, discovered at run time with natural-language descriptions.
      • MCP connects agents to tools; A2A connects agents to agents; gRPC connects services fast.
      • Treat every MCP server and every tool result as a security boundary.

      14.8Quick check

      An agent must use five systems. Compare the effort with custom REST adapters and with MCP.

      With REST you write and maintain five custom adapters, and changes require code updates. With MCP the agent speaks one protocol to five servers (often already available), and discovers each server's tools at run time.

      How do local and remote MCP servers communicate?

      Local servers use standard input/output (stdio) on the same machine. Remote servers use HTTP with streaming responses.

      Why does MCP use readable JSON-RPC with descriptions instead of fast binary gRPC?

      The model needs to read natural-language descriptions of each tool and its inputs to decide when and how to call it. Binary formats are faster but meaningless to a language model.

      Your inventory agent needs to place an order with another company's agent. MCP or A2A?

      A2A: it lets your agent read the supplier agent's Agent Card, delegate the task and receive status updates, without either side exposing internal code.

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "MCP vs API: Simplifying AI Agent Integration with External Data"; "A2A vs MCP: AI Agent Communication Explained"; "MCP vs gRPC"; "MCP vs ADK"
      • Reference guides: AI Fundamental-1, Module 2; AI Fundamentals-2, Module 7

      Section 15 · Mind-map branch 11

      Frameworks, ADK and agent skills

      About 20 minutes · Builds on Sections 13 and 14

      • What agent frameworks do for you
      • The main framework families and their best-known members
      • How to pick a framework for a project
      • Graph-based orchestration, with a LangGraph sketch
      • Agent skills: SKILL.md files and progressive disclosure
      In one line

      Agent frameworks are libraries that supply the plumbing every AI app needs (model calls, tools, memory, loops, multi-agent coordination, tracing), and agent skills are packaged instructions that teach an agent how to do a specific job.

      15.1Why use a framework?

      You can build an agent with a plain API call and a loop (Section 13). But real projects quickly need the same extras: retries, memory, document loaders, vector store connectors, branching logic, saving state between steps, human approval pauses, and logs of every step. Frameworks provide these so you don't rebuild them each time.

      Think of it like

      Building a house with a ready-made frame and standard fittings instead of cutting every beam yourself. You still design the house, but you don't reinvent doors and plumbing.

      15.2The framework families

      FamilyIdeaGood for
      Linear workflows
      LangChain, LlamaIndex      		Chain steps in a fixed order; LlamaIndex specialises in data and RAGRAG apps, document Q&A, simple pipelines
      Stateful graphs
      LangGraph, Semantic Kernel      		Steps are nodes, transitions are edges; loops, branches, saved state, human pausesProduction agents that must be controllable and auditable
      Role-based teams
      CrewAI, ChatDev      		Define agents as roles with goals ("researcher", "writer") that hand work to each otherContent pipelines, simulated teams
      Conversational multi-agent
      AutoGen (Microsoft is folding it into Microsoft Agent Framework)      		Agents talk to each other freely to solve a problemResearch, exploratory problem solving
      Visual builders
      LangFlow, Flowise      		Drag-and-drop canvas that generates the flowQuick prototypes and demos
      Agent Development Kit (ADK)Google's toolkit built around agents, tools, memory, events and runnersBuilding and orchestrating multi-agent apps end to end

      15.3Choosing a framework

      15.4Graph orchestration in practice

      Graph frameworks model an app as a state (shared data), nodes (steps that update the state) and edges (which step comes next, possibly depending on the state). Here is a support-ticket flow:

      Python · the classify-and-route part in LangGraph
      from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

class Ticket(TypedDict):
    text: str
    category: str
    reply: str

def classify(state: Ticket):
    # In a real app, ask an LLM to classify; a keyword check keeps the sketch short.
    return {"category": "billing" if "invoice" in state["text"].lower() else "technical"}

def billing_agent(state: Ticket):
    return {"reply": "I've found your invoice and will resend it."}

def tech_agent(state: Ticket):
    return {"reply": "Try restarting the device, then update the firmware."}

graph = StateGraph(Ticket)
graph.add_node("classify", classify)
graph.add_node("billing", billing_agent)
graph.add_node("technical", tech_agent)
graph.add_edge(START, "classify")
graph.add_conditional_edges("classify", lambda s: s["category"],
                            {"billing": "billing", "technical": "technical"})
graph.add_edge("billing", END)
graph.add_edge("technical", END)

app = graph.compile()
print(app.invoke({"text": "Please resend my invoice"})["reply"])
      I've found your invoice and will resend it.

      15.5Agent skills

      An agent skill is a folder that teaches an agent how to do one kind of task. At its heart is a SKILL.md file: a short header with a name and a description, followed by step-by-step instructions. The folder can also hold scripts, templates and reference files. Skills are the agent's procedural memory (Section 13).

      SKILL.md · an example skill
      ---
name: incident-triage
description: Use when a production alert or 5xx error is reported. Gathers evidence and proposes a fix.
---

# Incident triage

1. Check the error rate on the monitoring dashboard for the last 30 minutes.
2. List deployments from the last 24 hours; a recent deploy is the most likely cause.
3. Run `scripts/collect_logs.sh <service>` and look for the first error.
4. If a deploy is the cause, propose a rollback. Never roll back without human approval.
5. Write a summary: impact, likely cause, evidence, proposed action.

      Skill

      Teaches how: a procedure, checklist or house style. "How we triage incidents."

      MCP server

      Gives access: a live connection to a system. "Read the monitoring dashboard."

      System prompt

      Always-on rules for every task. "Be concise; never share customer data."

      Real world
      • Document Q&A: LlamaIndex or LangChain to load PDFs, chunk them and run RAG.
      • Enterprise operations: LangGraph or Semantic Kernel for an incident agent with approval steps and full logs.
      • Content teams: a CrewAI crew where a researcher gathers sources, a writer drafts and an editor checks facts and style.
      • Coding agents: skills for "write a migration", "run our release checklist" or "follow our API style guide".
      • Hackathons and pilots: LangFlow or Flowise to show a working flow in an afternoon.
      Common mistakes
      • Choosing the most-starred framework instead of the one that fits the workflow.
      • Adding a heavy framework for a single model call. Plain SDK code is clearer for simple apps.
      • Hiding prompts deep inside framework defaults; you can't debug what you can't see. Turn on tracing.
      • Writing skill descriptions that are vague ("helps with stuff"); the agent then never loads the skill, or loads the wrong one.

      15.6Key terms

      TermMeaning
      Agent frameworkA library providing the building blocks for AI apps and agents.
      OrchestrationCoordinating the steps, tools and agents of an application.
      State / node / edgeShared data / a step / a transition in a graph framework.
      ADKAgent Development Kit: Google's toolkit of agents, tools, memory, events and runners.
      Agent skill / SKILL.mdA packaged procedure an agent can load; its instruction file.
      Progressive disclosureLoading a skill's details only when the task needs them.
      TracingRecording every model call, tool call and decision for debugging.

      15.7Key takeaways

      • Frameworks save you from rebuilding loops, memory, connectors and tracing.
      • Pick by workflow shape: linear (LangChain, LlamaIndex), graph (LangGraph), roles (CrewAI), open conversation (AutoGen), prototype (LangFlow, Flowise).
      • Graph frameworks make agent behaviour explicit, testable and auditable.
      • Skills teach procedures and load progressively; MCP gives access to systems.

      15.8Quick check

      A bank wants a production agent with fixed approval steps and a full audit trail. Which family?

      A stateful graph framework such as LangGraph or Semantic Kernel (or ADK), because the steps, branches and human approval points are explicit and every transition can be logged.

      What is the difference between an agent skill and an MCP server?

      A skill teaches the agent how to do a task (instructions, scripts). An MCP server gives it access to a live system (tools and data). An agent often uses a skill that tells it which MCP tools to call.

      Why does progressive disclosure matter when an agent has 200 skills?

      Loading all 200 full instruction files would fill the context window. Keeping only names and descriptions loaded, and opening a skill's body only when needed, keeps the agent fast, cheap and focused.

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "Agentic AI Frameworks Explained: Workflows, Multi-Agent, & Production"; "MCP vs ADK"; "What AI Agent Skills Are and How They Work"; "MCP vs Skills"

      Section 16 · Mind-map branch 12

      AI and software engineering

      About 18 minutes · Builds on Section 13

      • The five steps from traditional coding to agentic engineering
      • Deterministic code vs probabilistic AI behaviour
      • How agents.md / CLAUDE.md files steer coding agents
      • A safe workflow for working with a coding agent
      • How the developer's job is changing
      In one line

      AI is moving software development from writing every line by hand towards describing what you want and verifying what an AI produces; the engineer's job shifts from typing behaviour to shaping, constraining and checking it.

      16.1The spectrum of delegation

      StageWho writes the codeWho checks itExample
      TraditionalDeveloperDeveloper, reviewers, testsHand-written payment logic
      AI-assistedDeveloper, with suggestionsDeveloperTab-completing a function in the IDE
      Vibe codingAI, from plain-language requestsOften only "does it seem to work?"A weekend prototype or personal tool
      Agentic codingAgent, across many filesAgent runs tests; human reviews the change"Upgrade this library and fix what breaks"
      Agentic engineeringAgents, inside guardrailsAutomated evaluations, verification layers, humans at key gatesA team where agents handle routine changes under strict CI checks
      Deterministic vs probabilistic

      Traditional code is deterministic: input A always gives output B, so you test it once and trust it. AI output is probabilistic: the same request can produce different code, and some of it will be wrong. That is why agentic engineering is mostly about verification: tests, type checks, linters, reviews and limits on what the agent may do.

      16.2Instruction files: agents.md and CLAUDE.md

      Coding agents read a Markdown file in the project root (called AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or similar, depending on the tool) before they start. It is the project's standing brief: how to build, how to test, what style to follow, what never to do. Files can also sit in sub-folders; the one closest to the code being edited takes priority over the ones above it.

      AGENTS.md · an example project brief
      # Project: QuickCart checkout service

## Commands
- Install: `pnpm install`
- Test: `pnpm test` (must pass before every commit)
- Lint: `pnpm lint --fix`

## Rules
- TypeScript strict mode. No `any`.
- Money is stored in paise as integers, never floats.
- Never edit files in /migrations by hand; generate them with `pnpm db:migrate:new`.
- Do not add new dependencies without asking.

## Where things are
- API handlers: src/api/   · Business logic: src/domain/   · Tests: tests/
      Think of it like

      The onboarding document you would give a new contractor on day one: how to run the project, the house rules, and the things that will get them in trouble. The agent reads it every session, so it doesn't repeat the same mistakes.

      16.3A safe workflow with a coding agent

      Weak task

      "Fix the checkout bug."

      Strong task

      "Orders over ₹10,000 fail at checkout with error 500 since yesterday's deploy. Find the cause, add a failing test that reproduces it, then fix it. Don't change the payment provider code. Done means pnpm test passes."

      16.4Where AI helps across the lifecycle

      AI IDEs

      Editors with codebase-aware chat, multi-file edits and agent modes.

      AI code review

      Automated review comments for bugs, security issues and style before a human looks.

      Tests

      Generating unit tests, especially for old code that has none.

      Modernisation

      Explaining and untangling legacy code (COBOL, old Java) and migrating it.

      Docs and onboarding

      Explaining an unfamiliar repository; drafting docs and changelogs.

      Real world
      • Routine maintenance: agents bump dependency versions, fix the breaking changes and open a pull request with passing tests.
      • Legacy migration: banks and insurers use AI to explain and translate decades-old code, with heavy test coverage as the safety net.
      • Startups: founders vibe-code prototypes in days, then bring in engineers to harden them before real users arrive.
      • Security teams: AI review flags injection risks and leaked secrets in every pull request.
      Common mistakes
      • Merging AI code you don't understand. You are still responsible for it.
      • Vibe-coding something that handles money, health or personal data, then shipping it without tests or review.
      • Pasting secrets (API keys, passwords, customer data) into prompts.
      • Letting an agent run destructive commands (deleting data, force-pushing) without approval.
      • Skipping the instruction file, then correcting the same mistakes in every session.

      16.5Key terms

      TermMeaning
      AI-assisted codingAI suggests; the developer stays in control line by line.
      Vibe codingBuilding by describing intent and iterating on what the AI produces.
      Agentic codingAn agent plans, edits, runs and debugs code with light supervision.
      Agentic engineeringDesigning the environment, constraints and checks in which agents work.
      Deterministic / probabilisticSame input always gives same output / output varies by probability.
      AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.mdProject instruction files that coding agents read first.
      CI (continuous integration)Automatic tests and checks that run on every change.

      16.6Key takeaways

      • Development is moving along a spectrum from writing code to shaping and verifying AI-written code.
      • AI output is probabilistic, so tests, reviews and guardrails matter more, not less.
      • Instruction files give agents the project's rules every session.
      • Good tasks state the goal, the constraints and how to verify "done".
      • Agentic engineering does not remove engineering; it moves it to design, boundaries and verification.

      16.7Quick check

      What is the main difference between vibe coding and agentic engineering?

      Vibe coding relies on describing intent and accepting output that seems to work. Agentic engineering designs the environment around the agent: instruction files, tests, checks, permissions and review gates, so its output is verified.

      A monorepo has AGENTS.md at the root and another in /payments. Which applies when the agent edits /payments/refund.ts?

      Both are read, but the /payments file is closest to the code, so its rules take priority where they conflict with the root file.

      Write the three parts every good coding-agent task should include.

      The goal (what and why), the constraints (what not to touch, style rules), and the verification (how you will know it is done, such as specific tests passing).

      Sources and further watching

      • IBM Technology: "Agentic Engineering vs Software Engineering: Beyond Vibe Coding"; "AI Model vs Agentic Harness"; "5 AI Agent Terms You Need to Know"
      • Reference guide: AI Fundamental-1, Module 1
