      Senior developer notes · LangChain 1.x (Python)

      LangChain v1 Field Guide

      One document that takes you from "what is LangChain?" to building, controlling, testing and shipping production agents with LangChain v1. Every chapter has a plain explanation, a diagram where it helps, and runnable code.

      How to read this

      Parts I–III are the core: read them in order. Parts IV–VI can be read as needed. Part VII ties everything together in one project. Code targets langchain>=1.0 on Python 3.10+. Model names are examples; swap in whichever provider and model you use.

      Chapters marked with a green dot in the contents have Example boxes: simple flowcharts and code that show the idea in action. New to LangChain? Follow the recommended learning order.

      Chapter 1 · Foundations

      What is LangChain v1?

      LangChainnoun · open-source framework

      An open-source framework for building applications and agents powered by large language models (LLMs). It gives you one standard interface to any model provider, a library of integrations (tools, vector stores, loaders), and a ready-made agent you can customise. In v1, the centre of LangChain is create_agent: a production-ready agent loop built on the LangGraph runtime and customised through middleware.

      LangChain 1.0 was released in October 2025 as the first stable major version. The team kept the parts developers actually used, removed or relocated the rest, and committed to no breaking changes until 2.0. The short version of what changed:

      • One way to build agents. from langchain.agents import create_agent replaces LangGraph's create_react_agent. The older AgentExecutor and initialize_agent now live in langchain-classic.
      • Middleware lets you hook into every step of the agent loop (before the model call, around tool calls, after the agent finishes) for summarisation, human approval, PII redaction, retries and more.
      • Built on LangGraph. Every agent gets persistence, streaming, human-in-the-loop and time travel for free, because it runs as a LangGraph graph.
      • Standard content blocks. message.content_blocks gives the same shape for text, reasoning, tool calls and images across supported providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google GenAI, AWS and Ollama, with more being added). Citations appear as annotations on text blocks.
      • A slimmer package. The langchain namespace now holds only agents, models, messages, tools and embeddings. Old chains, retrievers and the hub moved to langchain-classic.
      Example

      Legacy LangChain vs LangChain v1

      The common agent path is now much shorter. You call create_agent(), and LangGraph runs the loop for you.

      Legacy (more explicit)LangChain v1
      LLMModel
      Agent setupcreate_agent()
      AgentAgent + tools
      Executor (AgentExecutor)LangGraph runtime
      Tool loopTool loop
      ResponseResponse

      Think of LangChain v1 as three layers you can choose between depending on how much control you need: LangChain (quick, high-level agents), LangGraph (custom workflows and full control) and Deep Agents (long-running agents with planning and sub-agents, built on LangChain).

      Example

      Without LangChain vs with LangChain

      An LLM on its own follows User → LLM → Answer. LangChain adds an application layer around the LLM, so it can decide when to use tools, fetch information, call APIs, do calculations and complete multi-step tasks.

      Real-world example

      Logistics TAT Assistant

      A user asks: "Why was plant TAT high yesterday?" (TAT = turnaround time, how long a vehicle spends in the plant.) The LLM does not know the company's vehicle records. A LangChain agent can investigate using controlled tools:

      The code for this agent is in Chapter 10.

      Example

      Each part, in plain words

      ComponentThink of it asExample
      LLMBrainGroq / OpenAI / Anthropic
      ToolHands / actionSQL query, API call, Python function
      AgentDecision makerChooses which tool to use
      MessagesCommunicationUser request / response
      MiddlewareSupervisorSecurity / logging / approval
      StateWorking notebookCurrent analysis
      LangGraphWorkflow engineComplex stateful workflow
      Easy definition

      LangChain connects an LLM to tools, data, APIs and application logic so it can perform useful multi-step tasks rather than only generate text.

      Chapter 2 · Foundations

      The problem LangChain solves

      Calling an LLM once is easy. Building a reliable application around it is not. As soon as you go past a single prompt you hit the same set of problems every team hits:

      ProblemWithout a frameworkLangChain v1 answer
      Provider lock-inEach SDK (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Ollama) has its own request and response format. Switching means rewriting.init_chat_model("provider:model") with one interface: invoke, stream, batch, bind_tools.
      Tool callingHand-write JSON schemas, parse tool calls, run functions, feed results back, loop until done.@tool builds the schema from your function. create_agent runs the loop.
      MemoryStore and trim conversation history yourself. Context windows overflow.Checkpointers save each thread. SummarizationMiddleware trims old turns.
      Using your own dataWrite loaders for PDFs, web pages and databases; chunk, embed and search them.Hundreds of document loaders, text splitters, embedding models and vector stores behind standard interfaces.
      Reliable outputAsk for JSON and hope. Parse, validate, retry.response_format=MySchema returns a validated Pydantic object.
      Safety and controlAgents can send emails or delete data with no checkpoint.HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses for approval; limits and PII middleware enforce policy.
      DebuggingPrint statements across a multi-step loop.LangSmith tracing shows every model call, tool call, token count and latency.

      The proof is how little code a working agent takes:

      first_agent.py
      from langchain.agents import create_agent

def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get the current weather for a city."""
    return f"It is always sunny in {city}!"

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",   # any "provider:model" string
    tools=[get_weather],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.",
)

result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Pune?"}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
      Chapter 3 · Foundations

      Where to use LangChain (and where not to)

      Customer support agents

      Look up orders, search the help centre, open tickets, hand off to a human for refunds.

      Chat with your documents

      RAG over PDFs, wikis, Confluence, SharePoint or a database, with cited answers.

      Internal copilots

      Agents that query SQL, call internal APIs, draft emails and fill forms for employees.

      Data extraction

      Turn invoices, resumes or contracts into validated structured records.

      Research assistants

      Search the web, read pages, plan, and write a report (Deep Agents).

      Multi-model products

      Apps that must switch providers by cost, region or capability, or fall back on outage.

      When something else fits better

      A single prompt, one provider

      If you only call one model once with a fixed prompt, the provider's SDK is simpler.

      Complex, deterministic workflows

      Branching, parallel steps and loops you design yourself: use LangGraph directly (Chapter 22).

      Long autonomous tasks

      Multi-hour work with planning and a file system: start with Deep Agents (Chapter 23).

      Rule of thumb

      The official docs now suggest Deep Agents as the batteries-included starting point, create_agent when you want to build and customise the agent harness yourself, and LangGraph when you need to mix fixed workflow steps with agent steps. This guide teaches create_agent first because Deep Agents is built on it: once you understand it, Deep Agents is easy to pick up.

      Chapter 4 · Foundations

      The ecosystem map

      "LangChain" is a family of packages. Knowing which package owns what saves you hours of import errors.

      PackageWhat it holdsInstall when
      langchaincreate_agent, middleware, init_chat_model, @tool, messagesAlways
      langchain-coreBase abstractions, prompts, Runnables / LCEL, documentsComes with langchain
      langgraphGraph runtime, checkpointers, stores, Command, StateGraphComes with langchain
      langchain-openai, langchain-anthropic, …Provider chat models and embeddingsFor each provider you use
      langchain-communityCommunity loaders, tools and storesFor loaders such as PDF or web
      langchain-text-splittersChunking documentsRAG
      langchain[mcp]langchain.mcp.MCPAdapter: MCP servers as LangChain tools (replaces langchain-mcp-adapters)MCP (needs 1.4+)
      langchain-classicLegacy chains (LLMChain, ConversationChain), AgentExecutor, langchain.retrievers (e.g. MultiQueryRetriever), indexing API, hub, CacheBackedEmbeddings, community re-exportsOnly for old code
      deepagentscreate_deep_agentLong-running agents. Still pre-1.0, so expect API changes between minor versions.
      langsmithTracing and evaluation SDKAlways in production
      Example

      A slimmer package

      LangChain v1 keeps the main package focused on modern pieces. Legacy APIs and integrations moved to a separate package.

      langchain

      Modern agent APIs · middleware · core abstractions. Use this for new code.

      langchain-classic

      Legacy APIs and integrations (old chains, AgentExecutor, hub). Only for old code.

      Chapter 5 · Foundations

      Install and set up

      1. Python 3.10 or newer. LangChain v1 dropped 3.9. Check with python --version.
      2. Create a virtual environment so project packages stay separate.
      3. Install the core and one provider.
      4. Set API keys as environment variables, never in code.
      terminal (Windows PowerShell)
      python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1          # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate

pip install -U langchain langchain-anthropic langchain-openai
pip install -U "langchain[mcp]" langchain-community langchain-text-splitters
pip install -U python-dotenv langsmith
      .env
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=lsv2_...
LANGSMITH_PROJECT=langchain-v1-learning
      at the top of every script
      from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()   # reads .env into environment variables
      Example

      Multiple LLM providers in one .env

      Keep one key per provider in .env. Each provider's package finds its own key automatically.

      .env
      GROQ_API_KEY=...
OPENAI_API_KEY=...
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
      using the Groq key
      # pip install langchain-groq
from langchain_groq import ChatGroq

model = ChatGroq(
    model="openai/gpt-oss-120b",
    temperature=0,
)   # reads GROQ_API_KEY from the environment
      Remember

      API keys authenticate providers. They are not tools. Three keys let you choose between three LLM providers; they don't give the agent three actions.

      Recommended project layout

      folder structure
      my-agent/
├── .env
├── pyproject.toml
├── langgraph.json          # for deployment (Chapter 26)
├── src/
│   ├── agent.py            # create_agent(...) lives here
│   ├── tools.py            # @tool functions
│   ├── middleware.py       # custom middleware
│   ├── prompts.py          # system prompts
│   └── rag/ingest.py       # document indexing
└── tests/
    ├── test_tools.py
    └── test_agent.py
      Chapter 6 · Building blocks

      Chat models

      A chat model takes a list of messages and returns an AIMessage. LangChain gives every provider the same interface, so the rest of your code never changes when you switch.

      Two ways to create a model

      models.py
      # 1. Universal initialiser: "provider:model"
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model(
    "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
    temperature=0,        # 0 = deterministic, higher = more creative
    max_tokens=1024,      # cap the answer length
    timeout=30,           # seconds
    max_retries=6,        # default; retries 429 / 5xx / network errors with backoff
)                         # (raise to 10-15 for long-running agents)

# 2. Provider class, when you need provider-specific options
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
gpt = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-5.4-mini", temperature=0)

# Local model, no API key, via Ollama
local = init_chat_model("ollama:llama3.1")

      The five methods you will use

      model_methods.py
      # invoke: one request, full answer
response = model.invoke("Explain RAG in one sentence.")
print(response.content)          # the text
print(response.usage_metadata)   # {'input_tokens': 14, 'output_tokens': 31, ...}

# stream: tokens as they arrive (for chat UIs)
for chunk in model.stream("Write a haiku about graphs."):
    print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)

# batch: many independent requests in parallel
answers = model.batch(["What is 2+2?", "Capital of Japan?"])

# async versions: ainvoke, astream, abatch
# response = await model.ainvoke("Hello")

# bind_tools / with_structured_output: see Chapters 9 and 11
      ParameterMeaningTypical value
      temperatureRandomness of the answer0 for agents and extraction, 0.7 for writing
      max_tokensMaximum output length512–4096
      timeoutSeconds to wait before failing30–120
      max_retriesAutomatic retries with exponential backoff on 429, 5xx and network errors (not 401/404)Default 6; 10–15 for long agent runs
      rate_limiterInMemoryRateLimiter to stay under provider quotasAs needed
      rate_limit.py
      from langchain.rate_limiters import InMemoryRateLimiter

rate_limiter = InMemoryRateLimiter(
    requests_per_second=0.1,     # one request every 10 seconds
    check_every_n_seconds=0.1,
    max_bucket_size=10,
)
model = init_chat_model("gpt-5.5", model_provider="openai", rate_limiter=rate_limiter)
# Limits the number of requests over time only, not the size of each request.

      Newer model features in 1.x

      FeatureWhat it gives youNeeds
      model.profileA dictionary of capabilities, e.g. image_inputs, reasoning_output (beta)langchain>=1.1
      reasoning_effort="high"One standard parameter for how hard reasoning models thinklangchain-core>=1.5.2 + recent provider package
      Standard exceptionsModelRateLimitError, ModelTimeoutError, ContextOverflowError in langchain_core.exceptions, each with is_retryableRecent langchain-core
      batch_as_completed()Get batch results as each finishes; limit parallel calls with config={"max_concurrency": 5}All 1.x
      Breaking change in langchain-anthropic

      It no longer defaults max_tokens to 1024. The default is now higher and depends on the model. Set max_tokens yourself if you relied on the old cap.

      Multimodal input

      vision.py
      message = {
    "role": "user",
    "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?"},
        {"type": "image", "url": "https://example.com/invoice.png"},
        # or: {"type": "image", "base64": "...", "mime_type": "image/png"}
    ],
}
print(model.invoke([message]).content)
      Chapter 7 · Building blocks

      Messages and standard content blocks

      Messages are the unit of conversation. There are four types you need to know:

      ClassRoleWho creates it
      SystemMessagesystemYou: instructions and persona
      HumanMessageuserThe user's input
      AIMessageassistantThe model: text and/or tool_calls
      ToolMessagetoolThe agent, after running a tool; links back via tool_call_id
      messages.py
      from langchain.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage, AIMessage

conversation = [
    SystemMessage("You are a concise travel assistant."),
    HumanMessage("Suggest one city in Japan."),
    AIMessage("Kyoto."),
    HumanMessage("Why that one?"),
]
reply = model.invoke(conversation)

# Dict shorthand works everywhere too:
reply = model.invoke([{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}])

      Standard content blocks (new in v1)

      Providers return rich content in different shapes: Anthropic has "thinking" blocks, OpenAI has "reasoning" items, both have tool calls and citations. message.content_blocks normalises them into one list of typed dictionaries, so your UI code handles every provider the same way.

      content_blocks.py
      response = model.invoke("What is 17 * 23? Think first.")

for block in response.content_blocks:
    if block["type"] == "reasoning":
        print("THINKING:", block.get("reasoning"))
    elif block["type"] == "text":
        print("ANSWER:", block["text"])
    elif block["type"] == "tool_call":
        print("TOOL:", block["name"], block["args"])

print(response.text)   # v1: .text is a property (it was a method .text() in v0)
      Example

      Many providers, one standard shape

      Each provider formats its replies differently. Standard content blocks turn them all into the same block types, so your code reads every provider the same way.

      Remember

      Content blocks = how content is represented. Tools = what actions the agent can perform. Provider / model = which LLM is used. Content blocks are not the way to connect multiple tools or API keys.

      • The old .text() form still works with a deprecation warning and will be removed in v2.
      • Standard blocks are not written into .content by default. To opt in, set the environment variable LC_OUTPUT_VERSION=v1 or pass output_version="v1" to init_chat_model.
      • ToolMessage has an artifact field for data that should be kept but not sent to the model.
      typed multimodal input
      from langchain.messages import HumanMessage

msg = HumanMessage(content_blocks=[
    {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image."},
    {"type": "image", "url": "https://example.com/photo.jpg"},
    # image blocks also accept "base64" + "mime_type", or a provider "file_id"
])
      Chapter 8 · Building blocks

      Prompts and LCEL

      In v1, most agents only need a system_prompt string. Prompt templates and the LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) still live in langchain_core and remain useful for fixed, non-agent pipelines: summarisers, classifiers, translators.

      prompt_template.py
      from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You translate text into {language}. Reply with the translation only."),
    ("user", "{text}"),
])

# LCEL: the | operator pipes the output of one step into the next
chain = prompt | model | StrOutputParser()

print(chain.invoke({"language": "Hindi", "text": "Good morning"}))

      Everything joined with | is a Runnable, so the chain automatically gets invoke, stream, batch and async versions.

      Writing a good system prompt for an agent

      prompts.py
      SUPPORT_PROMPT = """You are Asha, a support agent for AutoPlant.

## Goal
Resolve the customer's issue in as few turns as possible.

## Tools
- Use `lookup_order` before answering any question about an order.
- Use `search_kb` for product and policy questions. Cite the article title.
- Never promise a refund. Use `escalate_to_human` for refunds.

## Style
Short paragraphs. Plain language. Ask one clarifying question when unsure.
"""
      Prompt checklist

      Role, goal, when to use each tool, what never to do, output style. Put rules about tools in the prompt and in each tool's docstring.

      Chapter 9 · Building blocks

      Tools

      A tool is a Python function the model can ask to run. The model never runs code itself: it returns a tool call (name + arguments), your agent runs the function, and the result goes back to the model as a ToolMessage.

      Example

      What a tool is, and what it is not

      A tool is a callable operation the agent is allowed to request: a Python function, a database operation, an API wrapper, a calculator, a search function, or a controlled business action. It is easy to confuse with these other things:

      ThingMeaning
      ToolAn action the agent can invoke
      API keyAn authentication credential (a password for a provider)
      ModelThe LLM used for reasoning and generating text
      Content blockThe standard representation of message / model content

      Defining tools with @tool

      tools.py
      from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
def search_database(query: str, limit: int = 10) -> str:
    """Search the customer database for records matching the query.

    Args:
        query: Search terms, e.g. a name or email.
        limit: Maximum number of results to return.
    """
    return f"Found {limit} results for '{query}'"

# The name, docstring and type hints become the schema the model sees:
print(search_database.name)          # search_database
print(search_database.args)          # {'query': {...}, 'limit': {...}}
print(search_database.invoke({"query": "Ravi"}))
      The docstring is the prompt

      The model chooses tools from their name and description alone. Write the docstring as instructions: what it does, when to use it, and what each argument means.

      Rich argument schemas with Pydantic

      tools_pydantic.py
      from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class WeatherInput(BaseModel):
    location: str = Field(description="City name or coordinates")
    units: Literal["celsius", "fahrenheit"] = Field(default="celsius")
    include_forecast: bool = Field(default=False, description="Add a 5-day forecast")

@tool(args_schema=WeatherInput)
def get_weather(location: str, units: str = "celsius", include_forecast: bool = False) -> str:
    """Get current weather and an optional forecast."""
    temp = 22 if units == "celsius" else 72
    return f"{location}: {temp}°{units[0].upper()}" + (" | 5-day: sunny" if include_forecast else "")

      Tools that read state, context and memory: ToolRuntime

      Add a parameter typed ToolRuntime and LangChain injects it at run time. The model never sees this parameter.

      tools_runtime.py
      from dataclasses import dataclass
from langchain.tools import tool, ToolRuntime

@dataclass
class Context:
    user_id: str

@tool
def get_my_orders(runtime: ToolRuntime[Context]) -> str:
    """Get the current user's recent orders."""
    user_id = runtime.context.user_id          # per-request data (Chapter 14)
    history = runtime.state["messages"]        # the conversation so far
    store = runtime.store                      # long-term memory (Chapter 13)
    runtime.stream_writer({"status": "fetching orders"})  # custom stream event
    return f"Orders for {user_id}: #1042 (shipped), #1051 (processing)"

      Other runtime fields: runtime.config, runtime.tool_call_id, and (with langgraph>=1.1.5) runtime.execution_info (thread ID, run ID, attempt number) and runtime.server_info (assistant, graph and user; None outside LangGraph Server).

      Reserved names

      config and runtime cannot be used as your own tool argument names. ToolRuntime replaces the older InjectedState, InjectedStore, InjectedToolCallId and get_runtime().

      More @tool options and return types

      tool_options.py
      from langchain.messages import ToolMessage
from langgraph.types import Command

@tool("web_search")                                   # custom name
def search(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the web for information."""
    return f"Results for {query}"

@tool("calculator", description="Evaluate a maths expression.")  # custom description
def calc(expression: str) -> str:
    return str(eval(expression))   # demo only: never eval untrusted input

@tool(return_direct=True)                             # agent stops and returns this output
def final_quote(product: str) -> str:
    """Return the official price quote for a product."""
    return f"{product}: ₹4,999"

@tool
def set_ticket(ticket_id: str, runtime: ToolRuntime) -> Command:
    """Attach a support ticket ID to this conversation."""
    return Command(update={
        "ticket_id": ticket_id,                       # updates agent state
        "messages": [ToolMessage(f"Ticket {ticket_id} attached",
                                 tool_call_id=runtime.tool_call_id)],  # required
    })

      Tools may also return a dict or a list of multimodal content blocks. A Command return must include a ToolMessage with the matching tool_call_id, otherwise the agent raises a ValueError.

      Using tools directly with a model

      bind_tools.py
      model_with_tools = model.bind_tools([get_weather])
msg = model_with_tools.invoke("Is it raining in Mumbai?")
print(msg.tool_calls)
# [{'name': 'get_weather', 'args': {'location': 'Mumbai'}, 'id': 'toolu_01...'}]

      You rarely need this by hand; create_agent does it for you. It is useful for understanding and for single-step tool selection.

      Chapter 10 · Agents

      create_agent: the heart of v1

      An agent is a model that decides, step by step, which tools to call until it can answer. This is the ReAct pattern (Reason + Act). create_agent builds that loop as a LangGraph graph.

      Full signature, explained

      agent_full.py
      from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",  # string or a model instance
    tools=[search_database, get_weather], # list of tools (or [] for none)
    system_prompt=SUPPORT_PROMPT,         # str or SystemMessage
    response_format=None,                 # schema type, or ToolStrategy / ProviderStrategy (Ch. 11)
    middleware=[],                        # list of middleware (Ch. 16)
    checkpointer=None,                    # short-term memory (Ch. 12)
    store=None,                           # long-term memory (Ch. 13)
    context_schema=None,                  # type of runtime context (Ch. 14)
    state_schema=None,                    # extra state fields (Ch. 12)
    name="support_agent",                 # useful in multi-agent systems
    # advanced: interrupt_before, interrupt_after, debug, cache, transformers
)

      Invoking and reading the result

      run_agent.py
      result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Find customer Ravi and the weather in his city, Pune."}]}
)

for m in result["messages"]:
    m.pretty_print()
      ================ Human Message ================ Find customer Ravi and the weather in his city, Pune. ================== Ai Message ================== Tool Calls: search_database(query="Ravi"), get_weather(location="Pune") ================= Tool Message ================= Found 10 results for 'Ravi' ================= Tool Message ================= Pune: 22°C ================== Ai Message ================== I found Ravi's record. It's currently 22°C in Pune.
      Example

      One way to build an agent (with Groq)

      A complete agent: a model, one tool, a system prompt, and one question.

      weather_agent.py
      from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_groq import ChatGroq

model = ChatGroq(
    model="openai/gpt-oss-120b",
    temperature=0,
)

def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get the weather for a city."""
    return f"The weather in {city} is sunny."

agent = create_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[get_weather],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.",
)

response = agent.invoke({
    "messages": [{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "What is the weather in New York?"
    }]
})

print(response["messages"][-1].content)
      Real-world example

      Practical logistics agent

      The Logistics TAT Assistant from Chapter 1, as code. Each function is one tool. The one-line docstring under each function is required: it is what the model reads to decide when to use that tool.

      logistics_agent.py
      from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain_groq import ChatGroq

model = ChatGroq(model="openai/gpt-oss-120b", temperature=0)

def query_vehicle_data(date: str) -> str:
    """Get the vehicle records for a date."""
    return "1500 vehicles"

def calculate_stage_tat(records: str) -> dict:
    """Calculate yard, plant and total TAT from vehicle records."""
    return {
        "yard_tat": "00:48",
        "plant_tat": "03:12",
        "total_tat": "04:00"
    }

def get_kpi_summary() -> str:
    """Get the TAT KPI summary compared with the target."""
    return "Plant TAT is 12% above target."

agent = create_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[
        query_vehicle_data,
        calculate_stage_tat,
        get_kpi_summary
    ],
    system_prompt="You are a logistics analytics assistant."
)

response = agent.invoke({
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Why was plant TAT high yesterday?"}]
})
print(response["messages"][-1].content)

      The functions return fixed sample values so you can run it right away. In a real project, replace their bodies with queries to your own vehicle database.

      Handling tool errors

      By default, a tool exception is raised. Usually you want the model to see the error and try again. Use the wrap_tool_call middleware (more in Chapter 16):

      tool_errors.py
      from langchain.agents.middleware import wrap_tool_call
from langchain.messages import ToolMessage

@wrap_tool_call
def handle_tool_errors(request, handler):
    try:
        return handler(request)
    except Exception as e:
        return ToolMessage(
            content=f"Tool error: {e}. Check the arguments and try again.",
            tool_call_id=request.tool_call["id"],
        )

agent = create_agent(model, tools=[search_database], middleware=[handle_tool_errors])

      Since langchain 1.3.14 there is also a built-in version:

      tool_error_middleware.py
      from langchain.agents.middleware import ToolErrorMiddleware, ToolRetryMiddleware

def on_error(exc, request) -> str | None:
    if isinstance(exc, ValueError):
        return f"`{request.tool_call['name']}` failed with {type(exc).__name__}. Fix the arguments."
    return None          # None = let the exception propagate

agent = create_agent(model, tools=[search_database], middleware=[
    ToolErrorMiddleware(on_error),            # also accepts aon_error= (async) and tools=[...]
    ToolRetryMiddleware(on_failure="error"),  # listed after it, so retries happen first
])
      Chapter 11 · Agents

      Structured output

      When code (not a person) consumes the answer, you want a validated object, not free text. Pass a schema to response_format; the result appears in result["structured_response"].

      structured_agent.py
      from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.structured_output import ToolStrategy, ProviderStrategy

class ContactInfo(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: str
    phone: str = Field(description="Phone number with country code")

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.4-mini",
    tools=[],
    response_format=ToolStrategy(ContactInfo),
)

result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user",
    "content": "Extract: John Doe, john@example.com, +1 555 123 4567"}]})

contact = result["structured_response"]
print(contact.email)   # john@example.com
      StrategyHow it worksUse when
      ProviderStrategy(Schema)Uses the provider's native JSON-schema modeProvider supports it (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini …): most reliable
      ToolStrategy(Schema)Exposes the schema as a special tool the model "calls"Works with any tool-calling model; retries on validation errors
      Schema (bare)LangChain uses ProviderStrategy if the model supports native structured output, otherwise ToolStrategyDefault choice. JSON-schema dicts are not auto-detected: wrap them in a strategy explicitly

      Without an agent, use the model directly:

      with_structured_output.py
      extractor = model.with_structured_output(ContactInfo)
info = extractor.invoke("Priya Shah, priya@corp.in, +91 98200 00000")
print(info.name)   # Priya Shah
      v1 improvement

      Structured output is generated inside the main agent loop, not by an extra model call afterwards. That saves a request and cost on every run.

      Chapter 12 · Agents

      Short-term memory (conversation threads)

      By default an agent forgets everything between invoke calls. Add a checkpointer and pass a thread_id: the agent saves its state after every step and reloads it on the next call with the same thread.

      Example

      State, persistence, streaming and human-in-the-loop

      Every agent run has these four supporting pieces. This chapter covers state and persistence; streaming is Chapter 15 and human approval is Chapter 17.

      memory.py
      from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

agent = create_agent(model, tools=[], checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42-chat-1"}}
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi, I'm Piyush."}]}, config)
r = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What's my name?"}]}, config)
print(r["messages"][-1].content)   # "Your name is Piyush."

# A different thread_id is a fresh conversation
other = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42-chat-2"}}
      CheckpointerPackageUse for
      InMemorySaverlanggraphDevelopment, notebooks, tests
      SqliteSaverlanggraph-checkpoint-sqliteSingle-machine apps
      PostgresSaverlanggraph-checkpoint-postgresProduction

      Keeping long conversations inside the context window

      summarize.py
      from langchain.agents.middleware import SummarizationMiddleware

agent = create_agent(
    model,
    tools=[],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
    middleware=[
        SummarizationMiddleware(
            model="openai:gpt-5.4-mini",   # a cheap model writes the summary
            trigger=("tokens", 4000),       # summarise once history passes 4,000 tokens
            keep=("messages", 20),          # keep the last 20 messages verbatim
        )
    ],
)
      Version note

      max_tokens_before_summary and messages_to_keep (seen in early 1.0 tutorials) are deprecated: use trigger and keep. Without trigger, summarisation never runs. keep defaults to ("messages", 20). trigger also accepts ("fraction", 0.8) of the context window, a dict (all conditions must be met) or a list (any one is enough). summary_prefix is deprecated in favour of summary_prompt.

      Custom state

      Agent state is a dictionary with at least messages. Extend it to carry your own fields across steps. In v1 custom state must be a TypedDict.

      custom_state.py
      from langchain.agents import AgentState

class SupportState(AgentState):
    customer_tier: str
    ticket_id: str | None

agent = create_agent(model, tools=[...], state_schema=SupportState)
agent.invoke({"messages": [...], "customer_tier": "gold", "ticket_id": None})
      Chapter 13 · Agents

      Long-term memory (across conversations)

      Short-term memory belongs to one thread. Long-term memory belongs to a user or organisation and is shared by every thread. It lives in a store: a key-value database organised by namespaces.

      long_term_memory.py
      from dataclasses import dataclass
from langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore
from langchain.tools import tool, ToolRuntime

@dataclass
class Context:
    user_id: str

@tool
def save_preference(key: str, value: str, runtime: ToolRuntime[Context]) -> str:
    """Remember a user preference for future conversations."""
    runtime.store.put(("prefs", runtime.context.user_id), key, {"value": value})
    return f"Saved {key} = {value}"

@tool
def get_preferences(runtime: ToolRuntime[Context]) -> str:
    """Recall everything we know about the user's preferences."""
    items = runtime.store.search(("prefs", runtime.context.user_id), limit=100)  # default limit is 10
    return "\n".join(f"{i.key}: {i.value['value']}" for i in items) or "No preferences yet."

store = InMemoryStore()   # production: PostgresStore
agent = create_agent(model, tools=[save_preference, get_preferences],
                     store=store, context_schema=Context)

agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "I prefer answers in Hindi."}]},
             context=Context(user_id="42"))
# ...a week later, in a brand-new thread:
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG."}]},
             context=Context(user_id="42"))
      Chapter 14 · Agents

      Runtime context and context engineering

      Context engineering means giving the model the right information and tools at the right moment. Most agent failures are context failures: the model lacked a fact, saw too many tools, or had a stale prompt. v1 gives you three levers.

      SourceLifetimeExampleAccess
      Runtime contextOne invokeuser ID, role, API keys, DB connectionruntime.context
      StateOne threadmessages, uploaded file names, ticket IDruntime.state / request.state
      StoreForeveruser preferences, learned factsruntime.store

      Dynamic system prompt

      dynamic_prompt.py
      from typing import TypedDict
from langchain.agents.middleware import dynamic_prompt, ModelRequest

class Context(TypedDict):
    user_role: str

@dynamic_prompt
def role_based_prompt(request: ModelRequest) -> str:
    role = request.runtime.context.get("user_role", "user")
    base = "You are a helpful assistant."
    if role == "expert":
        return base + " Give detailed technical answers with code."
    if role == "beginner":
        return base + " Explain simply, avoid jargon, use analogies."
    return base

agent = create_agent(model, tools=[], middleware=[role_based_prompt], context_schema=Context)
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is a vector?"}]},
             context={"user_role": "beginner"})

      Dynamic model selection

      dynamic_model.py
      from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import wrap_model_call, ModelRequest, ModelResponse
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

basic = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.4-mini")
advanced = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6")

@wrap_model_call
def pick_model(request: ModelRequest, handler) -> ModelResponse:
    # Long conversations are usually harder: switch to the stronger model
    model = advanced if len(request.state["messages"]) > 10 else basic
    return handler(request.override(model=model))

agent = create_agent(basic, tools=[...], middleware=[pick_model])

      Dynamic tool selection

      Too many tools confuse models. LLMToolSelectorMiddleware(model=..., max_tools=3, always_include=[...]) uses a model to pick the relevant few before each main call (it uses the agent's main model unless you pass a cheaper one); or filter request.tools yourself in wrap_model_call based on user permissions.

      tool_filter.py
      @wrap_model_call
def tools_by_permission(request: ModelRequest, handler) -> ModelResponse:
    if request.runtime.context.get("user_role") != "admin":
        request = request.override(tools=[t for t in request.tools if not t.name.startswith("admin_")])
    return handler(request)

      request.override(...) also accepts messages=, system_message= and response_format=. Use request.messages as a shortcut for request.state["messages"].

      Chapter 15 · Agents

      Streaming

      Agents can take many seconds. Streaming shows progress as it happens: which tool is running, and the answer token by token.

      stream_modeWhat you receiveGood for
      "updates"The state change after each step (model step, tools step)Progress UI: "Searching database…"
      "messages"(token_chunk, metadata) as the LLM generatesChat UIs with typing effect
      "custom"Anything your tools send through stream_writerTool progress bars
      "values"The full state after each stepDebugging
      streaming.py
      inputs = {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Delhi and Goa?"}]}

# Step-by-step progress
for chunk in agent.stream(inputs, stream_mode="updates"):
    for step, data in chunk.items():
        print(f"[{step}]", data["messages"][-1].content_blocks)

# Token-by-token
for token, metadata in agent.stream(inputs, stream_mode="messages"):
    if metadata["langgraph_node"] == "model" and token.text:
        print(token.text, end="", flush=True)

# Several modes at once
for mode, chunk in agent.stream(inputs, stream_mode=["updates", "custom"]):
    print(mode, chunk)

      Newer streaming formats

      The code above uses the default format, which yields tuples. The current docs show two newer options:

      • version="v2" on stream gives every chunk the same dict shape: {"type": ..., "ns": ..., "data": ...}.
      • agent.stream_events(..., version="v3") (new in LangChain 1.3) is the recommended API for new apps. It gives typed streams for messages, tool calls and values.
      streaming_v2_v3.py
      # v2: uniform dict chunks
for chunk in agent.stream(inputs, stream_mode="messages", version="v2"):
    if chunk["type"] == "messages":
        token, metadata = chunk["data"]
        if metadata["langgraph_node"] == "model" and token.text:
            print(token.text, end="", flush=True)

# v3 event streaming: recommended for new applications (langchain 1.3+)
stream = agent.stream_events(inputs, version="v3")
for kind, item in stream.interleave("messages", "tool_calls"):
    if kind == "messages":
        for t in item.text:
            print(t, end="", flush=True)
    else:
        print(f"\nTool call: {item.tool_name}({item.input}) -> {item.output}")
      Chapter 16 · Control

      Middleware: the defining feature of v1

      Middleware is code that runs at fixed points in the agent loop. It is how you add memory trimming, approvals, guardrails, retries, logging, model switching and prompt changes without rewriting the agent.

      Example

      Middleware, the simple view

      Think of middleware as a supervisor around the agent. It can inspect, change, restrict, retry, log or pause each step.

      Use casePurposeBuilt-in option
      SecurityBlock unauthorized tool calls@wrap_tool_call check, ToolCallLimitMiddleware
      PII protectionRedact sensitive informationPIIMiddleware
      LoggingRecord execution@before_model / @after_model
      RetriesRecover from temporary failuresToolRetryMiddleware, ModelRetryMiddleware
      Human approvalPause before sensitive actionsHumanInTheLoopMiddleware (Ch. 17)

      The detailed version, with every hook point, is Figure 16.1 below.

      HookRunsTypical use
      before_agentOnce, at the start of invokeLoad user profile, input guardrails
      before_modelBefore each model callTrim/summarise messages, inject context, enforce limits
      wrap_model_callAround each model callSwitch model, filter tools, retry, cache, fallback
      after_modelAfter each model replyOutput guardrails, human approval, logging
      wrap_tool_callAround each tool executionError handling, retries, permission checks, timing
      after_agentOnce, at the endSave memories, analytics, final checks

      Built-in middleware

      MiddlewareWhat it does
      SummarizationMiddlewareSummarises old messages when history gets long
      HumanInTheLoopMiddlewarePauses before chosen tools for approve / edit / reject
      PIIMiddlewareDetects emails, card numbers, IPs etc.; redacts, masks, hashes or blocks
      ModelCallLimitMiddlewareCaps model calls per run or per thread (stops runaway loops)
      ToolCallLimitMiddlewareCaps calls to a specific tool or all tools
      ModelFallbackMiddlewareTries backup models if the primary fails
      ToolRetryMiddleware / ModelRetryMiddlewareRetries with exponential backoff
      LLMToolSelectorMiddlewareUses a small model to pick relevant tools
      TodoListMiddlewareGives the agent a write_todos planning tool
      ContextEditingMiddlewareClears old tool outputs to save tokens
      ToolErrorMiddlewareTurns tool exceptions into error messages the model can react to (1.3.14+)
      ProviderToolSearchMiddlewareLets the provider search a large set of tools on demand
      ShellToolMiddlewareGives the agent a shell inside a workspace, with an execution policy
      FilesystemFileSearchMiddlewareGlob and grep search over a folder
      LLMToolEmulatorFakes tool results with a model, for testing
      FilesystemMiddleware, SubAgentMiddleware, RubricMiddlewareFrom the deepagents package: virtual files, sub-agents, rubric-checked answers
      builtin_middleware.py
      from langchain.agents.middleware import (
    PIIMiddleware, ModelCallLimitMiddleware, ToolCallLimitMiddleware,
    ModelFallbackMiddleware, ToolRetryMiddleware,
)

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
    tools=[search_database, get_weather],
    middleware=[
        PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True),
        PIIMiddleware("credit_card", strategy="mask"),   # "block" raises an exception instead
        ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=8, exit_behavior="end"),
        ToolCallLimitMiddleware(tool_name="search_database", run_limit=3),
        ModelFallbackMiddleware("openai:gpt-5.4-mini"),
        ToolRetryMiddleware(max_retries=3, backoff_factor=2.0),
    ],
)
      Defaults worth knowing

      PII: built-in types are email, credit_card, ip, mac_address, url; add your own with detector=. apply_to_input is on by default; apply_to_output and apply_to_tool_results are off. strategy="block" raises an exception, so catch it.
      Retries: ToolRetryMiddleware / ModelRetryMiddleware default to max_retries=2, backoff_factor=2.0, initial_delay=1.0, max_delay=60.0, jitter=True, on_failure="continue".
      Limits: ToolCallLimitMiddleware exit_behavior defaults to "continue" (also "error", "end"). ModelCallLimitMiddleware takes "end" or "error"; its thread_limit needs a checkpointer.

      Order matters

      Middleware runs like layers of an onion. before_* hooks run first to last; after_* hooks run last to first; the first wrap_* middleware is the outermost wrapper.

      Writing custom middleware: decorators

      custom_decorators.py
      from langchain.agents.middleware import before_model, after_model, AgentState
from langgraph.runtime import Runtime

@before_model
def log_call(state: AgentState, runtime: Runtime) -> dict | None:
    print(f"Calling model with {len(state['messages'])} messages")
    return None   # None = change nothing

@after_model(can_jump_to=["end"])
def block_banned_words(state: AgentState, runtime: Runtime) -> dict | None:
    last = state["messages"][-1]
    if "confidential" in last.text.lower():
        return {
            "messages": [{"role": "assistant", "content": "I can't share that."}],
            "jump_to": "end",          # skip straight to the end of the run
        }
    return None

      Writing custom middleware: classes

      Use a class when the middleware needs configuration, several hooks or its own state fields.

      custom_class.py
      import time
from typing_extensions import NotRequired
from langchain.agents.middleware import AgentMiddleware, AgentState

class TimingState(AgentState):
    model_ms: NotRequired[list[float]]   # extra fields should be optional

class TimingMiddleware(AgentMiddleware[TimingState]):
    state_schema = TimingState          # adds a field to agent state

    def __init__(self, slow_ms: float = 5000):
        super().__init__()
        self.slow_ms = slow_ms

    def wrap_model_call(self, request, handler):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        response = handler(request)
        ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        if ms > self.slow_ms:
            print(f"Slow model call: {ms:.0f} ms")
        return response

    def after_agent(self, state, runtime):
        print("Run finished with", len(state["messages"]), "messages")
        return None

agent = create_agent(model, tools=[], middleware=[TimingMiddleware(slow_ms=3000)])

      In class hooks, allow jumps with the @hook_config(can_jump_to=["end"]) decorator. jump_to can be "end", "tools" or "model". Besides state_schema, a middleware class can also declare tools it adds to the agent.

      Chapter 17 · Control

      Human in the loop

      Some actions should never happen without a person saying yes: sending email, paying, deleting, deploying. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses the agent right before those tool calls, saves the state, and waits for a decision.

      hitl.py
      from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import HumanInTheLoopMiddleware
from langchain.tools import tool
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from langgraph.types import Command

@tool
def send_email(to: str, subject: str, body: str) -> str:
    """Send an email."""
    return f"Email sent to {to}"

@tool
def read_inbox() -> str:
    """Read the latest emails."""
    return "1 new email from boss@corp.com: 'Send the Q3 report to the client.'"

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
    tools=[send_email, read_inbox],
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),            # required: the pause must be saved
    middleware=[HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(
        interrupt_on={
            "send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]},
            "read_inbox": False,             # safe: never pause
        },
        description_prefix="Approval needed",
    )],
)

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "inbox-1"}}
result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Handle my inbox."}]}, config)

# The run paused. Show the pending action to a human:
print(result["__interrupt__"])

# Option A: approve
agent.invoke(Command(resume={"decisions": [{"type": "approve"}]}), config)

# Option B: edit the arguments first
agent.invoke(Command(resume={"decisions": [{
    "type": "edit",
    "edited_action": {"name": "send_email",
                      "args": {"to": "client@acme.com", "subject": "Q3 report", "body": "Attached."}},
}]}), config)

# Option C: reject with feedback the model will see
agent.invoke(Command(resume={"decisions": [{
    "type": "reject", "message": "Don't email the client yet; wait for finance sign-off."
}]}), config)

      More HITL details

      • Fourth decision, respond: {"type": "respond", "message": "..."} returns the human's text as a successful tool result. Use it only for "ask the user" tools, never to deny an action.
      • True shorthand: interrupt_on={"send_email": True} allows all decisions.
      • Conditional pauses: add "when": fn to a tool's config to pause only when fn(request) returns true (1.3.3+).
      • Payload: the interrupt holds action_requests (name, arguments, description) and review_configs (action name, allowed decisions). description_prefix defaults to "Tool execution requires approval".
      • Several paused calls: send one decision per call, in the same order.
      • Newer read style: the docs now use agent.invoke(..., version="v2") and read result.interrupts. result["__interrupt__"] still works with plain invoke.
      Chapter 18 · Control

      Guardrails

      Guardrails are checks that keep an agent safe and on-topic. Layer them: cheap deterministic checks first, model-based checks where needed.

      LayerHookExample
      Inputbefore_agentBlock prompt-injection phrases, off-topic requests, PII
      Actionwrap_tool_call / HITLOnly admins may call delete_user; approve payments
      CostLimit middlewareMax 10 model calls, max 3 web searches per run
      Outputafter_agentCheck the final answer with a small "judge" model
      guardrails.py
      from langchain.agents.middleware import before_agent, after_agent
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain.messages import AIMessage

BLOCKED = ["ignore previous instructions", "reveal your system prompt"]

@before_agent(can_jump_to=["end"])
def input_guard(state, runtime):
    text = state["messages"][-1].text.lower()
    if any(p in text for p in BLOCKED):
        return {"messages": [{"role": "assistant",
                 "content": "I can't help with that request."}], "jump_to": "end"}
    return None

judge = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.4-mini", temperature=0)

@after_agent(can_jump_to=["end"])
def output_guard(state, runtime):
    last = state["messages"][-1]
    if not isinstance(last, AIMessage):
        return None
    verdict = judge.invoke(
        f"Reply SAFE or UNSAFE. Does this answer leak secrets or give harmful advice?\n\n{last.text}"
    ).text
    if "UNSAFE" in verdict:
        # Same id = replace the unsafe message. A new message would only be appended.
        return {"messages": [AIMessage(content="I can't share that answer.", id=last.id)]}
    return None
      Chapter 19 · Knowledge and scale

      RAG: answering from your own data

      Retrieval-Augmented Generation means: find the passages of your documents that relate to the question, put them in the prompt, and let the model answer from them. It reduces made-up answers and lets the model use private, up-to-date information.

      Step 1: index documents

      rag/ingest.py
      from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader, WebBaseLoader
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_core.vectorstores import InMemoryVectorStore

# Load
docs = PyPDFLoader("policies/refund_policy.pdf").load()
docs += WebBaseLoader("https://example.com/help/shipping").load()

# Split: overlapping chunks keep sentences from being cut in half
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200, add_start_index=True)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs)
print(len(chunks), "chunks")

# Embed + store
embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small")
vector_store = InMemoryVectorStore(embeddings)   # swap for Chroma / PGVector / Pinecone
vector_store.add_documents(chunks)

      Step 2a: agentic RAG (the agent decides when to search)

      rag/agentic.py
      from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain.agents import create_agent

@tool(response_format="content_and_artifact")
def retrieve_policy(query: str):
    """Search company policy documents. Use for any refund, shipping or warranty question."""
    found = vector_store.similarity_search(query, k=4)
    text = "\n\n".join(f"[{d.metadata.get('source')}]\n{d.page_content}" for d in found)
    return text, found          # text goes to the model; docs kept as an artifact

agent = create_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",
    tools=[retrieve_policy],
    system_prompt="Answer only from retrieved policy text. Cite the source in brackets. "
                  "If the documents don't contain the answer, say so.",
)

      Step 2b: two-step RAG (always retrieve, one model call)

      rag/two_step.py
      from langchain.agents.middleware import dynamic_prompt, ModelRequest

@dynamic_prompt
def inject_context(request: ModelRequest) -> str:
    question = request.state["messages"][-1].text
    docs = vector_store.similarity_search(question, k=4)
    context = "\n\n".join(d.page_content for d in docs)
    return f"Answer using only this context:\n\n{context}"

rag_agent = create_agent(model, tools=[], middleware=[inject_context])
      Two-step RAGAgentic RAG
      RetrievalAlways, onceWhen the model decides; can search several times
      Latency and costLow, predictableHigher, variable
      Best forFAQ bots, document Q&AResearch, multi-hop questions, mixing data with other tools
      Hybrid RAGCombines both: always retrieve first, then let the agent search again or check its answer when the first context isn't enough.

      RAG component choices

      ComponentPopular options
      LoadersPyPDFLoader, WebBaseLoader, CSVLoader, Docx2txtLoader, DirectoryLoader, Notion, Confluence, Google Drive
      SplittersRecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (default), MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter, token-based, code-aware splitters
      EmbeddingsOpenAI text-embedding-3-small, Google, Cohere, Voyage, HuggingFace local models, Ollama
      Vector storesInMemory (dev), Chroma, FAISS (local), PGVector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Elasticsearch
      Where the official tutorial went

      The docs' RAG tutorial (/langchain/rag) now redirects to "RAG with Deep Agents", built on create_deep_agent. Concepts (2-step, agentic, hybrid) are on the Retrieval page. The create_agent code in this chapter is still valid.

      Quality tips

      Tune chunk size (500–1500 chars) and overlap (10–20%). Store useful metadata (source, page, date) and filter on it. Evaluate retrieval separately from generation: if the right chunk is not retrieved, no prompt will fix the answer.

      Chapter 20 · Knowledge and scale

      MCP: plug in external tool servers

      The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for exposing tools and data to AI apps. Thousands of MCP servers exist (GitHub, Slack, file systems, databases). LangChain now ships MCP support built in as langchain.mcp (beta, needs langchain[mcp]>=1.4.0). It replaces the separate langchain-mcp-adapters package.

      mcp_agent.py
      # pip install -U "langchain[mcp]"
import asyncio
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter

# Standard "mcpServers" config: the transport is worked out from each entry
config = {
    "mcpServers": {
        "math": {"command": "python", "args": ["servers/math_server.py"]},  # local, stdio
        "weather": {"url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp"},                    # remote, HTTP
    }
}

async def main():
    async with MCPAdapter(config) as adapter:
        tools = await adapter.list_tools()   # names get a server prefix: math_add, math_multiply...
        agent = create_agent("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6", tools)
        result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "(3 + 5) x 12?"}]})
        print(result["messages"][-1].content)

asyncio.run(main())

# One server only:
#   MCPAdapter("https://example.com/mcp")         # a plain string must be an http(s) URL
#   MCPAdapter(Path("servers/math_server.py"))    # a local script is passed as a Path
      • Importing langchain.mcp shows a LangChainBetaWarning because the API is still in beta.
      • If a server asks for input partway through a call ("elicitation"), the run pauses like human-in-the-loop and resumes with Command(resume={"responses": {...}}).
      • MCP tool errors reach the model as ToolMessage(status="error"), so the agent can recover.
      • MCP prompts and resources are not wrapped yet; only tools are. The SSE transport is deprecated and WebSocket is not supported.
      • Authentication is set on a fastmcp.Client.
      On an older 1.x release?

      Below langchain 1.4, use the separate package: from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient. Give each server a "transport" key ("stdio" or "http"), then call await client.get_tools().

      servers/math_server.py (build your own MCP server)
      from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Math")

@mcp.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers."""
    return a + b

@mcp.tool()
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiply two numbers."""
    return a * b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")
      Chapter 21 · Knowledge and scale

      Multi-agent systems

      One agent with 40 tools gets confused. Split the work: specialised agents with a few tools each, coordinated by a supervisor. The simplest pattern in v1 is sub-agents as tools.

      supervisor.py
      calendar_agent = create_agent(model, tools=[create_event, find_free_slot],
    system_prompt="You schedule meetings. Confirm the exact time you booked.")
email_agent = create_agent(model, tools=[draft_email, send_email],
    system_prompt="You write and send professional emails.")

@tool
def schedule_meeting(request: str) -> str:
    """Schedule a meeting. Describe who, when and how long in plain language."""
    r = calendar_agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": request}]})
    return r["messages"][-1].text

@tool
def handle_email(request: str) -> str:
    """Draft or send an email. Describe recipient and content in plain language."""
    r = email_agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": request}]})
    return r["messages"][-1].text

supervisor = create_agent(
    model,
    tools=[schedule_meeting, handle_email],
    system_prompt="You are a personal assistant. Break requests into steps and delegate.",
)
supervisor.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user",
    "content": "Book 30 min with Meera tomorrow afternoon and email her the invite."}]})
      PatternHowUse when
      SubagentsThe main agent calls specialist agents as tools (shown above). Subagents keep no memory between calls.Clear separation of domains
      HandoffsTools return Command(update={...}) to change a state field such as current_step; @wrap_model_call middleware swaps prompt and tools based on it. With separate agent subgraphs, use Command(goto="sales_agent", graph=Command.PARENT).Triage then specialist, step-by-step flows
      SkillsOne agent loads specialised prompts and knowledge only when neededMany domains, one conversation
      RouterA routing step classifies the input, sends it to one or more agents, and combines the resultsDistinct request types
      Custom workflowAgents are nodes in a LangGraph StateGraphFixed, auditable workflows
      Chapter 22 · Knowledge and scale

      Dropping down to LangGraph

      create_agent is a LangGraph graph with a fixed shape. When you need a different shape (fixed steps, branches, parallel work, loops you control), build the graph yourself. You keep the same checkpointers, streaming and interrupts.

      Example

      LangChain v1 is built on LangGraph

      The standard create_agent() agent already runs on the LangGraph runtime. You do not need to build a graph by hand for every simple agent.

      Example

      LangChain v1 vs LangGraph

      QuestionLangChain v1LangGraph
      Primary goalBuild agents simplyControl workflows explicitly
      AbstractionHigher-levelLower-level orchestration
      Simple agentExcellent fitPossible but more manual
      Complex branchingUse lower-level capabilitiesExcellent fit
      Stateful workflowsSupported by runtimeCore strength
      Complex multi-agent workflowsPossibleExcellent fit
      Example

      Annotation and state

      Annotations (types) describe the shape of the information carried through a workflow. Every step reads this state, and the model, tools and router all work from it. Structured state matters most in explicit LangGraph workflows like the one below.

      state.py
      from typing import TypedDict

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    user_query: str
    result: str
    retry_count: int
      Mental model

      State is a typed dictionary. Nodes are functions that read state and return updates. Edges decide which node runs next. Compile it and you get a Runnable with invoke and stream.

      graph_workflow.py · classify → route → respond
      from typing import Literal, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain.agents import create_agent

llm = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.4-mini", temperature=0)
tech_agent = create_agent(llm, tools=[], system_prompt="You are technical support.")

class State(TypedDict):
    question: str
    category: str
    answer: str

def classify(state: State) -> dict:
    label = llm.invoke(
        f"Classify as 'billing' or 'technical'. One word only.\n\n{state['question']}"
    ).text.strip().lower()
    return {"category": label}

def billing(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"answer": llm.invoke(f"As billing support, answer: {state['question']}").text}

def technical(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"answer": tech_agent.invoke(   # a create_agent agent can be a node
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": state["question"]}]}
    )["messages"][-1].text}

def route(state: State) -> Literal["billing", "technical"]:
    return "billing" if "billing" in state["category"] else "technical"

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("classify", classify)
builder.add_node("billing", billing)
builder.add_node("technical", technical)
builder.add_edge(START, "classify")
builder.add_conditional_edges("classify", route)
builder.add_edge("billing", END)
builder.add_edge("technical", END)

graph = builder.compile()
print(graph.invoke({"question": "Why was I charged twice?"})["answer"])
      NeedUse
      Model + tools in a loop, customised with hookscreate_agent + middleware
      Fixed sequence or branches you designLangGraph StateGraph
      Parallel fan-out (e.g. summarise 50 docs, then merge)LangGraph Send API
      Long research or coding tasks with planningDeep Agents
      Chapter 23 · Knowledge and scale

      Deep Agents

      Simple agents are "shallow": they work well for a few steps but lose track on long tasks. deepagents is built on create_agent and adds what tools like Claude Code use: a virtual file system for notes, sub-agents (the task tool) with isolated context, and a detailed system prompt. Since v0.7, planning is opt-in: add middleware=[TodoListMiddleware()] (from langchain.agents.middleware).

      Other options in the docs: subagents=, skills=, memory=["./AGENTS.md"], permissions=, interrupt_on=, pluggable storage and sandbox backends, and automatic prompt caching on Anthropic models. The package is still pre-1.0, so its API can change.

      deep_research.py
      # pip install deepagents tavily-python
from deepagents import create_deep_agent
from tavily import TavilyClient

tavily = TavilyClient()

def internet_search(query: str, max_results: int = 5) -> dict:
    """Search the web for current information."""
    return tavily.search(query, max_results=max_results)

agent = create_deep_agent(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6",   # pass a model explicitly: the default is deprecated
    tools=[internet_search],
    system_prompt="You are an expert researcher. Plan first, save notes to files, "
                  "then write a well-cited report to /final_report.md.",
)

result = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user",
    "content": "Compare LangChain v1 and other agent frameworks for enterprise use."}]})
# Files live in agent state under absolute paths; each value is a dict
print(result["files"]["/final_report.md"]["content"])
print(result["messages"][-1].content)   # the agent's final message

      The current Deep Agents quickstart suggests the provider's built-in web search (for example {"type": "web_search"}) instead of a separate search API like Tavily.

      Chapter 24 · Production

      LangSmith: observe and evaluate

      You cannot improve what you cannot see. Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and an API key, and every run is recorded: each model call with its prompt and output, each tool call, tokens, cost and latency. No code changes are needed.

      Evaluation: test answers against a dataset

      evaluate.py
      from langsmith import Client

client = Client()
dataset = client.create_dataset("support-qa")
client.create_examples(
    dataset_id=dataset.id,
    examples=[
        {"inputs": {"question": "How long do refunds take?"},
         "outputs": {"answer": "5-7 business days"}},
        {"inputs": {"question": "Do you ship to Sri Lanka?"},
         "outputs": {"answer": "Yes, in 10-14 days"}},
    ],
)

def target(inputs: dict) -> dict:
    r = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": inputs["question"]}]})
    return {"answer": r["messages"][-1].text}

def mentions_expected(outputs: dict, reference_outputs: dict) -> bool:
    return reference_outputs["answer"].lower() in outputs["answer"].lower()

client.evaluate(target, data="support-qa", evaluators=[mentions_expected],
                experiment_prefix="v1-prompt")

      Run this after every prompt or model change and compare experiments side by side. For subjective quality, use an LLM-as-judge evaluator; for agents, also check the trajectory (did it call the right tools in a sensible order?) with the agentevals package.

def test_weather_celsius():

      from langchain_core.language_models.fake_chat_models import GenericFakeChatModel
from langchain.messages import AIMessage
from langchain.agents import create_agent

def test_agent_returns_model_reply():
    fake = GenericFakeChatModel(messages=iter([AIMessage("Hello from the fake model")]))
    agent = create_agent(fake, tools=[])
    out = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]})

      Chapter 26 · Production

      Deployment

      Option A: Agent Server (LangSmith Deployment)

      The Agent Server (formerly LangGraph Server) gives you a REST API with threads, streaming, background runs, persistence and human-in-the-loop endpoints out of the box. Run it locally first:

      langgraph.json
      {
  "dependencies": ["."],
  "graphs": { "support_agent": "./src/agent.py:agent" },
  "env": ".env"
}
      terminal
      pip install -U "langgraph-cli[inmem]"
langgraph dev        # local server + LangGraph Studio (needs Python 3.11+)

      When it works locally, connect the GitHub repo in LangSmith to deploy, or use langgraph build -t my-agent-image to produce a Docker image for your own infrastructure.

      No checkpointer needed on the server

      The Agent Server provides persistence automatically. When you serve with langgraph dev or deploy, don't pass your own checkpointer or store to create_agent.

      Option B: your own FastAPI service

      server.py
      from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel
from src.agent import agent   # built with a Postgres checkpointer in production

app = FastAPI()

class ChatIn(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    message: str

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(body: ChatIn):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": body.thread_id}}
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": body.message}]}, config)
    return {"reply": result["messages"][-1].text}

@app.post("/chat/stream")
async def chat_stream(body: ChatIn):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": body.thread_id}}
    async def tokens():
        async for token, meta in agent.astream(
            {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": body.message}]}, config, stream_mode="messages"
        ):
            if meta.get("langgraph_node") == "model" and token.text:   # skip tool output
                yield token.text
    return StreamingResponse(tokens(), media_type="text/plain")

      v0.xv1

      prompt= argumentsystem_prompt=
      pre_model_hook / post_model_hookbefore_model / after_model middleware

      Structured output via extra LLM callToolStrategy / ProviderStrategy in the main loop

      from langchain import hublangchain_classic or LangSmith client

      Python 3.9Python 3.10+

      ToolNode(handle_tool_errors=...)@wrap_tool_call or ToolErrorMiddleware
