      RAG Field Guide

      Retrieval-Augmented Generation from first principles to production. The guide covers the full pipeline and every major RAG architecture, from Naive RAG to Graph, Agentic, Self-RAG, Temporal and Federated RAG. Each architecture has a diagram, Python code, reference repos and a clear answer to which RAG to use when.

      How to read this

      Parts I–III teach the building blocks that every RAG system shares: read them in order. Part IV is the RAG catalog. It has about 60 architectures in 10 families, and every one is described on the same card layout, so you can compare them. Use the decision tree in Chapter 24 to pick the right one for a problem. Code is Python 3.10+, uses Claude through the official anthropic SDK and uses LangGraph for the agentic patterns. Every example builds on the small shared module rag_common.py from Chapter 3.

      Chapter 1 · Foundations

      What RAG is and why it exists

      Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)noun · architecture pattern

      A pattern where, before a language model answers, the system retrieves relevant pieces of information from an external knowledge source. It then adds them to the prompt, and the model generates an answer grounded in that evidence, ideally with citations.

      The three problems a plain LLM cannot solve

      A large language model stores what it learned in its weights. This is called parametric memory. That memory has three hard limits in an enterprise setting:

      1 · It is frozen

      Training stops at a cutoff date. Yesterday's price change, this morning's incident and last week's policy update are not in the weights.

      2 · It is public

      The model never saw your contracts, tickets, wiki, codebase or database. It cannot answer "what is our refund policy?"

      3 · It cannot show its work

      When it does not know, it may hallucinate a fluent but wrong answer, and it cannot point to a source you can check.

      RAG fixes all three without retraining. Knowledge lives in an external store that you can update at any time, filter by user permissions and cite. The model's job shifts from remembering facts to reading and reasoning over evidence.

      Think of it like

      A closed-book exam compared with an open-book exam. Without RAG the model answers from memory. With RAG a librarian (the retriever) first fetches the right pages, and the student (the LLM) writes the answer from them and cites the page numbers. Most RAG engineering is about making the librarian fetch the right pages.

      Where the idea came from

      The name comes from Lewis et al., 2020, "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (Facebook AI Research, NeurIPS 2020, arXiv:2005.11401). That paper joined a seq2seq generator (BART), the parametric memory, to a dense vector index of Wikipedia searched with DPR, the non-parametric memory. It trained the two together end to end. Today "RAG" means the general pattern of putting retrieved text into an LLM prompt, and the retriever and generator are usually not trained together. You plug in an off-the-shelf embedding model and an off-the-shelf LLM such as Claude.

      RAG compared with the alternatives

      RAG is one of five ways to give a model knowledge or behaviour it does not have. They are not rivals. Each one changes a different thing:

      ApproachWhat it changesFresh data?Cost profileBest for
      Prompt engineeringInstructions and examples in the promptOnly what you paste inCheapestTone, format, task framing
      RAGWhat evidence the model sees, per queryYes: update the indexIndex build + a retrieval step on every queryLarge, changing, private or permissioned knowledge that needs citations
      Long contextPut the whole corpus in the promptYes, if you re-send itPays for every token on every callOne long document or a small corpus; whole-document reasoning
      CAG (cache-augmented)Preload a fixed corpus once and cache itOnly when the cache is rebuiltCheap repeat reads via prompt cachingSmall, stable corpus (a manual or FAQ) with many questions
      Fine-tuningThe model's weights: behaviour, style, domain skillsNo: retrain to updateTraining cost + its own hostingOutput format, domain jargon, a narrow skill; not facts that change
      Common misconception

      "Million-token context windows make RAG obsolete." They do not. Sending a large corpus with every query multiplies cost and latency. Models also use information in the middle of a very long prompt less reliably (Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle", arXiv:2307.03172). And you still need per-user access control and fresh data. In practice the two combine: retrieve the 20 most relevant documents, then use the long context to read them whole. See LongRAG (A7), CAG (A8) and Self-Route (E5) in the catalog.

      The evolution of RAG, in one picture

      The research survey by Gao et al. (arXiv:2312.10997) describes three generations: Naive → Advanced → Modular. Since 2024 the field has added a fourth wave of agentic, graph-based and self-correcting systems, where the LLM itself decides when, what and how often to retrieve.

      What a RAG engineer actually does

      Building a demo takes an afternoon. Building a RAG system people trust is mostly this work:

      • Data work: parsing messy PDFs, tables and scans; choosing chunk boundaries; attaching metadata such as source, date, owner and permissions.
      • Retrieval quality: embeddings, hybrid keyword + vector search, reranking and query rewriting, so the right passage reaches the top 5.
      • Architecture choice: knowing when simple RAG is enough and when you need graph, multi-hop, agentic or SQL retrieval. That is what Part IV is for.
      • Grounded generation: prompts that force citations and an honest "I don't know".
      • Evaluation: measuring retrieval (recall@k, MRR) and answers (faithfulness, relevance) on a test set, so every change is an experiment, not a guess.
      • Production: incremental re-indexing, access control, latency and cost budgets, monitoring, and defence against prompt injection hidden in documents.
      Real-world example

      An HR policy assistant

      An employee asks: "Can I carry over unused leave into next year?" The LLM alone might quote a typical policy from the internet, which is wrong for this company. A RAG system searches the company handbook. It finds the "Leave carry-over" section, which says "up to 5 days, used by 31 March". It passes that section to Claude, and Claude answers with a citation to the exact page. When HR edits the handbook, the index is updated that night and the next answer is correct, with no model retraining. You will build exactly this in Chapter 3.

      Key takeaways

      • RAG = retrieve evidence → augment the prompt → generate a grounded, cited answer.
      • It solves stale knowledge, private data and unverifiable answers without retraining.
      • Use fine-tuning for behaviour, RAG for knowledge. Long context and CAG suit small, stable corpora, and they often combine with RAG.
      • The hard part is retrieval quality and choosing the right architecture, not the LLM call.

      Quick check

      Your product catalogue changes daily and support agents need cited answers. RAG or fine-tuning?

      RAG. The facts change daily (fine-tuning would be stale within a day), and citations require retrieved sources.

      You want every answer formatted as a strict JSON object in your company's tone. Which approach?

      That is behaviour, not knowledge. Start with prompting and structured outputs. Consider fine-tuning only if prompting cannot hold the format.

      Why can't you simply put all 50,000 company documents in a 1M-token prompt?

      They do not fit. Even a subset that fits costs tokens on every query, is slower, is read less reliably in the middle, and ignores per-user permissions. Retrieve first, then read.

      Chapter 2 · Foundations

      The RAG pipeline end to end

      Every RAG system, from a 60-line script to Microsoft GraphRAG, has the same two halves. An indexing pipeline runs offline, whenever documents change, and turns raw documents into a searchable index. A query pipeline runs online, for every question, and turns a question into a grounded answer. Learn this map once and every architecture in Part IV becomes "the same map with a few boxes changed".

      The indexing pipeline, stage by stage

      StageWhat it doesKey decisionTypical failureDeep dive
      Load + parseReads files and APIs and extracts clean text, tables and structureWhich parser (layout-aware or plain text); whether to OCR scansTables flattened into nonsense; headers and footers repeated on every chunkCh 5
      ChunkSplits documents into retrievable passagesSize, overlap, boundaries (sentence, heading, semantic)The answer is split across two chunks; a chunk has no context ("it increased by 5%")Ch 6
      EnrichAdds metadata: source, title, section, date, permissions, languageWhich fields you will filter on laterNo date means old and new policy versions compete; no ACL means data leaksCh 6
      EmbedTurns each chunk into a vector that captures its meaningEmbedding model (quality, language, dimensions, cost)A general model misses domain jargon; mixing model versions in one indexCh 7
      IndexStores vectors (ANN index) and often a keyword (BM25) index tooVector database, index type, filtering, hybrid searchRecall drops because ANN parameters are tuned for speed onlyCh 8

      The query pipeline, stage by stage

      StageWhat it doesKey decisionTypical failureDeep dive
      Transform queryRewrites, expands or splits the user's questionRewrite, multi-query, HyDE, decomposition, routingVague follow-ups ("what about last year?") retrieve nothing usefulCh 10
      RetrieveFinds candidate chunks (top 20–100)Dense, sparse or hybrid; metadata filters; kThe right chunk is at rank 40 and never seenCh 9
      RerankRe-scores candidates with a stronger model and keeps the best fewCross-encoder or LLM reranker; how many to keepSkipped, so near-duplicates and off-topic chunks fill the promptCh 11
      Build contextOrders, deduplicates and compresses the chunks into a prompt with source IDsOrder, token budget, citation formatKey evidence buried in the middle; the context budget blown on duplicatesCh 12
      GenerateThe LLM answers from the context and cites sourcesModel, grounding instructions, refusal ruleThe model "fills gaps" from memory and hallucinatesCh 12

      What one indexed chunk looks like

      A chunk is more than text. Metadata is what lets you filter ("only 2026 policies", "only documents this user may see"), cite ("Handbook §4.2, p. 12") and update ("delete every chunk of doc 881 and re-index it").

      one record in the index
      {
  "id": "handbook-2026#leave-carry-over#0",
  "doc_id": "handbook-2026",
  "text": "Leave carry-over: employees may carry over up to 5 unused days into the next calendar year. Carried-over days must be used by 31 March.",
  "embedding": [0.0213, -0.0871, 0.0442, "... 384 numbers ..."],
  "metadata": {
    "title": "Employee Handbook 2026",
    "section": "4.2 Leave carry-over",
    "page": 12,
    "source_url": "https://intranet.example.com/handbook-2026.pdf",
    "updated_at": "2026-01-15",
    "department": "HR",
    "allowed_groups": ["all-employees"],
    "language": "en"
  }
}

      Why RAG systems fail: the seven failure points

      Barnett et al., "Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System" (arXiv:2401.05856, 2024), studied three real RAG deployments and found failures cluster at seven points. Keep this list nearby when you debug.

      #Failure pointWhat you seeUsual fix
      FP1Missing contentThe answer is not in the corpus, but the model answers anywayA refusal instruction; a relevance threshold; CRAG-style web fallback (E2)
      FP2Missed the top-ranked documentsThe right chunk exists but ranks below the cut-offHybrid search, a better embedding model, query rewriting, a larger k + reranking
      FP3Not in context (consolidation)Retrieved, but dropped when the context was trimmedRerank before trimming; compress; increase the budget
      FP4Not extractedIn the prompt, but the model ignores it or misreads itLess noise; put the best evidence first; a stronger model
      FP5Wrong formatIgnores the requested table, list or JSONStructured outputs; clearer instructions
      FP6Incorrect specificityToo general, or too detailed for the questionQuery rewriting; answer-style instructions
      FP7IncompleteAnswers part of a multi-part questionQuery decomposition (B3); multi-hop RAG (D1)
      Debugging rule

      When an answer is wrong, first check whether the right chunk was retrieved. If it was not, the problem is retrieval: chunking, embeddings, search or the query (FP1–FP3). If it was, the problem is generation: the prompt, context order or model (FP4–FP7). This one check halves debugging time.

      A realistic latency and cost budget

      Numbers vary with hardware and models, but the shape is stable. Generation dominates. Each extra LLM call that an advanced architecture adds (rewriting, grading, reflection) adds roughly a second or more and costs extra.

      StepTypical latencyNotes
      Embed the query (local small model)5–30 msAn API embedding adds a network round trip (≈50–200 ms)
      ANN vector search (1M vectors, HNSW)2–20 msPlus BM25 for hybrid: similar
      Cross-encoder rerank of 50 candidates50–300 msGPU helps a lot; API rerankers ≈100–300 ms
      LLM query rewrite (small model)0.3–1.5 sOptional; one extra call
      LLM answer generation1–10 sDominated by output length; stream it to the user

      Key takeaways

      • Indexing runs offline and once per change. Querying runs online and once per question. Design both.
      • Metadata is half of a chunk's value: it enables filtering, citations, permissions and updates.
      • Debug in order: was the right chunk retrieved? Then was it used?
      • Every advanced architecture is this pipeline with stages added, swapped or looped.

      Quick check

      Users get answers from last year's policy even though the new one is indexed. Which stage do you fix?

      Enrichment and retrieval: add updated_at or a version to the metadata, then filter or boost the newest version, or delete superseded chunks on re-index. Time-sensitive corpora may need Temporal RAG (G6).

      The correct chunk is retrieved at rank 3, but the answer still ignores it. Which failure point is this?

      FP4, not extracted. It is a generation-side problem: reduce noise in the context, put the best evidence first and tighten the grounding prompt.

      Chapter 3 · Foundations

      Your first RAG in about 60 lines of Python

      This chapter builds a complete, working RAG system with no framework and no database: Python, numpy, a local embedding model and Claude. Seeing every step in plain code is the best way to understand what LangChain, LlamaIndex and vector databases do for you later. You will also create two files that every later example in this guide imports:

      • rag_common.py: shared helpers: llm(), llm_parse(), embed(), chunk_text(), a tiny VectorIndex and a grounded answer().
      • sample_docs.py: a small fictional company corpus ("Northwind Robotics": HR policies, expenses, security, two robot products, an incident report and an org chart). It is designed so that later chapters can show multi-hop, temporal, graph and permission problems on the same data.

      Step 0 · Set up

      terminal (Windows PowerShell)
      python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1            # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -U anthropic sentence-transformers numpy pydantic

$env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "sk-ant-..."   # macOS/Linux: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
      Models used in this guide

      claude-opus-5-5 writes the answers. The much cheaper claude-haiku-5-5 does helper work such as rewriting queries, grading documents and routing. Embeddings come from BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, a free 384-dimension model that runs on a laptop CPU (about 130 MB download on first use). Anthropic does not sell its own embedding model. Its docs point to Voyage AI, and Chapter 7 shows how to swap models.

      Step 1 · The shared helpers: rag_common.py

      rag_common.py
      """Shared helpers used by every example in the RAG Field Guide.

pip install -U anthropic sentence-transformers numpy pydantic
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import anthropic
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"              # writes the final answers
FAST_MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5"        # cheap helper calls: rewrite, grade, route
EMBED_MODEL = "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"  # 384-dim local embedding model
QUERY_PREFIX = "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "

client = anthropic.Anthropic()         # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
_embedder: SentenceTransformer | None = None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- LLM calls
def llm(prompt: str, system: str = "", model: str = MODEL, max_tokens: int = 4000) -> str:
    """Send one user message to Claude and return the reply text."""
    kwargs = {"model": model, "max_tokens": max_tokens,
              "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
    if system:
        kwargs["system"] = system
    if model == MODEL:
        # If a safety classifier declines, the API re-runs the request on a fallback model.
        resp = client.beta.messages.create(
            betas=["server-side-fallback-2026-07-01"], fallbacks="default", **kwargs)
    else:
        resp = client.messages.create(**kwargs)
    if resp.stop_reason == "refusal":
        return "[the model declined this request]"
    return "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text").strip()


def llm_parse(prompt: str, schema, system: str = "", model: str = FAST_MODEL):
    """Ask Claude for output that matches a Pydantic model; returns a validated instance."""
    kwargs = {"model": model, "max_tokens": 2000, "output_format": schema,
              "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
    if system:
        kwargs["system"] = system
    return client.messages.parse(**kwargs).parsed_output


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- embeddings
def embedder() -> SentenceTransformer:
    global _embedder
    if _embedder is None:
        _embedder = SentenceTransformer(EMBED_MODEL)
    return _embedder


def embed(texts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    """Embed passages. Rows are unit length, so a dot product equals cosine similarity."""
    return embedder().encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True, convert_to_numpy=True)


def embed_query(query: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """BGE models retrieve better when short queries carry an instruction prefix."""
    return embed([QUERY_PREFIX + query])[0]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- chunking
@dataclass
class Chunk:
    id: str
    text: str
    meta: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


def chunk_text(text: str, size: int = 800, overlap: int = 120) -> list[str]:
    """Pack sentences into ~size-character chunks; each chunk repeats ~overlap chars of the last."""
    sentences = [s.strip() for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+|\n{2,}", text.strip()) if s.strip()]
    chunks, cur = [], ""
    for s in sentences:
        if cur and len(cur) + len(s) + 1 > size:
            chunks.append(cur)
            tail = cur[-overlap:].split(" ", 1)[-1] if overlap else ""
            cur = f"{tail} {s}".strip()
        else:
            cur = f"{cur} {s}".strip()
    if cur:
        chunks.append(cur)
    return chunks


def make_chunks(docs: dict[str, dict], size: int = 800, overlap: int = 120) -> list[Chunk]:
    """docs = {doc_id: {"title": ..., "text": ..., other metadata...}} -> list of Chunk."""
    out = []
    for doc_id, d in docs.items():
        meta = {k: v for k, v in d.items() if k != "text"} | {"doc_id": doc_id}
        for i, piece in enumerate(chunk_text(d["text"], size, overlap)):
            out.append(Chunk(id=f"{doc_id}#{i}", text=piece, meta=meta))
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- vector index
class VectorIndex:
    """A tiny in-memory vector index: exact cosine search with numpy."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.chunks: list[Chunk] = []
        self.vecs: np.ndarray | None = None

    def add(self, chunks: list[Chunk]) -> None:
        v = embed([c.text for c in chunks])
        self.vecs = v if self.vecs is None else np.vstack([self.vecs, v])
        self.chunks.extend(chunks)

    def search(self, query: str, k: int = 4, where: dict | None = None) -> list[tuple[float, Chunk]]:
        """Return the k most similar chunks as (score, chunk); `where` filters on metadata."""
        scores = self.vecs @ embed_query(query)
        hits = []
        for i in np.argsort(-scores):
            c = self.chunks[i]
            if where and any(c.meta.get(key) != val for key, val in where.items()):
                continue
            hits.append((float(scores[i]), c))
            if len(hits) == k:
                break
        return hits


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- grounded answer
ANSWER_SYSTEM = """You answer questions using ONLY the numbered sources provided.
Rules:
- Cite every claim with its source number in square brackets, e.g. [2].
- If the sources do not contain the answer, say exactly: "I don't know based on the provided documents."
- Do not use outside knowledge. Be concise."""


def format_context(hits: list[tuple[float, Chunk]]) -> str:
    blocks = []
    for n, (_, c) in enumerate(hits, start=1):
        label = c.meta.get("title", c.meta.get("doc_id", c.id))
        blocks.append(f"[{n}] ({label}, updated {c.meta.get('updated_at', 'n/a')})\n{c.text}")
    return "\n\n".join(blocks)


def answer(question: str, hits: list[tuple[float, Chunk]], model: str = MODEL) -> str:
    prompt = f"Sources:\n\n{format_context(hits)}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    return llm(prompt, system=ANSWER_SYSTEM, model=model)

      Step 2 · The sample corpus: sample_docs.py

      The documents are short so the examples run fast, but they contain the traps real corpora have. The meal limit was changed by a later update (a temporal conflict). One answer needs facts from two documents (multi-hop). The security policy is visible only to some groups (permissions). And people, products and teams link to each other (graph structure).

      sample_docs.py
      """A small fictional corpus used by every example in this guide."""
DOCS = {
    "leave-policy": {

        "allowed_groups": ["all-employees"],

      Step 3 · Index, retrieve and answer: first_rag.py

      first_rag.py
      from rag_common import VectorIndex, answer, make_chunks
from sample_docs import DOCS

# ---- indexing (offline): chunk -> embed -> store
index = VectorIndex()
index.add(make_chunks(DOCS))
print(f"Indexed {len(index.chunks)} chunks from {len(DOCS)} documents\n")

# ---- query (online): retrieve -> augment -> generate
for question in [
    "How many unused leave days can I carry over, and by when must I use them?",
    "What does error E17 mean on a rover?",
    "What is the company's stock price?",          # not in the corpus: should refuse
]:
    hits = index.search(question, k=3)
    print("Q:", question)
    for score, chunk in hits:
        print(f"   {score:.3f}  {chunk.id}")
    print("A:", answer(question, hits), "\n")
      Indexed 9 chunks from 8 documents Q: How many unused leave days can I carry over, and by when must I use them? 0.781 leave-policy#0 0.612 leave-policy#1 0.534 expense-update-2026#0 A: You can carry over up to 5 unused days into the next calendar year, and they must be used by 31 March, after which they expire [1]. Q: What does error E17 mean on a rover? 0.744 rover-r2#0 0.655 rover-r3#0 0.571 incident-2026-03#0 A: E17 means the battery is overheating: stop the rover and let it cool for 30 minutes [1]. Rover R3 uses the same error codes [2]. Q: What is the company's stock price? ... A: I don't know based on the provided documents.

      NoteScores and chunk counts above are illustrative. Your exact numbers depend on the library versions, and the answer wording will vary from run to run.

      What each part is doing

      1. Chunking (chunk_text) packs whole sentences into pieces of about 800 characters, with a small overlap so a fact on a boundary appears in both neighbours.
      2. Embedding (embed) maps each chunk to 384 numbers. Vectors are normalised to length 1, so vecs @ query computes the cosine similarity with every chunk in one matrix multiply.
      3. Retrieval (search) sorts all chunks by similarity and returns the top k. This is exact search: fine for thousands of chunks. Millions need an ANN index (Chapter 8).
      4. Augmentation (format_context) numbers each chunk and adds its title and date, so the model can cite [1] and tell old versions from new ones.
      5. Generation (answer) uses a system prompt with three rules: only use the sources, cite them, and say "I don't know" otherwise. That last rule is your main defence against failure point FP1.

      Try these and watch it break (on purpose)

      This naive pipeline has real weaknesses. Each one is fixed by a later chapter or catalog card:

      Ask thisWhat goes wrongFixed by
      "What is the international meal allowance?"Both the 2025 value (90) and the 2026 update (100) are retrieved; the model may pick the wrong oneDate-aware prompt, metadata filters, Temporal RAG (G6)
      "Who does the incident commander of INC-2026-031 report to?"Needs two hops: incident → Mei Chen → org chart → Daniel OkaforMulti-hop RAG (D1), Graph RAG (G1)
      "E42" (a two-character query)Dense embeddings handle short codes and IDs poorlyHybrid BM25 + vector search (A5)
      A contractor asks about laptop encryptionThe security policy is restricted, but this index ignores permissionsMetadata filtering, permission-aware RAG (I8)
      "Compare R2 and R3 battery and payload"Works only if both product sheets make the top kQuery decomposition (B3), larger k + reranking (A4)
      Permission filter

      index.search(q, where={"department": "HR"}) shows the idea of metadata filtering, but this toy version only does equality checks. Real permission checks test list membership (is the user's group in allowed_groups?) and must run inside the vector database before ranking, not after. See Chapter 8 and card I8.

      Key takeaways

      • A RAG system is about 60 lines of code: chunk, embed, search, prompt, generate. Frameworks add convenience, not magic.
      • Normalised embeddings turn similarity search into a single matrix multiplication.
      • The grounding prompt (cite + refuse) matters as much as retrieval.
      • Every weakness you just saw has a named fix. That is what the rest of the guide is about.

      Quick check

      Why are the embeddings normalised?

      For unit-length vectors, the dot product equals cosine similarity. So vecs @ q ranks every chunk with one fast matrix multiply, with no division by vector lengths.

      Why does format_context include updated_at?

      So the model can see that the 2026 update supersedes the 2025 policy when both are retrieved. It is a cheap first defence against stale answers.

      Chapter 4 · Foundations

      How to read the RAG catalog

      "RAG" is now a family of about 65 named architectures. Most of them change only one or two boxes of the pipeline from Chapter 2. Part IV groups them into 10 families by what they change. Once you know which box a type changes, you know what problem it solves and what it costs.

      The ten families at a glance

      FamilyWhat it changesReach for it when…Chapter
      A · Core paradigmsThe overall pipeline shapeStarting any project; you need a baseline14
      B · Query transformationThe query before retrievalQueries are vague, short, multi-part or need routing15
      C · Index structureWhat a retrievable unit is and how it is embeddedChunks lose context; documents are long; precision is poor16
      D · Iterative and multi-stepHow many times you retrieve, and with whatAnswers need several facts that build on each other17
      E · Self-reflective and adaptiveWhether the system checks and corrects itselfRetrieval is sometimes wrong; question difficulty varies18
      F · AgenticWho controls retrieval: code or an LLM agentOpen-ended tasks, many sources and tools19
      G · Graph and structuredKnowledge stored as graphs, tables, SQL or time-stamped factsRelationships, global questions, numbers, time-sensitive facts20
      H · MultimodalNon-text content: images, page scans, video, audio, codeKnowledge lives in figures, slides, recordings or repos21
      I · System and deploymentWhere data lives and who may see itSilos, privacy, live data, many tenants, a specific domain22
      J · Trained RAGThe model weights themselves are trained for retrievalA fixed domain, a high volume of queries, ML capacity23

      How every card is laid out

      Each RAG type in Part IV gets one card with the same sections, so you can compare any two types side by side:

      1. One-line definition and any other names it is known by.
      2. Architecture diagram: the pipeline with the changed boxes highlighted in purple.
      3. How it works: the mechanism as numbered steps, taken from the original paper or docs.
      4. Use it when / avoid it when, plus real-world use cases.
      5. Python: a full runnable example for the core types, and a focused sketch of the key idea for the rest (a full-code companion section is planned).
      6. Pros and cons, and the main limitations.
      7. Ratings on five 1–5 scales (below).
      8. References: paper, official repo, docs and tutorials, each labeled.
      9. Compared with: the nearest alternatives and how to choose between them.

      The rating scales

      Build complexity
      ●●●○○medium

      Scale1 means5 means
      Build complexityAn afternoon with plain PythonA team-scale system: training, graphs, many services
      LatencyOne retrieval + one LLM callMany LLM calls or loops; seconds to minutes
      CostEmbeddings + one generationHeavy LLM use at indexing and/or query time
      Quality gainMarginal over a good baselineLarge gains on the problems it targets
      MaturityA research prototypeStandard practice, supported by major frameworks

      Ratings are an experienced practitioner's relative judgement, not benchmark results. "Quality gain" applies on the problem the type targets. GraphRAG scores high for global "what are the themes?" questions and adds little for simple lookups.

      Reference labels

      • official repo Code published by the paper's authors or the project's company.
      • community A third-party implementation or wrapper: useful, but check its activity.
      • paper The original research paper (arXiv ID given).
      • docs Official framework documentation or tutorial (LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Haystack, vendor docs).
      • inactive The repo is no longer maintained. Read it to understand the idea; do not depend on it.

      The complete index of RAG types

      Every type in the catalog, with a one-line summary. Click an ID to jump to its card.

      IDRAG typeIn one line
      A · Core paradigms
      A1Naive / Standard RAGIndex → retrieve top-k → stuff into prompt → generate
      A2Advanced RAGNaive + pre-retrieval (rewrite) and post-retrieval (rerank, compress) steps
      A3Modular RAGSwappable modules with routing, branching and loops (LEGO-style)
      A4Retrieve-and-Rerank RAGFast recall of many candidates, then a precise reranker picks the best few
      A5Hybrid RAGKeyword (BM25) + vector search fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
      A6Conversational RAGRewrites follow-up questions using chat history before retrieving
      A7Long-context RAG (LongRAG)Retrieve a few long units and let a long-context model read them whole
      A8Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG)No retrieval: preload a small corpus once and cache it
      B · Query transformation
      B1HyDEEmbed a hypothetical answer instead of the question
      B2Multi-query / RAG-FusionSeveral rewrites of the query, results fused with RRF
      B3Query decompositionSplit a complex question into sub-questions, answer each, combine
      B4Step-back RAGAlso retrieve for a more general "step-back" question
      B5Routing RAGSend each query to the right index, tool or prompt, or to none
      B6Rewrite-Retrieve-ReadAn LLM rewrites the query (and expands jargon) before retrieval
      C · Index structure
      C1Parent-document / small-to-bigMatch on small chunks, hand the LLM the bigger parent or window
      C2Hierarchical RAG (RAPTOR)A tree of recursive cluster summaries, searched at every level
      C3Contextual RetrievalAn LLM writes a context line for every chunk before indexing
      C4Late chunkingEmbed the whole document, then pool per chunk: context for free
      C5Multi-vector / ColBERT RAGOne vector per token; fine-grained late-interaction matching
      C6Proposition RAG (Dense X)Index atomic, self-contained facts instead of passages
      C7Memory-augmented RAG (MemoRAG)A global memory of the corpus drafts clues that guide retrieval
      D · Iterative and multi-step
      D1Multi-hop RAG (IRCoT)Interleave reasoning steps with retrieval to chain facts
      D2Iterative RAG (Iter-RetGen)Use each draft answer to retrieve better evidence, then repeat
      D3Recursive RAGFollow references from retrieved nodes into deeper sources
      D4Active RAG (FLARE)Retrieve mid-generation whenever the model becomes unsure
      D5Chain-of-Retrieval (Self-Ask, CoRAG)Ask and answer follow-up questions step by step, each with retrieval
      E · Self-reflective and adaptive
      E1Self-RAGThe model decides when to retrieve and critiques its own output with reflection tokens
      E2Corrective RAG (CRAG)Grade the retrieved documents; if bad, rewrite and search the web
      E3Adaptive RAGClassify question difficulty → no retrieval, single-step or multi-step
      E4Speculative RAGA small drafter writes several answers; a large verifier picks one
      E5Self-RouteTry cheap RAG first; fall back to long context if the model says it cannot answer
      E6Noise-robust RAG (Chain-of-Note)Write a reading note per document; abstain if context is insufficient
      E7RL-trained search RAG (Search-R1)A reasoning model trained with RL to decide when and what to search
      F · Agentic
      F1Agentic RAGAn LLM agent uses retrieval as a tool in a reason-act loop
      F2Multi-agent RAGSpecialist agents (router, retriever, critic) collaborate
      F3Deep-research RAGPlan → many searches → read → write a long cited report
      F4Tool-augmented RAG (MCP)Retrieval mixed with live APIs and tools served over MCP
      F5Agent-memory RAGRAG over the agent's own long-term memory (Mem0, Letta)
      G · Graph and structured knowledge
      G1GraphRAG (Microsoft)Entity graph + community summaries; local, global and DRIFT search
      G2LightRAGLightweight graph + vectors with dual-level (entity/theme) retrieval
      G3HippoRAGMemory-inspired: knowledge graph + Personalized PageRank
      G4Knowledge-Graph RAG (Neo4j)Query a property graph with vector + Cypher retrievers
      G5KAGKnowledge-augmented generation with logical-form reasoning over a KG
      G6Temporal RAGTime-aware facts with validity intervals (bi-temporal graphs)

      H2Visual-document RAG (ColPali, VisRAG)Retrieve page images directly; no OCR

      H5Code RAGAST-aware chunks, symbol graphs and repo maps for code

      I2On-device / small-model RAGRAG designed for small local models (MiniRAG)

      I4Web-search RAGA live search API is the retriever (Perplexity-style)

      The honest rule of thumb

      Most production systems in 2026 are A5 Hybrid + A4 Rerank + C1/C3 better chunks, plus one specialised type for their hardest problem: G7 SQL for numbers, G1/G2 graphs for relationships, F1 agentic for open-ended tasks, I8 for permissions. Start with the simplest type that could work, measure it (Chapter 24), and add complexity only where the measurements say it is needed.

      Chapter 5 · Ingestion and indexing

      Loading and parsing documents

      Garbage in, garbage out applies to RAG more than anywhere else. If a parser flattens a table into a jumble of numbers, drops a heading or repeats the page footer 200 times, no embedding model or reranker can recover. In real projects, parsing problems cause more bad answers than model problems, yet they are the least visible part of the pipeline. Always look at the parsed text before you index it.

      What makes documents hard

      ContentThe problemWhat good parsing keeps
      Born-digital PDFText exists, but reading order across columns, headers and footers is lostReading order, headings, page numbers
      Scanned PDF / imagesNo text layer at allOCR text, with confidence; layout
      TablesRows and columns become a stream of cellsTable structure as Markdown/HTML, plus a caption
      SlidesLittle text; meaning lives in layout and picturesSlide titles, speaker notes, image captions
      HTML / wikiNavigation, cookie banners and ads mixed with contentMain content only, heading hierarchy, links
      DOCX / emailTracked changes, quoted replies, signaturesFinal text, thread structure, sender and date
      Formulas / codeSymbols mangled by plain-text extractionLaTeX for maths, fenced code blocks

      Choosing a parser (2026)

      ToolBest atRunsLicence note
      PyMuPDF (2.x, includes the former pymupdf4llm)Very fast extraction of born-digital PDFs; to_markdown() with automatic layout analysis; OCR hookLocal, CPUAGPL-3.0 or commercial
      Docling (docling-project/docling)Layout, reading order, table structure and formulas across PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX and HTML; one unified document modelLocal (air-gapped OK)MIT
      UnstructuredMany formats → typed "elements" (Title, NarrativeText, Table); chunk_by_titleLocal; hosted platform adds VLM/OCRApache-2.0
      Marker (datalab-to/marker)PDF → Markdown with tables and equations; optional LLM passLocal, GPU helpsWeights: free under $5M revenue
      MinerU (opendatalab/MinerU)Scientific and Chinese/English PDFs, formulas, complex tablesLocal, GPUCustom licence (Apache-based, terms at very large scale)
      LlamaParseHosted agentic parsing of difficult documentsCloud, per-page creditsCommercial
      Claude (vision)The hardest pages: charts, handwritten forms, weird layouts. Send the PDF and ask for MarkdownAPIPay per token: use selectively
      Rule of thumb

      Use PyMuPDF for clean digital PDFs at scale. Use Docling as the default for mixed enterprise documents with tables. Send only the pages that defeat both to a vision model (Claude or a VLM-based parser). Tag every chunk with the parser that produced it, so you can re-parse one class of documents later.

      Code: a practical parser with a fast path and a quality path

      install
      pip install -U pymupdf docling
      parse_docs.py
      """Parse PDFs into page-tagged Markdown: fast path (PyMuPDF), quality path (Docling)."""
import re
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import pymupdf                                   # PyMuPDF
from docling.document_converter import DocumentConverter


def parse_fast(path: str) -> list[dict]:
    """One record per page with plain text. Good for clean, born-digital PDFs."""
    pages = []
    with pymupdf.open(path) as doc:
        for i, page in enumerate(doc, start=1):
            pages.append({"page": i, "text": page.get_text("text")})
    return pages


def parse_quality(path: str) -> str:
    """Layout-aware Markdown (headings, reading order, tables). Slower; use for complex files."""
    result = DocumentConverter().convert(path)
    return result.document.export_to_markdown()


def needs_ocr(pages: list[dict], min_chars: int = 40) -> bool:
    """Scanned PDFs have (almost) no text layer."""
    empty = sum(1 for p in pages if len(p["text"].strip()) < min_chars)
    return empty > len(pages) / 2


def strip_repeated_lines(pages: list[dict], min_share: float = 0.6) -> list[dict]:
    """Remove headers/footers: short lines that repeat on most pages."""
    counts = Counter(line.strip() for p in pages for line in set(p["text"].splitlines())
                     if 0 < len(line.strip()) < 80)
    repeated = {line for line, n in counts.items() if n >= max(3, min_share * len(pages))}
    for p in pages:
        p["text"] = "\n".join(l for l in p["text"].splitlines() if l.strip() not in repeated)
    return pages


def clean(text: str) -> str:
    text = re.sub(r"(\w)-\n(\w)", r"\1\2", text)     # re-join hyphenated line breaks
    text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text)
    return re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", text).strip()


def parse(path: str, has_tables: bool = False) -> dict:
    pages = parse_fast(path)
    if has_tables or needs_ocr(pages):
        # Docling's default pipeline runs OCR on scanned pages and rebuilds table structure.
        return {"source": Path(path).name, "parser": "docling", "markdown": parse_quality(path)}
    pages = strip_repeated_lines(pages)
    md = "\n\n".join(f"<!-- page {p['page']} -->\n{clean(p['text'])}" for p in pages)
    return {"source": Path(path).name, "parser": "pymupdf", "markdown": md}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    doc = parse("handbook.pdf")
    print(doc["parser"], len(doc["markdown"]), "chars")
    print(doc["markdown"][:800])

      The <!-- page N --> markers survive chunking, so each chunk can carry its page number for citations ("Handbook, p. 12").

      Code: let Claude parse the pages nothing else can

      Claude reads PDFs natively, including charts and scanned pages. It costs more than a local parser, so use it as the last resort for pages that fail a quality check: too little text, broken tables or an OCR result full of gibberish.

      parse_with_claude.py
      import base64

from rag_common import MODEL, client

PROMPT = """Convert this document to clean Markdown for a search index.
- Keep headings (#, ##), lists and the reading order.
- Render every table as a Markdown table.
- Describe each chart or figure in one or two sentences inside [Figure: ...].
- Mark each page start with <!-- page N -->.
Output only the Markdown."""


def pdf_to_markdown(path: str) -> str:
    data = base64.standard_b64encode(open(path, "rb").read()).decode()
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=16000,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
            {"type": "document",
             "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": data}},
            {"type": "text", "text": PROMPT},
        ]}],
    )
    return "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")


print(pdf_to_markdown("quarterly-report.pdf")[:1000])
      Limits

      A single request accepts up to 32 MB and a limited number of pages (600, or 100 on 200k-context models), and every page costs input tokens. Split big files and send only the pages that need vision. For large volumes, a VLM-based parser (Docling with GraniteDocling, MinerU, Marker with --use_llm) is usually cheaper.

      Metadata to capture while parsing

      You will never have an easier moment to collect metadata than during parsing. Capture at least:

      • Identity: doc_id, source URL or path, a content hash (to skip unchanged files on re-index).
      • Structure: title, section path ("4 Leave › 4.2 Carry-over"), page number.
      • Time: created and updated dates, effective date, version. Temporal RAG depends on these.
      • Access: owner, department, the groups allowed to read it. Permission-aware RAG (I8) depends on these.
      • Provenance: the parser and its version, OCR used (yes/no), language.

      Common mistakes

      • Never looking at the parsed output. Print 20 random parsed pages before indexing anything.
      • One parser for everything. Route by document type. The fast path handles 80% of documents; spend money only on the rest.
      • Losing tables. Keep them as Markdown tables. For important tables, also store a one-line natural-language summary as a separate chunk ("Table 3: meal allowances by region").
      • Indexing boilerplate. Repeated headers, footers, legal disclaimers and navigation menus pollute every search. Strip them.

      Key takeaways

      • Parsing quality caps retrieval quality. Inspect the output.
      • Normalise everything to Markdown that keeps headings, tables and page markers.
      • Use the fast path for most files, layout-aware parsing for complex ones, and vision for the hardest pages.
      • Collect identity, structure, time and access metadata now. Later chapters depend on it.

      Quick check

      Half the pages of a PDF return almost no text. What happened, and what do you do?

      It is a scan with no text layer. Route it to OCR: Docling's pipeline, or a VLM such as Claude for difficult pages.

      Why keep page markers in the parsed Markdown?

      They flow into chunk metadata, so answers can cite "p. 12" and users can verify the source.

      Chapter 6 · Ingestion and indexing

      Chunking strategies

      A chunk is the unit you retrieve. Chunking decides what the retriever can find and what the LLM will read. Make chunks too big and the embedding blurs several topics, so they rank poorly and waste context. Make them too small and they lose the context that gives them meaning: "it increased by 5%" says nothing about what increased. There is no universal best size, but there is a sensible default and a clear way to measure.

      The strategies at a glance

      StrategyHow it splitsStrengthsWeaknessesUse for
      Fixed-sizeEvery N tokens, optional overlapTrivial, predictableCuts sentences and tables mid-wayQuick baselines, uniform text
      RecursiveTries paragraph → line → sentence → word separators until pieces fitRespects natural boundaries; a strong defaultIgnores document semanticsThe default for prose
      Sentence-basedPacks whole sentences up to a sizeNever breaks a sentenceNeeds a good sentence splitter per languageQ&A over prose
      Structure-awareSplits on Markdown/HTML headings, then recursively within sectionsChunks align with topics; heading path becomes metadataNeeds good parsing (Ch 5)Manuals, policies, docs, wikis
      SemanticEmbeds sentences; cuts where similarity between neighbours dropsTopic-coherent chunksExtra embedding cost; uneven sizesLong, loosely structured text (transcripts)
      Parent–child (C1)Small children for matching, large parents for readingPrecise matching plus full contextTwo stores; more tokensLong documents
      Contextual (C3)An LLM prefixes each chunk with a situating sentenceBig recall gains (−35% to −49% failures)One LLM call per chunk at ingestHigh-value corpora
      Late chunking (C4)Embed the whole document, pool tokens per chunkContext without LLM callsNeeds a long-context embedding modelCheap contextual chunks
      Proposition (C6)An LLM rewrites text into atomic factsVery precise for factoid QAExpensive; loses narrativeFact-dense corpora
      LLM / agenticAn LLM decides the boundariesHighest recall in some testsSlow and costly at scaleSmall, high-value sets
      SpecialisedCode by AST (functions/classes); tables by row groups with headers repeated; chats by turn/threadRespects the format's logicOne splitter per formatCode (H5), tables (G8), tickets

      What the research says about size and overlap

      Chroma's study "Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval" (trychroma.com/research/evaluating-chunking, July 2024) measured token-level recall and precision across 5 corpora and 472 queries:

      ChunkerRecallNote
      LLM chunker (GPT-4o)91.9Best recall, low precision, expensive
      Cluster-semantic, 400 tokens91.3Strong
      Recursive, 400 tokens, no overlap89.5Simple and strong
      Recursive, 200 tokens, no overlap88.1Good precision
      Recursive 800 tokens, 400 overlap (a common framework default)85.4Below average
      Semantic (Kamradt-style default)83.6Defaults matter
      Good defaults to start from

      Recursive splitting at 256–512 tokens, with 0–15% overlap, applied inside structural sections, and with the section's heading path added to each chunk. Overlap mostly adds duplicate tokens, so use a little at most. Then tune size on your evaluation set (Chapter 13): the best size depends on your documents and questions.

      Code: four chunkers you will actually use

      install
      pip install -U langchain-text-splitters tiktoken
      chunkers.py
      """Structure-aware, recursive, semantic and 'breadcrumb' chunking."""
import re

import numpy as np
from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

from rag_common import Chunk, embed

# 1) Structure first: split Markdown on headings; heading text goes into metadata.
header_splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(
    headers_to_split_on=[("#", "h1"), ("##", "h2"), ("###", "h3")], strip_headers=False)

# 2) Then recursive splitting inside each section, measured in tokens.
recursive = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_tiktoken_encoder(chunk_size=400, chunk_overlap=40)


def structure_chunks(markdown: str, doc_id: str, base_meta: dict) -> list[Chunk]:
    out = []
    for section in header_splitter.split_text(markdown):          # Documents with .metadata
        path = " > ".join(section.metadata[k] for k in ("h1", "h2", "h3") if k in section.metadata)
        for j, piece in enumerate(recursive.split_text(section.page_content)):
            # 3) Breadcrumb: prepend the heading path so the chunk keeps its context.
            text = f"{path}\n\n{piece}" if path else piece
            out.append(Chunk(id=f"{doc_id}#{len(out)}", text=text,
                             meta=base_meta | {"section": path, "doc_id": doc_id}))
    return out


# 4) Semantic chunking: cut where neighbouring sentences stop being similar.
def semantic_chunks(text: str, percentile: float = 90, max_chars: int = 1500) -> list[str]:
    sents = [s.strip() for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text) if s.strip()]
    if len(sents) < 3:
        return [" ".join(sents)]
    vecs = embed(sents)
    distance = 1 - np.sum(vecs[:-1] * vecs[1:], axis=1)   # cosine distance between neighbours
    threshold = np.percentile(distance, percentile)
    chunks, cur = [], [sents[0]]
    for sent, d in zip(sents[1:], distance):
        if d > threshold or sum(len(s) for s in cur) > max_chars:
            chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
            cur = [sent]
        else:
            cur.append(sent)
    chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
    return chunks


if __name__ == "__main__":
    md = """# Employee Handbook
## 4 Leave
### 4.2 Carry-over
Employees may carry over up to 5 unused days. Carried-over days must be used by 31 March.
## 5 Expenses
The international meal allowance is 100 EUR per day."""
    for c in structure_chunks(md, "handbook", {"updated_at": "2026-07-01"}):
        print(c.id, "|", c.meta["section"], "|", c.text.replace("\n", " ")[:90])
      handbook#0 | Employee Handbook | Employee Handbook # Employee Handbook handbook#1 | Employee Handbook > 4 Leave > 4.2 Carry-over | Employee Handbook > 4 Leave > 4.2 Carry-over ### 4.2 Carry-over Employees may carry... handbook#2 | Employee Handbook > 5 Expenses | Employee Handbook > 5 Expenses ## 5 Expenses The international meal...

      The breadcrumb ("Employee Handbook > 4 Leave > 4.2 Carry-over") is a free, cheap form of contextualisation. The chunk now says what the 5 days refer to even when it is retrieved on its own. Contextual Retrieval (card C3) takes the same idea further with an LLM-written context sentence.

      Chunking for other content types

      • Tables: keep the header row with every row group. Store a natural-language summary chunk for each important table. Very large tables belong in SQL or Table RAG (G7, G8).
      • Code: split by function and class with tree-sitter and keep the file path and signature in metadata (H5).
      • Conversations, tickets, email: chunk by thread or turn window and keep the speaker and timestamp.
      • Transcripts: semantic or fixed time windows (for example 60–120 seconds) with start and end timestamps (H4).
      • Slides: one chunk per slide: title + body + speaker notes + image caption.

      Common mistakes

      • Keeping a framework default (for example 1000 characters, 200 overlap) without ever measuring it.
      • Large overlap "to be safe". It duplicates content in the top-k and wastes context; prefer structure-aware boundaries.
      • Chunks without metadata. Every chunk needs its source, section, page, date and permissions (Ch 2).
      • Re-chunking without re-embedding. Changing the chunking requires rebuilding the index. Version your chunking config.

      Key takeaways

      • Split by structure first, recursively inside sections (256–512 tokens), with little or no overlap.
      • Add the heading path to each chunk; it costs nothing and helps retrieval.
      • Context-adding techniques (C3 contextual, C4 late, C1 parent–child) fix "chunks without meaning".
      • Measure: chunk size is a hyperparameter, not a belief.

      Quick check

      Your chunks are 2,000 tokens and retrieval precision is poor. Why?

      Large chunks mix several topics, so their embedding is an average that matches many queries weakly. Use smaller chunks, and use parent–child (C1) if the LLM still needs the bigger context.

      What does a breadcrumb add to a chunk?

      The section path ("Handbook > Leave > Carry-over") gives an isolated chunk its topic. This improves both the embedding and BM25 matching at no extra cost.

      Chapter 7 · Ingestion and indexing

      Embedding models

      Embeddingnoun · vector representation

      A fixed-length list of numbers that represents the meaning of a text (or image). Texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions, so "how many vacation days do I get?" lands near "employees receive 24 days of paid annual leave" even though they share almost no words.

      Retrieval embedding models are bi-encoders. The query and each document are encoded separately, so you can embed millions of documents once, offline, and compare a new query to all of them with fast vector maths. Similarity is usually cosine similarity: the angle between two vectors. For unit-length vectors this equals the dot product.

      Kinds of embeddings

      KindWhat it isGood atExamples
      DenseOne vector of 384–4096 floats per textMeaning, paraphrase, cross-lingualbge, Qwen3-Embedding, Voyage, OpenAI, Cohere
      Sparse (lexical)A weight per vocabulary term; mostly zerosExact terms: IDs, codes, names, jargonBM25, SPLADE, ELSER, miniCOIL
      Multi-vectorOne vector per token (late interaction)Fine-grained matching, out-of-domain robustnessColBERTv2, bge-m3, jina-v4 (C5)
      MatryoshkaTrained so the first N dimensions still workCut storage by truncating vectorsOpenAI v3, Voyage 4, nomic, Qwen3, arctic-embed
      MultilingualOne space for 100+ languagesCross-lingual search (I6)bge-m3, multilingual-e5, Cohere, Qwen3
      MultimodalText and images (and more) in one spaceImage and page retrieval (H1, H2)CLIP/SigLIP, voyage-multimodal-3.5, Cohere embed v5, gemini-embedding-2
      Domain-tunedTrained on law, finance, code, medicineJargon-heavy corporavoyage-law-2, voyage-finance-2, voyage-code-4, MedCPT
      Contextual chunkEach chunk embedded with awareness of its whole documentChunks that need context (C3, C4)voyage-context-4, late chunking (Jina)

      Leaderboards move

      Check the MTEB leaderboard, and look at the retrieval scores for your languages, not the overall average. Then confirm the choice on your own evaluation set (below). Benchmark rank and your-data rank often differ.

      How to choose: six questions

      1. Languages? English only, or multilingual and cross-lingual.
      2. Data can leave your network? If not, use open weights locally.
      3. Input length? Long chunks or late chunking need 8k+ context models.
      4. Storage budget? 1M chunks × 1024 dims × 4 bytes ≈ 4 GB in float32, ≈ 1 GB in int8 and ≈ 128 MB in binary. Matryoshka truncation and quantization cut it further.
      5. Latency? A local small model embeds a query in milliseconds; an API adds a network round trip.
      6. Domain jargon? Consider a domain model, or fine-tune on your own pairs (below).

      Code: compare embedding models on your own data

      This is the most valuable 30 lines in the chapter: a recall@k harness. Write 20–50 real questions, note which document answers each, and compare models in a few minutes.

      compare_embedders.py
      import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

from rag_common import make_chunks
from sample_docs import DOCS

# question -> the doc_id that contains the answer (write 20-50 of these from real users)
GOLD = {
    "How many leave days can I carry over?": "leave-policy",
    "What does E17 mean?": "rover-r2",
    "Who must I tell about a security incident and how fast?": "security-policy",
    "When was the firmware 4.1 bug fixed?": "incident-2026-03",
    "What is the payload of the R3?": "rover-r3",
    "Who does Tomas Ruiz report to?": "org-chart",
}
MODELS = {   # name -> (model id, query prefix, document prefix)
    "bge-small": ("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5",
                  "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ", ""),
    "nomic-v1.5": ("nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5", "search_query: ", "search_document: "),
    "arctic-l-v2": ("Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-l-v2.0", "query: ", ""),
}

chunks = make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0)
for name, (model_id, qp, dp) in MODELS.items():
    model = SentenceTransformer(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
    D = model.encode([dp + c.text for c in chunks], normalize_embeddings=True)
    hits = {1: 0, 3: 0}
    for question, gold_doc in GOLD.items():
        q = model.encode(qp + question, normalize_embeddings=True)
        ranked = [chunks[i].meta["doc_id"] for i in np.argsort(-(D @ q))]
        for k in hits:
            hits[k] += gold_doc in ranked[:k]
    print(f"{name:12s} recall@1={hits[1]/len(GOLD):.2f}  recall@3={hits[3]/len(GOLD):.2f}")
