        return llm_rerank(q, candidates, top_n=k)            # RankGPT-style, ~1-3 s
    return cross_encoder_rerank(q, candidates, top_n=k)      # ~50-150 ms on CPU


def ask(question: str, min_score: float = 0.2) -> str:
    best = cross_encoder_rerank(question, index.search(question, k=30), top_n=4,
                                min_score=min_score)
    if not best:                     # the reranker doubles as a relevance gate
        return REFUSAL               # no LLM call, no hallucination risk
    return answer(question, best)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    gold = [  # (question, doc that answers it), deliberately paraphrased
        ("how long until a drained R3 is mostly charged again?", "rover-r3"),
        ("my robot says its battery is too hot, what now?", "rover-r2"),
        ("deadline to tell security about a breach", "security-policy"),
        ("why did the Rotterdam robots halt in March?", "incident-2026-03"),
        ("can I book premium economy for a 9-hour flight?", "expense-policy-2025"),
        ("how many weeks off at full pay for the main caregiver of a newborn?", "leave-policy"),
        ("what changed about meal money abroad in 2026?", "expense-update-2026"),
        ("who is the CEO's direct report for product?", "org-chart"),
    ]
    print("hybrid only        ", evaluate(first_stage, gold, k=1))
    print("hybrid + rerank    ", evaluate(two_stage, gold, k=1))
    print("hybrid + LLM rerank", evaluate(lambda q, k: two_stage(q, k, reranker="llm"), gold, k=1))
    print()
    print(ask("What should I do if the rover battery overheats?"))
    print(ask("What is the company's share price today?"))     # gate should refuse
      hybrid only {'hit@k': 0.62, 'MRR': 0.62} hybrid + rerank {'hit@k': 0.88, 'MRR': 0.88} hybrid + LLM rerank {'hit@k': 1.0, 'MRR': 1.0} Stop the rover and let it cool for 30 minutes; E17 means the battery is overheating [1]. I don't know based on the provided documents.

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • One of the largest precision gains available, and it works with any first stage
      • Fewer, better chunks: shorter prompts, lower cost, fewer distractions
      • A calibrated relevance score enables refusal and confidence display
      • Mature tooling: sentence-transformers, rerankers, hosted APIs
      Cons
      • Adds 50 ms (small model on CPU) to 3 s (LLM reranker) per query
      • Cannot recover passages the first stage missed
      • Thresholds must be calibrated per model and per domain
      • English MS MARCO models are weaker on other languages and specialist jargon; pick a multilingual or domain model

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●●○○○low
      Cost
      ●●○○○low
      Quality gain
      ●●●●○high
      Maturity
      ●●●●●very high

      References

      • paper Nogueira & Cho, "Passage Re-ranking with BERT" arXiv:1901.04085 · the cross-encoder reranker
      • paper Sun et al., "Is ChatGPT Good at Search? Investigating LLMs as Re-Ranking Agents" (RankGPT) EMNLP 2023 · arXiv:2304.09542
      • official repo sunnweiwei/RankGPT inactive no commits since 2024 · read for the sliding-window permutation idea
      • official repo AnswerDotAI/rerankers ~1.6k★ · one API over cross-encoders, ColBERT, LLM and hosted rerankers (arXiv:2408.17344)
      • docs Sentence Transformers: cross-encoder usage
      • docs Anthropic, "Introducing Contextual Retrieval" reranking: 49% → 67% fewer retrieval failures

      Compared with

      • vs A5 Hybrid: they solve different problems. Hybrid search improves recall (get the right chunk into the candidates) and reranking improves precision (put it first). Use both.
      • vs C5 ColBERT: late interaction is a middle ground. It is more precise than a single vector and cheaper than a cross-encoder, and can be the first stage or the reranker.
      • vs E2 CRAG: CRAG also grades retrieved documents, but it then acts on a bad grade by rewriting the query or searching the web. A4 only reorders and cuts.

      A5 Hybrid RAG

      Also called: hybrid search, sparse + dense retrieval, BM25 + vector with RRF

      Run a keyword search (BM25) and a vector search side by side and merge the two rankings, usually with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so you catch both exact terms and paraphrases.

      How it works

      1. Index twice: each chunk gets a dense embedding and a sparse representation, either BM25 term statistics or a learned sparse model such as SPLADE (Ch 7).
      2. Search both with the same query, taking 20–50 results from each.
      3. Fuse. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009) gives each document Σ 1/(k + rank) over the lists it appears in, with k = 60. It uses only ranks, so the two score scales never need to agree. The alternative is a weighted (convex) combination: normalise both score lists to 0–1, then compute α·dense + (1−α)·sparse. This can be slightly better when tuned, but it is sensitive to normalisation.
      4. Continue as usual: optionally rerank (A4), then generate.

      Dense and sparse retrievers fail on different queries. Dense models blur rare tokens, so "E42" looks much like "E17". BM25 has no idea that "time off" means "leave". Fusing them gives a retriever that is rarely terrible, which is why every major vector database now ships hybrid search natively.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Queries contain codes, SKUs, error numbers, names, acronyms or legal citations
      • Users mix keyword-style queries ("E42 reset") with natural questions
      • Your domain vocabulary is rare in the embedder's training data
      • By default in production: it costs almost nothing

      Avoid it when

      • The language has no good tokenizer for BM25 and no learned sparse model (use multilingual dense search plus reranking)
      • Content is not text-like (image or audio embeddings)
      • You measured it and BM25 adds nothing: some paraphrase-heavy corpora behave this way

      Real-world use cases

      • IT and robotics support: error codes, firmware versions and part numbers
      • Legal search: exact statute numbers together with conceptual questions
      • E-commerce: product IDs and brand names alongside "warm waterproof jacket for hiking"

      Python (full example)

      This compares dense-only, BM25-only, RRF and weighted fusion on two kinds of query: keyword queries (codes and product names) and paraphrase queries. It then sweeps the weight α. You will see each single retriever win on one kind of query and the fused versions do well on both.

      hybrid_rag.py
      """A5 Hybrid RAG: BM25 + dense vectors, fused two ways (RRF and weighted), then measured.

pip install -U anthropic sentence-transformers numpy pydantic bm25s
Needs: rag_common.py, sample_docs.py, retrievers.py (HybridIndex, rrf), eval_retrieval.py
"""
import numpy as np

from eval_retrieval import evaluate
from rag_common import Chunk, answer, make_chunks
from retrievers import HybridIndex
from sample_docs import DOCS

index = HybridIndex(make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0))
Hits = list[tuple[float, Chunk]]


def dense_only(q: str, k: int) -> Hits:
    return [(s, index.chunks[i]) for i, s in index.dense(q, k)]


def sparse_only(q: str, k: int) -> Hits:
    return [(s, index.chunks[i]) for i, s in index.sparse(q, k)]


def hybrid_rrf(q: str, k: int) -> Hits:
    return index.search(q, k=k)           # rrf([dense, sparse]) with k=60, from Chapter 9


def _minmax(pairs: list[tuple[int, float]]) -> dict[int, float]:
    if not pairs:
        return {}
    scores = np.array([s for _, s in pairs])
    lo, hi = scores.min(), scores.max()
    return {i: (s - lo) / (hi - lo) if hi > lo else 1.0 for i, s in pairs}


def hybrid_weighted(q: str, k: int, alpha: float = 0.5, fetch: int = 30) -> Hits:
    """Convex combination: alpha * dense + (1 - alpha) * bm25, each min-max normalised."""
    dense, sparse = _minmax(index.dense(q, fetch)), _minmax(index.sparse(q, fetch))
    fused = {i: alpha * dense.get(i, 0.0) + (1 - alpha) * sparse.get(i, 0.0)
             for i in dense.keys() | sparse.keys()}
    top = sorted(fused.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:k]
    return [(score, index.chunks[i]) for i, score in top]


KEYWORD = [("E42", "rover-r2"), ("E17", "rover-r2"), ("firmware 4.1", "incident-2026-03"),
           ("FinTrack", "expense-policy-2025"), ("PeopleHub", "leave-policy")]
PARAPHRASE = [("what if my robot can't see where it is going?", "rover-r2"),
              ("time off after having a baby", "leave-policy"),
              ("who keeps our laptops and passwords safe?", "security-policy"),
              ("biggest load the newest robot can carry", "rover-r3"),
              ("why did dozens of robots freeze at one site?", "incident-2026-03")]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"{'retriever':18s} {'keyword hit@1':>14s} {'paraphrase hit@1':>17s}")
    for name, fn in [("dense only", dense_only), ("BM25 only", sparse_only),
                     ("hybrid RRF", hybrid_rrf), ("hybrid weighted", hybrid_weighted)]:
        kw, pp = evaluate(fn, KEYWORD, k=1), evaluate(fn, PARAPHRASE, k=1)
        print(f"{name:18s} {kw['hit@k']:>14.2f} {pp['hit@k']:>17.2f}")

    print("\nalpha sweep (0 = BM25 only, 1 = dense only), all 10 queries, hit@1:")
    for alpha in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0):
        r = evaluate(lambda q, k: hybrid_weighted(q, k, alpha=alpha), KEYWORD + PARAPHRASE, k=1)
        print(f"  alpha={alpha:.2f}  {r['hit@k']:.2f}")

    q = "What does error E42 mean?"
    print("\n" + answer(q, hybrid_rrf(q, 3)))
      retriever keyword hit@1 paraphrase hit@1 dense only 0.40 0.80 BM25 only 1.00 0.40 hybrid RRF 1.00 0.80 hybrid weighted 1.00 0.80 alpha sweep (0 = BM25 only, 1 = dense only), all 10 queries, hit@1: alpha=0.00 0.70 alpha=0.25 0.90 alpha=0.50 0.90 alpha=0.75 0.80 alpha=1.00 0.60

      Production swap. In production, let the database do the fusion. Qdrant, Weaviate, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Milvus, Pinecone and pgvector (with full-text search) all support it. Here is the same idea in Qdrant's Query API, using the fastembed BM25 model for the sparse side:

      qdrant_hybrid.py (sketch)
      # pip install -U qdrant-client fastembed
from fastembed import SparseTextEmbedding
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models

from rag_common import embed, embed_query, make_chunks
from sample_docs import DOCS

chunks = make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0)
bm25 = SparseTextEmbedding("Qdrant/bm25")
db = QdrantClient(":memory:")
db.create_collection(
    "northwind",
    vectors_config={"dense": models.VectorParams(size=384, distance=models.Distance.COSINE)},
    sparse_vectors_config={"sparse": models.SparseVectorParams(modifier=models.Modifier.IDF)},
)
dense_vecs = embed([c.text for c in chunks])
sparse_vecs = list(bm25.embed([c.text for c in chunks]))
db.upsert("northwind", points=[
    models.PointStruct(id=i, payload={"id": c.id, "text": c.text}, vector={
        "dense": dense_vecs[i].tolist(),
        "sparse": models.SparseVector(indices=sparse_vecs[i].indices.tolist(),
                                      values=sparse_vecs[i].values.tolist())})
    for i, c in enumerate(chunks)])


def hybrid_search(query: str, k: int = 5):
    q_sparse = next(iter(bm25.query_embed(query)))
    return db.query_points(
        "northwind",
        prefetch=[
            models.Prefetch(query=models.SparseVector(indices=q_sparse.indices.tolist(),
                                                      values=q_sparse.values.tolist()),
                            using="sparse", limit=30),
            models.Prefetch(query=embed_query(query).tolist(), using="dense", limit=30),
        ],
        query=models.FusionQuery(fusion=models.Fusion.RRF),    # fusion runs inside Qdrant
        limit=k,
    ).points


for p in hybrid_search("E42"):
    print(round(p.score, 3), p.payload["id"])

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Fixes the biggest blind spot of dense retrieval (exact terms) at almost no cost
      • RRF needs no tuning and no score calibration
      • BM25 is fast, explainable and has no model to host
      • Native in every major vector database
      Cons
      • Two indexes to keep in sync on every update
      • BM25 depends on tokenisation and stop words, which is weak for some languages
      • Fusion can promote a keyword match that is off-topic, so pair it with reranking
      • Weighted fusion needs α tuned per corpus, and the best value drifts as data changes

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●○○○○very low
      Cost
      ●○○○○very low
      Quality gain
      ●●●●○high
      Maturity
      ●●●●●very high

      References

      • paper Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher, "Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learning methods" SIGIR 2009 · k = 60
      • docs Qdrant: hybrid and multi-stage queries prefetch + RRF / DBSF fusion
      • docs Weaviate: hybrid search alpha-weighted fusion
      • docs Haystack tutorial 33: hybrid retrieval BM25 + embedding retriever + DocumentJoiner
      • community xhluca/bm25s ~1.8k★, active · fast pure-Python BM25 used in this guide

      Compared with

      • vs A1 Naive (dense only): hybrid search is nearly free, so it should be your default. Dense-only search is the exception you choose after measuring.
      • vs B2 RAG-Fusion: both use RRF. A5 fuses different retrievers on one query, while B2 fuses one retriever over several LLM-written queries. A5 costs no LLM call.
      • vs learned sparse (SPLADE, BM42, miniCOIL): these replace BM25 on the sparse side with a model that also expands terms. They are a drop-in upgrade inside the same hybrid design.

      A6 Conversational RAG

      Also called: history-aware RAG, chat RAG, condense-question RAG, contextual query rewriting

      Before retrieving, rewrite the user's latest message into a standalone question using the chat history, so "and abroad?" becomes "What is the international meal allowance?"

      How it works

      1. Condense. A cheap LLM call receives the last few turns and the new message and returns one self-contained question. On the first turn, skip this step.
      2. Retrieve with the standalone question, never with the raw follow-up: "since when?" on its own retrieves nothing useful.
      3. Generate with the sources and the recent history, so the answer can say "the international allowance went up from 90 to 100 EUR" in context.
      4. Store the turn. Keep history bounded: summarise or drop old turns, and do not keep old retrieved chunks forever.

      The task has a research name, question-in-context rewriting (the CANARD dataset, Elgohary et al., 2019). Frameworks package it: LangChain's create_history_aware_retriever (now in langchain-classic), the LangGraph agentic-RAG tutorial, and LlamaIndex's CondensePlusContextChatEngine.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Any chat interface where users ask follow-up questions
      • Messages use pronouns, ellipsis or "what about…" phrasing
      • Topics shift during a conversation

      Avoid it when

      • Single-shot search boxes (no history to use)
      • Latency is critical and follow-ups are rare (condense only when the message looks like a follow-up)
      • An agent already decides its own search queries (F1 does this implicitly)

      Real-world use cases

      • Help-desk and HR chatbots ("What's the meal allowance?" → "And abroad?" → "Since when?")
      • Customer-support chat over order and product data
      • Voice assistants, where follow-ups are short and pronoun-heavy

      Python (sketch)

      conversational_rag.py
      """A6 Conversational RAG: condense the follow-up, retrieve with it, answer with history + sources."""
from query_tools import condense                     # Chapter 10
from rag_common import ANSWER_SYSTEM, format_context, llm, make_chunks
from retrievers import HybridIndex
from sample_docs import DOCS

index = HybridIndex(make_chunks(DOCS, size=400, overlap=60))
history: list[tuple[str, str]] = []                  # (role, text)


def chat(user_msg: str) -> str:
    question = condense(history, user_msg) if history else user_msg     # 1) standalone question
    hits = index.search(question, k=4)                                  # 2) retrieve with it
    turns = "\n".join(f"{role}: {text}" for role, text in history[-6:])
    reply = llm(f"Conversation so far:\n{turns or '(none)'}\n\nSources:\n\n{format_context(hits)}\n\n"
                f"User: {user_msg}\n(Standalone meaning: {question})",
                system=ANSWER_SYSTEM)                                   # 3) answer in context
    history.extend([("user", user_msg), ("assistant", reply)])          # 4) remember the turn
    return reply


for msg in ["What is the domestic meal allowance?", "And abroad?", "Since when?"]:
    print(f"> {msg}\n{chat(msg)}\n")

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Fixes the most common failure in chat RAG: follow-ups retrieving nothing
      • One cheap helper call (Haiku-class model)
      • The rewritten question is visible, which makes debugging and logging easier
      Cons
      • Adds a sequential LLM call before retrieval (about 200–500 ms)
      • A wrong rewrite silently sends retrieval to the wrong topic
      • Long histories cost tokens and can drag in stale context

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●●○○○low
      Cost
      ●●○○○low
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●●●●very high

      References

      • paper Elgohary et al., "Can You Unpack That? Learning to Rewrite Questions-in-Context" (CANARD) EMNLP 2019
      • docs LangGraph: agentic RAG tutorial history-aware retrieval inside a graph
      • docs LangChain: RAG tutorial chat history and retrieval
      • official repo run-llama/llama_index CondensePlusContextChatEngine

      Compared with

      • vs B6 Rewrite-Retrieve-Read: both rewrite the query. A6 rewrites using chat history and B6 rewrites into document vocabulary. A good condense prompt can do both at once.
      • vs F5 Agent memory: A6 uses the current conversation only. Agent memory retrieves facts from past sessions.

      A7 Long-context RAG (LongRAG)

      Also called: LongRAG (Jiang et al., 2024), long retriever + long reader, "retrieve documents, not chunks"

      Make the retrieval units long (whole documents or groups of related documents, about 4K tokens each), retrieve only a handful, and let a long-context model read them in full.

      How it works

      1. Build long retrieval units. The paper groups related Wikipedia pages (linked by hyperlinks) into units of about 4K tokens, roughly 30× longer than classic 100-word passages. Your equivalent might be whole documents, or all documents about one product.
      2. Retrieve a few units. Embedders cannot represent 4K tokens well, so a unit is scored by its best-matching smaller piece. Fewer than 8 units are returned, about 30K tokens.
      3. Read everything. A long-context model (GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 in the paper) reads the units in full and extracts the answer.

      With no training at all, LongRAG reached 62.7 exact match on Natural Questions and 64.3 on HotpotQA, comparable to fine-tuned RAG systems of its time. Because there are far fewer units, the retriever's job becomes much easier. Note that there is a second, unrelated paper also called "LongRAG" (Zhao et al., EMNLP 2024) about long-context QA, so cite the arXiv ID.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Answers depend on context spread across a document (contracts, reports, manuals)
      • Chunking keeps breaking the meaning, such as tables, definitions and cross-references
      • You can afford ~30K input tokens per query (or cache them)

      Avoid it when

      • You have high query volume with tight cost or latency limits
      • Answers are short facts inside huge corpora (chunk-level retrieval plus reranking is cheaper)
      • Documents need permission filtering at the passage level

      Real-world use cases

      • Contract review: retrieve the three most relevant contracts and read each one whole
      • Analyst Q&A over annual reports or research papers
      • Incident analysis: retrieve whole post-mortems, not fragments

      Python (sketch)

      long_rag.py
      """A7 LongRAG sketch: retrieve a few LONG units and let a long-context model read them whole."""
from collections import defaultdict

from rag_common import MODEL, VectorIndex, llm, make_chunks
from sample_docs import DOCS

# 1) Long retrieval units. Here: all documents of one department.
#    (The paper groups hyperlinked Wikipedia pages into ~4K-token units.)
units: dict[str, list[str]] = defaultdict(list)
for doc_id, d in DOCS.items():
    units[d["department"]].append(doc_id)

# 2) Score a unit by its best-matching small chunk: embedders cannot encode 4K tokens well.
index = VectorIndex()
index.add(make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0))


def retrieve_units(question: str, n_units: int = 2, scan: int = 30) -> list[str]:
    best: dict[str, float] = {}
    for score, c in index.search(question, k=scan):
        unit = DOCS[c.meta["doc_id"]]["department"]
        best[unit] = max(best.get(unit, 0.0), score)
    return sorted(best, key=best.get, reverse=True)[:n_units]


def long_rag(question: str) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
    picked = retrieve_units(question)
    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"<document title='{DOCS[i]['title']}' updated='{DOCS[i]['updated_at']}'>\n"
        f"{DOCS[i]['text']}\n</document>"
        for unit in picked for i in units[unit])          # whole documents, not chunks
    reply = llm(f"{context}\n\nUsing only the documents above, answer the question and quote "
                f"the sentences you relied on.\n\nQuestion: {question}", model=MODEL)
    return reply, picked


reply, picked = long_rag("Which firmware fixed the March 2026 E42 incident, and when did it ship?")
print("units read:", picked, "\n", reply)

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • No information lost at chunk boundaries
      • Retrieval becomes easier: far fewer, more distinctive units
      • No training needed; it gets better as long-context models improve
      Cons
      • ~30K input tokens per query: 10–50× the cost of chunk RAG unless cached
      • Slower time to first token
      • Models still use the middle of long prompts less reliably ("lost in the middle")
      • The official repo is a research artifact and no longer maintained

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●●●○○medium
      Cost
      ●●●●○high
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●○○○low

      References

      • paper Jiang, Ma & Chen, "LongRAG: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Long-context LLMs" arXiv:2406.15319
      • official repo TIGER-AI-Lab/LongRAG inactive ~250★ · no commits since Aug 2024
      • paper Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts" arXiv:2307.03172 · why ordering still matters

      Compared with

      • vs C1 Parent-document: C1 matches small chunks and expands them to a parent section. LongRAG goes further, to whole documents or groups of documents. Try C1 first because it is cheaper.
      • vs A8 CAG: CAG sends everything and does no retrieval. LongRAG still retrieves, so it scales to corpora far larger than a context window.
      • vs E5 Self-Route: Self-Route uses cheap chunk RAG first and switches to long context only when the model says it cannot answer.

      A8 Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG)

      Also called: retrieval-free RAG, "just put it all in the prompt", KV-cache preloading

      If the knowledge base is small and stable, skip retrieval entirely. Load all of it into the model's context once, cache it, and answer every question against the cached copy.

      How it works

      1. Preload: put the whole knowledge base into the context and compute the model's key-value (KV) cache for it once.
      2. Query: append the question to the cached prefix and generate. There is no retrieval step, so retrieval cannot fail.
      3. Reset: truncate the cache back to the knowledge-base prefix after each question, so questions do not leak into each other.

      The CAG paper (Chan et al., WWW 2025) used Llama-3.1-8B. CAG beat sparse and dense RAG on SQuAD and on small and medium HotpotQA sets. On the largest HotpotQA set it scored 0.7407 against 0.7535 for sparse RAG, roughly level, but generated in 2.26 s instead of 92 s compared with feeding the same context without a cache. On hosted APIs, the equivalent is prompt caching. Anthropic's own guidance in the Contextual Retrieval post is that if your knowledge base is smaller than about 200,000 tokens (roughly 500 pages), you can simply include all of it in the prompt.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • The corpus is small (under ~200K tokens) and changes rarely
      • Many questions hit the same corpus within the cache lifetime
      • Questions need the whole picture ("what are all the exceptions to…?")
      • You want to remove retrieval as a failure point

      Avoid it when

      • The corpus is large, grows or changes often (every change rebuilds the cache)
      • Different users may see different documents (one shared cache cannot enforce permissions)
      • Query volume is low, so the cache expires between questions
      • You need passage-level provenance from a retrieval log

      Real-world use cases

      • A product-manual or policy-handbook assistant (one manual, many users)
      • An onboarding bot over a fixed set of HR documents
      • Q&A over one long contract or report during a review session

      Python (sketch)

      With Claude, CAG is prompt caching: mark the knowledge-base block with cache_control. The first call writes the cache, and later calls read it at a fraction of the normal input price (0.05× on Claude Opus 5.5). A cached prefix must be at least 512 tokens on the 5.5 models and byte-identical on every call, which is why the documents are sorted. The default lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed on every hit; "ttl": "1h" keeps it for an hour at a higher write price.

      cag.py
      """A8 Cache-Augmented Generation with Claude prompt caching: no retriever, no index."""
from rag_common import MODEL, client
from sample_docs import DOCS

KB = "\n\n".join(                                    # sorted: the cached prefix must never change
    f"<document id='{doc_id}' title='{d['title']}' updated='{d['updated_at']}'>\n{d['text']}\n</document>"
    for doc_id, d in sorted(DOCS.items()))

SYSTEM = [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Answer only from the documents below and cite document ids. "
                             "If documents conflict, prefer the most recent. "
                             "If the answer is not there, say you don't know."},
    {"type": "text", "text": KB, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}},
]


def ask(question: str) -> str:
    resp = client.beta.messages.create(
        model=MODEL, max_tokens=4000, system=SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],          # varies: after the cache
        betas=["server-side-fallback-2026-07-01"], fallbacks="default")
    u = resp.usage
    print(f"   [cache write {u.cache_creation_input_tokens} · cache read "
          f"{u.cache_read_input_tokens} · uncached {u.input_tokens} tokens]")
    if resp.stop_reason == "refusal":
        return "[the model declined this request]"
    return "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")


for q in ["What is the international meal allowance now?",          # 1st call writes the cache
          "Who does the incident commander of the March 2026 outage report to?",   # reads it
          "Compare Rover R2 and R3 battery life and payload."]:                 # reads it
    print("Q:", q)
    print("A:", ask(q), "\n")

      True KV-cache CAGWith an open model you can cache the knowledge base's KV tensors yourself. The official hhhuang/CAG repo does this with Hugging Face Transformers: compute a DynamicCache for the knowledge base once, generate each answer from a copy of it, then crop the cache back to the knowledge-base length. Prompt caching gives you the same effect on a hosted API without managing GPU memory.

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • No retrieval errors: the model sees everything
      • Simplest possible system: no chunking, embeddings or vector database
      • Handles "whole-corpus" questions that defeat top-k retrieval
      • With caching, repeat questions are cheap and fast
      Cons
      • Hard size limit: the context window, and quality drops well before it
      • Every corpus change invalidates the cache
      • No per-user permissions inside one shared cache
      • Without cache hits, every question pays for the whole corpus

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●○○○○very low
      Latency
      ●●○○○low
      Cost
      ●●○○○low
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●●○○medium

      References

      • paper Chan et al., "Don't Do RAG: When Cache-Augmented Generation is All You Need for Knowledge Tasks" WWW 2025 · arXiv:2412.15605
      • official repo hhhuang/CAG ~1.6k★ · KV-cache preloading with Transformers; no commits since May 2025
      • docs Claude docs: prompt caching cache_control, TTLs, minimum lengths, pricing
      • docs Anthropic, "Introducing Contextual Retrieval" "under ~200K tokens, just put it in the prompt"

      Compared with

      • vs A1 Naive: for a small corpus, CAG removes retrieval errors and is often simpler. RAG wins as soon as the corpus is large, changes often or needs permissions.
      • vs A7 LongRAG: LongRAG retrieves a few long units from a large corpus. CAG retrieves nothing from a small one.
      • vs J3 native-memory RAG: KBLaM and similar methods also put knowledge directly into the model's attention, but they need training. CAG works with any model today.

      Family A side by side

      TypeChangesFixesExtra cost per queryPick it when
      A1 NaiveNothing (baseline)No knowledge, no citations1 embed + 1 LLM callAlways, as the baseline
      A2 AdvancedSteps before and after retrievalVocabulary mismatch, noisy context+1 helper call, +rerankerMeasured retrieval failures
      A3 ModularThe pipeline's shape (routes, loops)One pipeline cannot fit all questionsVaries per routeMixed question types
      A4 RerankAdds a precision stageRight chunk retrieved but ranked low+50 ms to 3 sAlmost always
      A5 HybridAdds a keyword retrieverCodes, names, rare terms~nothingDefault in production
      A6 ConversationalRewrites follow-ups"And abroad?" retrieving nothing+1 helper callAny chat interface
      A7 LongRAGLong retrieval units, long readerMeaning lost at chunk boundaries~30K input tokensAnswers spread across documents
      A8 CAGRemoves retrievalRetrieval errors on small corporaCache reads onlyCorpus under ~200K tokens, stable

      Key takeaways

      • Always build A1 first and measure it. Every other type must beat it on your evaluation set.
      • A5 hybrid + A4 rerank is the standard production core: hybrid improves recall, reranking improves precision, and together they cost very little.
      • A2 is a set of independent fixes, so test each with an ablation. A3 is an architecture style that many later cards are specific instances of.
      • Large context windows open two new options: A8 CAG for small, stable corpora and A7 LongRAG for reading whole documents. Both trade token cost for fewer retrieval errors.

      Quick check

      Your naive RAG answers "E42?" wrongly but "what does the lidar error mean?" correctly. Which card fixes this, and why?

      A5 Hybrid. Dense embeddings blur short codes, so "E42" looks much like "E17". BM25 matches the exact token, and RRF merges the two rankings without any score calibration.

      Reranking does not improve a question that keeps failing. What do you check first?

      Whether the correct chunk is in the candidate list at all (recall@fetch). A reranker can only reorder what stage 1 returns. If the chunk is missing, fix chunking, add hybrid search, use a better embedder or fetch more candidates.

      When is CAG the wrong choice even for a small corpus?

      When different users may see different documents, since one shared cache cannot enforce permissions. It is also wrong when the corpus changes so often that the cache is constantly rebuilt, or when traffic is so low that the cache expires between questions.

      Chapter 15 · The RAG catalog

      Family B · Query-transformation RAG

      Users write short, vague, multi-part or jargon-filled questions. Documents are written in a different voice. Family B fixes that mismatch before retrieval by changing the query, while the index stays as it is. All six types add an LLM call in front of the retriever (except semantic routing). That is why they are cheap to try and cheap to remove. Chapter 10 built the helper functions in query_tools.py. This chapter turns each one into a complete architecture, measures it, and shows when it backfires.

      If your queries are…TryWhy
      Short or vague, worded unlike the documentsB1 HyDE, B6 rewriteMove the query into "document space" before searching
      Ambiguous: one wording misses relevant documentsB2 multi-query / RAG-FusionSeveral wordings raise recall
      Multi-part: comparisons, "X and Y", chains of factsB3 decompositionOne retrieval cannot cover several targets
      Very specific, but the answer depends on a general ruleB4 step-backAlso retrieve the rule or principle
      About different domains, sources or toolsB5 routingSearch the right index, or none at all
      The shared risk: query drift

      Every transformation can move the query away from what the user meant. A rewrite might drop a product code, or HyDE might invent a wrong fact. Two habits protect you. First, always keep the original query in the mix: fuse it with the transformed one, or use it for BM25 and reranking. Second, measure on your evaluation set with and without the transformation (Chapter 13).

      B1 HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)

      Also called: hypothetical document embeddings, "answer-first retrieval", generate-then-retrieve

      Ask an LLM to write a fake passage that would answer the question, embed that passage, and search with its vector. A document is compared with a document instead of a question with a document.

      How it works

      1. Generate one or more hypothetical documents that answer the question. The paper sampled several with InstructGPT at temperature 0.7. The passages may contain wrong details, and that is acceptable.
      2. Embed them as documents, not as queries. With instruction-tuned embedders such as BGE, use the passage encoding without the query prefix.
      3. Average the hypothetical vectors together with the original query vector into one search vector.
      4. Search the real index with that vector. The dense "bottleneck" keeps the shared topic and shape of the fake answers and filters out their invented specifics.
      5. Generate the real answer from the real chunks, exactly as before.

      The paper (Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan, ACL 2023) used an unsupervised retriever, Contriever. On TREC DL19, HyDE lifted nDCG@10 from 44.5 to 61.3, close to a Contriever fine-tuned on MS MARCO (62.1) and above BM25 (50.6). On DL20 it went from 42.1 to 57.9. The gains come from zero-shot settings. With a strong, fine-tuned embedder the gap is smaller, and if the LLM lacks the domain knowledge, the fake passage can point the search in the wrong direction.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Questions are short or conversational and documents are long and formal
      • You have no labelled data to fine-tune an embedder (the zero-shot setting)
      • The LLM knows the general domain well (HR, IT, general science)

      Avoid it when

      • The LLM does not know your private terms and codes: it will invent meanings for "E42"
      • Queries are already precise keywords, IDs or names (use A5)
      • You need the lowest latency: generation adds 0.5–2 s before search can start

      Real-world use cases

      • Searching research papers or medical literature with lay questions ("why does my knee click?")
      • A new product search with no click data for fine-tuning
      • FAQ bots where users write one-line questions and articles are long

      Python (full example)

      This follows the paper: several passages from one cheap call, embedded as documents and averaged with the query vector. It also shows the production-safe variant, HyDE on the dense side only, with the user's exact words on the BM25 side, and prints the failure mode on a private code.

      hyde_rag.py
      """B1 HyDE: search with the embedding of hypothetical ANSWERS instead of the question.

pip install -U anthropic sentence-transformers numpy pydantic bm25s
Needs: rag_common.py, sample_docs.py, retrievers.py, eval_retrieval.py
"""
import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from eval_retrieval import evaluate
from rag_common import answer, embed, embed_query, llm_parse, make_chunks
from retrievers import HybridIndex, rrf
from sample_docs import DOCS

index = HybridIndex(make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0))     # index.vecs = passage vectors


class Passages(BaseModel):
    passages: list[str] = Field(description="Short hypothetical document passages")


def hypothetical_docs(question: str, n: int = 3) -> list[str]:
    """One cheap call -> n passages in different document styles (variety replaces sampling)."""
    out = llm_parse(
        f"Write {n} short passages (2-4 sentences each), each in the style of a different kind of "
        f"internal company document (policy, product manual, FAQ, incident report), that would "
        f"answer:\n{question}\nInvent plausible details if needed: they are only used as search keys.",
        Passages)
    return out.passages[:n]


def hyde_vector(question: str, n: int = 3) -> np.ndarray:
    """Mean of the fake passages (embedded as DOCUMENTS) and the query vector, re-normalised."""
    vecs = np.vstack([embed(hypothetical_docs(question, n)), embed_query(question)[None, :]])
    v = vecs.mean(axis=0)
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)


def dense_by_vector(vec: np.ndarray, k: int) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    scores = index.vecs @ vec
    return [(int(i), float(scores[i])) for i in np.argsort(-scores)[:k]]


def plain_dense(q: str, k: int):
    return [(s, index.chunks[i]) for i, s in index.dense(q, k)]


def hyde_dense(q: str, k: int):
    return [(s, index.chunks[i]) for i, s in dense_by_vector(hyde_vector(q), k)]


def hyde_hybrid(q: str, k: int, fetch: int = 30):
    """Production variant: HyDE vector for dense search, the user's exact words for BM25."""
    fused = rrf([dense_by_vector(hyde_vector(q), fetch), index.sparse(q, fetch)])
    return [(s, index.chunks[i]) for i, s in fused[:k]]


GOLD = [  # indirect questions: little word overlap with the documents
    ("I'm going to be a dad soon, how much time off do I get?", "leave-policy"),
    ("can I use a public chatbot with client information?", "security-policy"),
    ("the robot's laser eye is dirty, what now?", "rover-r2"),
    ("how quick is the newer warehouse bot?", "rover-r3"),
    ("who ran the response when the Dutch site's robots froze?", "incident-2026-03"),
    ("which executive is responsible for the products?", "org-chart"),
    ("do I have to keep the slip for a 30 euro taxi?", "expense-policy-2025"),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("plain dense ", evaluate(plain_dense, GOLD, k=1))
    print("HyDE dense  ", evaluate(hyde_dense, GOLD, k=1))
    print("HyDE hybrid ", evaluate(hyde_hybrid, GOLD, k=1))

    print("\nFailure mode: what HyDE searches with for a private code")
    for p in hypothetical_docs("What does error E42 mean?"):
        print("  -", p)                   # invented meanings: the dense side drifts

    q = "I'm going to be a dad soon, how much time off do I get?"
    print("\n" + answer(q, hyde_hybrid(q, 3)))
      plain dense {'hit@k': 0.57, 'MRR': 0.57} HyDE dense {'hit@k': 0.86, 'MRR': 0.86} HyDE hybrid {'hit@k': 0.86, 'MRR': 0.86} Failure mode: what HyDE searches with for a private code - Error E42 indicates a network timeout between the client and the server... - E42: Disk quota exceeded. Free up space or contact IT... As the secondary caregiver you receive 6 weeks of leave at full salary [1]...

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Large zero-shot gains without training or labelled data
      • Works with any embedder and any vector database: only the query changes
      • Fake details are filtered out by the embedding and never reach the user
      Cons
      • Adds a generation step before search, which increases time to first token
      • Fails when the LLM does not know the domain, and can confidently mislead the dense search
      • Smaller gains with strong fine-tuned embedders
      • Every query costs an LLM call (cache frequent queries)

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●●○○○low
      Cost
      ●●○○○low
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●●●○high

      References

      • paper Gao, Ma, Lin & Callan, "Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels" ACL 2023 · arXiv:2212.10496
      • official repo texttron/hyde ~580★ · reference implementation with Contriever; little activity since 2024
      • paper Wang, Yang & Wei, "Query2doc: Query Expansion with Large Language Models" arXiv:2303.07678 · the same idea for BM25 (see B6)
      • community langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch query-translation notebooks: HyDE, multi-query, fusion, decomposition, step-back

      Compared with

      • vs B6 Rewrite: B6 produces a better question, while HyDE produces a fake answer. HyDE helps dense search more. A rewrite is safer for keyword search and private codes.
      • vs C3 Contextual Retrieval: both close the question–document gap, but C3 does it once at indexing time (no query latency) and HyDE does it on every query.
      • vs fine-tuning the embedder (Ch 7): once you have a few thousand real (query, passage) pairs, a fine-tuned embedder usually beats HyDE with no per-query cost.

      B2 Multi-query RAG / RAG-Fusion

      Also called: multi-query retrieval, query expansion with fusion, RAG-Fusion (Rackauckas, 2024)

      Have an LLM write several different versions of the question, retrieve for each one, and merge the ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Documents found by many versions rise to the top.

      How it works

      1. Generate variants: one cheap LLM call writes 3–5 queries that ask for the same information in different words and from different angles.
      2. Retrieve for each (in parallel), including the original question.
      3. Fuse the lists with RRF, score = Σ 1/(60 + rank), the same formula hybrid search uses (A5).
      4. Generate from the fused top k. Optionally show the variants to the user as "related searches".

      "Multi-query" (LangChain's MultiQueryRetriever, now in langchain-classic) takes the union of the results. "RAG-Fusion" (the Raudaschl repo and Rackauckas' paper from Infineon) ranks them with RRF. An industry study in March 2026 (arXiv:2603.02153) is a useful warning. RAG-Fusion raised raw recall, but once a reranker and a top-k cut were added, the gain disappeared (Hit@10 went from 0.51 to 0.48) and latency went up. Measure it inside your full pipeline, not on its own.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Recall is the bottleneck: the right chunk is often missing from the candidates
      • Queries are ambiguous or very short ("rover keeps stopping")
      • You have no reranker, or a weak one
      • Users benefit from seeing alternative phrasings

      Avoid it when

      • You already have hybrid search + a strong reranker: measure first, because the gain may vanish
      • Latency matters: 1 LLM call + N retrievals before generation
      • Queries are precise lookups (IDs, names) where variants add only noise

      Real-world use cases

      • Technical support, where customers describe symptoms many different ways
      • Sales and product-knowledge assistants (Infineon's deployment in the paper)
      • Exploratory research search, where breadth matters more than speed

      Python (full example)

      This compares four setups on under-specified queries for recall and latency: single query, fusion, single + rerank, and fusion + rerank. This is the comparison the 2026 study recommends.

      fusion_rag.py
      """B2 Multi-query / RAG-Fusion: several rewrites, one ranking each, fused with RRF.

pip install -U anthropic sentence-transformers numpy pydantic bm25s
Needs: rag_common.py, sample_docs.py, retrievers.py, query_tools.py, rerankers.py, eval_retrieval.py
"""
import time

from eval_retrieval import evaluate
from query_tools import multi_query
from rag_common import answer, make_chunks
from rerankers import cross_encoder_rerank
from retrievers import HybridIndex, rrf
from sample_docs import DOCS

index = HybridIndex(make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0))


def single(q: str, k: int):
    return [(s, index.chunks[i]) for i, s in index.dense(q, k)]


def fusion(q: str, k: int, n: int = 4, fetch: int = 20):
    variants = multi_query(q, n)                 # [original] + n rewrites, one LLM call
    fused = rrf([index.dense(v, fetch) for v in variants])
    return [(s, index.chunks[i]) for i, s in fused[:k]]


def with_rerank(search):
    """Wrap any retriever: take 20 candidates, keep the cross-encoder's top k."""
    def run(q: str, k: int):
        return cross_encoder_rerank(q, search(q, 20), top_n=k)
    return run


GOLD = [  # under-specified queries, the case RAG-Fusion is meant for
    ("rover keeps stopping", "rover-r2"),
    ("money for food on trips abroad", "expense-update-2026"),
    ("who to tell about a hacked laptop", "security-policy"),
    ("how long does charging take on the big robot", "rover-r3"),
    ("time off for new parents", "leave-policy"),
    ("software bug in March", "incident-2026-03"),
    ("Priya's boss", "org-chart"),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"{'setup':18s} {'hit@3':>6s} {'MRR':>6s} {'ms/query':>9s}")
    for name, fn in [("single", single), ("fusion", fusion),
                     ("single + rerank", with_rerank(single)),
                     ("fusion + rerank", with_rerank(fusion))]:
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        r = evaluate(fn, GOLD, k=3)
        ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 / len(GOLD)
        print(f"{name:18s} {r['hit@k']:>6.2f} {r['MRR']:>6.2f} {ms:>9.0f}")

    q = "rover keeps stopping"
    print("\nvariants:", multi_query(q))
    print(answer(q, fusion(q, 4)))
      setup hit@3 MRR ms/query single 0.71 0.57 14 fusion 1.00 0.81 1450 single + rerank 0.86 0.79 95 fusion + rerank 1.00 0.93 1530

      Reading the resultOn a tiny corpus with a small embedder, fusion helps, but it costs about 100× the retrieval latency because of the LLM call. On a large corpus with a strong reranker, the 2026 study found no gain. Your evaluation set decides.

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Higher recall for vague and ambiguous queries
      • RRF needs no tuning; variants can run in parallel
      • Robust: one bad variant is outvoted by the others
      • The variants double as "did you mean / related searches"
      Cons
      • An LLM call plus N retrievals per query
      • Gains can vanish behind a good reranker (2026 industry study)
      • Variants can drift off-topic and pull in distractors
      • N times the load on the vector database

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●●●○○medium
      Cost
      ●●○○○low
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●●●○high

      References

      • paper Rackauckas, "RAG-Fusion: a New Take on Retrieval-Augmented Generation" arXiv:2402.03367 · Infineon deployment
      • paper "Scaling Retrieval Augmented Generation with RAG Fusion: Lessons from an Industry Deployment" arXiv:2603.02153 (Mar 2026) · gains vanish after reranking
      • community Raudaschl/rag-fusion ~960★, active · the original RAG-Fusion implementation
      • community langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch multi-query and RAG-Fusion notebooks

      Compared with

      • vs A5 Hybrid: both use RRF. A5 fuses different retrievers on one query with no LLM call. B2 fuses different queries. Do A5 first because it is free.
      • vs B3 Decomposition: B2's variants ask the same question in different words. B3's sub-questions ask different questions that together cover a complex one.
      • vs A4 Rerank: they overlap. If you can afford only one, a reranker usually gives more for less latency.

      B3 Query-decomposition RAG

      Also called: sub-question RAG, least-to-most RAG, question decomposition, "plan-and-retrieve"

      Split a complex question into simple sub-questions, retrieve and answer each one, then combine the partial answers into a final, cited answer.

      How it works

      1. Decompose: an LLM splits the question into the smallest set of simple, self-contained sub-questions. A simple question stays as one.
      2. Solve each: retrieve for the sub-question and write a short sub-answer with a cheap model.
        • Parallel (LlamaIndex's SubQuestionQueryEngine): for independent parts such as comparisons and lists.
        • Sequential (Least-to-Most prompting, Self-Ask): for dependent parts, where the next sub-question uses earlier answers.
      3. Synthesise: the strong model writes the final answer from all retrieved sources, using the sub-answers as notes, and cites the sources.

      The ideas come from reasoning research. Least-to-Most prompting (Zhou et al., ICLR 2023) solves easy sub-problems first. Self-Ask (Press et al., 2022) has the model ask itself follow-up questions, answers them with a search engine, and measures the "compositionality gap": models often know both facts but fail to combine them. Decomposing the question narrows that gap.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Questions compare things: "R2 vs R3 battery and payload"
      • Questions have several parts: "policy for X, and who approves it?"
      • Answers chain two or three facts (sequential mode)
      • The relevant chunks would never all appear in one top-k

      Avoid it when

      • Most questions are simple lookups: decomposition adds 2–4 LLM calls for nothing (route with E3)
      • The chain is long or open-ended (use D1 or F1)
      • Latency budgets are under a second

      Real-world use cases

      • Product comparisons and spec sheets ("compare plans A, B and C on price and limits")
      • Financial analysis across filings ("revenue growth of X vs Y in 2025")
      • Policy questions that combine a rule and an owner or approver

      Python (full example)

      Both modes are shown. Sub-answers use the fast model. The final synthesis uses the strong model and cites the real sources, not the sub-answers.

      decomposition_rag.py
      """B3 Query decomposition: split, retrieve + answer each part, then synthesise.

pip install -U anthropic sentence-transformers numpy pydantic bm25s
Needs: rag_common.py, sample_docs.py, retrievers.py, query_tools.py
"""
import re
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from query_tools import decompose
from rag_common import ANSWER_SYSTEM, FAST_MODEL, answer, format_context, llm, llm_parse, make_chunks
from retrievers import HybridIndex
from sample_docs import DOCS

index = HybridIndex(make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0))


def solve(sub_q: str, k: int = 3):
    """Retrieve for one sub-question and write a short note with the cheap model."""
    hits = index.search(sub_q, k=k)
    note = re.sub(r"\s*\[\d+\]", "", answer(sub_q, hits, model=FAST_MODEL))  # drop local [n]s
    return note, hits


def synthesise(question: str, notes: str, hits) -> str:
    unique = list({c.id: (s, c) for s, c in hits}.values())     # de-duplicate across sub-questions
    prompt = (f"Sources:\n\n{format_context(unique)}\n\n"
              f"Notes from answering sub-questions (a guide only; cite the sources, not the notes):\n"
              f"{notes}\n\nQuestion: {question}")
    return llm(prompt, system=ANSWER_SYSTEM)


def parallel_decomposition(question: str):
    """Independent parts (comparisons, 'X and Y'): solve them concurrently."""
    subs = decompose(question)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(solve, subs))
    notes = "\n".join(f"- {q} -> {note}" for q, (note, _) in zip(subs, results))
    hits = [h for _, hs in results for h in hs]
    return subs, synthesise(question, notes, hits)


class NextStep(BaseModel):
    done: bool = Field(description="True if the known facts are enough to answer")
    follow_up: str = Field("", description="The next single, simple question to look up")


def sequential_decomposition(question: str, max_steps: int = 4):
    """Dependent parts (least-to-most / self-ask): each step may use earlier answers."""
    facts, hits = [], []
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        known = "\n".join(facts) or "(nothing yet)"
        step = llm_parse(f"Question: {question}\nKnown facts:\n{known}\n\n"
                         "Are the known facts enough to answer? If not, give the next single, "
                         "simple question to look up.", NextStep)
        if step.done or not step.follow_up:
            break
        note, h = solve(step.follow_up)
        facts.append(f"- {step.follow_up} -> {note}")
        hits.extend(h)
    return facts, synthesise(question, "\n".join(facts), hits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    subs, final = parallel_decomposition(
        "Compare Rover R2 and Rover R3 on battery life, charging time and payload.")
    print("PARALLEL sub-questions:", subs, "\n", final, "\n")

    steps, final = sequential_decomposition(
        "Who does the incident commander of the March 2026 Rotterdam outage report to?")
    print("SEQUENTIAL steps:\n" + "\n".join(steps), "\n", final)
      PARALLEL sub-questions: ['What is the battery life, charging time and payload of Rover R2?', 'What is the battery life, charging time and payload of Rover R3?'] R3 has the longer battery life (12 h vs 10 h) [2][1], charges faster (60 vs 90 min to 80%) and carries twice the payload (300 kg vs 150 kg) [2][1]. SEQUENTIAL steps: - Who was the incident commander of the March 2026 Rotterdam outage? -> Mei Chen. - Who does Mei Chen report to? -> Daniel Okafor, the CEO. The incident commander, Mei Chen [1], reports to Daniel Okafor, the Chief Executive Officer [2].

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Each sub-question gets its own focused retrieval, so nothing is crowded out of the top k
      • Sub-answers make the reasoning visible and debuggable
      • Parallel mode keeps latency close to one extra round
      • Cheap model for sub-steps, strong model only for synthesis
      Cons
      • 2–6 extra LLM calls per question
      • A bad decomposition (missing or wrong part) fails silently
      • The sequential mode is slow and can loop; cap the steps
      • Over-decomposes simple questions unless you route first

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●●○○medium
      Latency
      ●●●○○medium
      Cost
      ●●●○○medium
      Quality gain
      ●●●●○high
      Maturity
      ●●●●○high

      References

      • paper Zhou et al., "Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models" ICLR 2023 · arXiv:2205.10625
      • paper Press et al., "Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models" (Self-Ask) arXiv:2210.03350
      • official repo ofirpress/self-ask inactive prompts and Bamboogle dataset; no commits since 2023
      • official repo run-llama/llama_index SubQuestionQueryEngine (parallel sub-questions over several tools)
      • community langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch decomposition notebook (answer recursively or individually)

      Compared with

      • vs B2 Multi-query: B2 rephrases one need. B3 splits several needs. A comparison question needs B3.
      • vs D1 Multi-hop (IRCoT): B3 plans its sub-questions up front (or one simple step at a time). IRCoT interleaves retrieval with full chain-of-thought reasoning and handles longer, less predictable chains.
      • vs G1 GraphRAG: for relationship chains over many entities, a graph can follow the links directly instead of asking one question per hop.

      B4 Step-back RAG

      Also called: step-back prompting, abstraction-first retrieval

      Before answering a very specific question, ask a more general "step-back" question about the underlying rule or concept, retrieve for both, and reason from the principle down to the specific case.

      How it works

      1. Abstract: a cheap LLM call writes the step-back question, for example "Who manages Mei Chen's projects in 2026?" → "What is Northwind's reporting structure?"
      2. Retrieve twice: for the original and for the step-back question. Merge and de-duplicate.
      3. Reason in two stages: the prompt asks the model to state the relevant principle or fact from the step-back results, then apply it to the specific question.

      Zheng et al. (Google DeepMind, ICLR 2024) reported gains with PaLM-2L of +7% on MMLU Physics, +11% on Chemistry, +27% on TimeQA and +7% on MuSiQue. The gains were largest on questions that need a principle or a broader time frame.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Specific cases are governed by general rules (policy, law, physics, compliance)
      • Questions include dates or details that the rule documents never mention
      • You want the answer to explain the rule, not just the verdict

      Avoid it when

      • Simple fact lookups: the general retrieval adds distracting context
      • The corpus has no "principle" documents to find

      Real-world use cases

      • Expense and travel-policy checks ("is this specific claim allowed?")
      • Legal and compliance Q&A, from the statute down to the case
      • STEM tutoring: retrieve the principle, then solve the problem

      Python (sketch)

      step_back_rag.py
      """B4 Step-back RAG: retrieve for the specific question AND a more general one."""
from query_tools import step_back                    # Chapter 10
from rag_common import ANSWER_SYSTEM, format_context, llm, make_chunks
from retrievers import HybridIndex
from sample_docs import DOCS

index = HybridIndex(make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0))


def step_back_rag(question: str, k: int = 3) -> tuple[str, str]:
    general = step_back(question)
    merged = {c.id: (s, c) for s, c in index.search(general, k=k) + index.search(question, k=k)}
    prompt = (f"Sources:\n\n{format_context(list(merged.values()))}\n\n"
              f"First state the general rule that applies (step-back question: {general}). "
              f"Then apply it to this specific case: {question}")
    return general, llm(prompt, system=ANSWER_SYSTEM)


general, reply = step_back_rag(
    "I was in Singapore on 3 July 2026 and spent 95 EUR on meals in one day. Is all of it covered?")
print("step-back question:", general, "\n", reply)

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Finds governing rules that the specific question never mentions
      • Answers explain their reasoning ("the rule is…, so…")
      • One cheap extra call; both retrievals run in parallel
      Cons
      • Too general a step-back pulls in irrelevant material
      • Doubles retrieval and context size
      • No official code; results depend on the prompt

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●●○○○low
      Cost
      ●●○○○low
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●●○○medium

      References

      • paper Zheng et al., "Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models" ICLR 2024 · arXiv:2310.06117 · no official repo
      • community langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch step-back notebook

      Compared with

      • vs B3 Decomposition: B3 goes down into simpler parts. B4 goes up to the general rule. They combine well: step back, then decompose.
      • vs B2 Multi-query: a step-back question is a deliberately more abstract variant. B2's variants stay at the same level.

      B5 Routing RAG

      Also called: query routing, semantic routing, logical routing, router query engine

      Classify each query first and send it to the right destination: a specific index, a SQL database, a tool, a different prompt, or no retrieval at all.

      How it works

      1. Define routes: each route is a destination plus a description or a handful of example utterances.
      2. Classify the query:
        • Semantic routing embeds the query and compares it with each route's examples. The semantic-router library does this in milliseconds and, from v1, can calibrate scores into probabilities so it can return "no route".
        • Logical routing asks an LLM to pick a route with structured output.
        • A cascade does both: semantic first, and the LLM only when the semantic router is unsure.
      3. Dispatch: search the chosen index (or several), call the tool, or skip retrieval. When no route is confident, fall back to searching everything.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Knowledge lives in several separate stores (wiki, tickets, SQL, code)
      • Many queries need no retrieval (greetings, general questions)
      • Routes need different prompts, models or permissions
      • A single index has grown too large and noisy

      Avoid it when

      • There is one homogeneous corpus: a router adds a failure point for no gain
      • Routes overlap heavily, so misroutes would be common (search everything and rerank instead)

      Real-world use cases

      • Enterprise assistants: HR vs IT vs finance knowledge bases
      • Support bots: billing questions to the account API, how-to questions to the docs, small talk to no retrieval
      • Guardrails: route off-topic or sensitive requests to a fixed response

      Python (sketch)

      A semantic router with the v1 semantic-router API, using the same BGE model as the rest of the guide, with an LLM router as the alternative.

      routing_rag.py
      """B5 Routing RAG: pick the right index (or none) before retrieving.

pip install -U "semantic-router[fastembed]>=1,<2" anthropic sentence-transformers bm25s pydantic
"""
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel
from semantic_router import IndexedRouter, Route
from semantic_router.encoders import FastEmbedEncoder

from rag_common import FAST_MODEL, answer, llm, llm_parse, make_chunks
from retrievers import HybridIndex
from sample_docs import DOCS

GROUPS = {"people": ["leave-policy", "org-chart"],
          "money": ["expense-policy-2025", "expense-update-2026"],
          "robots": ["rover-r2", "rover-r3", "incident-2026-03"],
          "security": ["security-policy"]}
INDEXES = {name: HybridIndex(make_chunks({d: DOCS[d] for d in ids}, size=300, overlap=0))
           for name, ids in GROUPS.items()}

# ---- semantic router: a few example utterances per route, matched in milliseconds
router = IndexedRouter(encoder=FastEmbedEncoder(name="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"), routes=[
    Route(name="people", utterances=["how much holiday do I get", "parental leave rules",
                                     "who is my manager's boss", "sick days and doctor's note"]),
    Route(name="money", utterances=["meal allowance on trips", "can I expense a taxi",
                                    "which flight class can I book", "how do I submit a receipt"]),
    Route(name="robots", utterances=["rover error code", "battery life of the R3",
                                     "robot stopped working", "firmware update problem"]),
    Route(name="security", utterances=["password rules", "report a security incident",
                                       "is laptop encryption required", "can I paste data into an AI tool"]),
    Route(name="chitchat", utterances=["hi there", "thanks a lot!", "what can you do?", "good morning"]),
])
# Without calibration the best route always wins. To allow "no route", call
# router.fit(X=[...labelled queries...], y=[route name or None, ...]) and set router.confidence_threshold.


# ---- logical router: an LLM chooses (slower, handles unusual phrasing)
class Choice(BaseModel):
    route: Literal["people", "money", "robots", "security", "chitchat"]


def llm_route(question: str) -> str:
    return llm_parse("Pick the knowledge base for this question: people (HR, leave, org chart), "
                     "money (expenses), robots (products, incidents), security, or chitchat.\n\n"
                     + question, Choice).route


def routed_rag(question: str, use_llm: bool = False) -> tuple[str | None, str]:
    route = llm_route(question) if use_llm else router(question).name
    if route == "chitchat":
        return route, llm(question, model=FAST_MODEL, max_tokens=300)
    names = [route] if route else list(INDEXES)      # no confident route: search everything
    hits = sorted((h for n in names for h in INDEXES[n].search(question, k=3)),
                  key=lambda h: h[0], reverse=True)[:4]
    return route, answer(question, hits)


for q in ["Hello!", "What does E17 mean on a rover?", "How many days of leave can I carry over?"]:
    print(q, "->", routed_rag(q))

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Smaller, cleaner search spaces give better precision
      • Skipping retrieval for chit-chat saves cost and avoids odd citations
      • Semantic routing adds only milliseconds
      • Each route can have its own prompt, model and permissions
      Cons
      • A misroute means the right document is never searched
      • Routes and their examples need upkeep as content grows
      • Cross-domain questions need several routes or a fallback

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●○○○○very low
      Cost
      ●○○○○very low
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●●●○high

      References

      • official repo aurelio-labs/semantic-router ~4.0k★, active · v1: IndexedRouter, calibrated confidence_threshold, DecisionRouter, Chain
      • docs Semantic Router v1 docs with a migration guide from 0.x (SemanticRouter/RouteLayer → IndexedRouter)
      • official repo run-llama/llama_index RouterQueryEngine, LLM and Pydantic selectors
      • official repo deepset-ai/haystack ConditionalRouter component
      • community langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch logical and semantic routing notebooks

      Compared with

      • vs E3 Adaptive RAG: E3 routes by difficulty (no, single-step or multi-step retrieval). B5 routes by topic or source. Production systems often do both.
      • vs A3 Modular: a router is the "conditional" flow pattern of modular RAG.
      • vs F1 Agentic: an agent can pick tools dynamically and call several of them. A router makes one fast decision up front.

      B6 Rewrite-Retrieve-Read

      Also called: query rewriting, query expansion, Query2doc (a related method)

      Insert a rewriting step in front of retrieval. An LLM, or a small trained rewriter, turns the user's wording into the query a search engine or index will match best.

      How it works

      1. Rewrite: turn the input into a good search query. This means expanding abbreviations, adding formal terms, removing chatter and splitting if needed. Ma et al. (EMNLP 2023) first used a prompted LLM, then a small trainable rewriter.
      2. Retrieve with the rewritten query. The paper used a web search engine, but any index works.
      3. Read: the LLM answers from the results.
      4. (Optional) train the rewriter: warm up a T5 rewriter on LLM-written rewrites, then improve it with reinforcement learning (PPO), rewarding rewrites that help the frozen reader answer correctly.

      A close relative is Query2doc (Wang et al., 2023). It appends an LLM-written pseudo-document to the query instead of replacing the query. That gives keyword search more matching terms, and it improved BM25 by 3–15% on MS MARCO and TREC DL without any fine-tuning.

      Use it when / avoid it when

      Use it when

      • Users use slang, abbreviations or internal nicknames that documents do not
      • The retriever is keyword-based or an external search API
      • You can supply a glossary of your organisation's terms

      Avoid it when

      • Queries are already well-formed: rewriting adds latency and drift risk
      • Exact strings matter (codes, quotes) and the rewriter might alter them; keep the original for BM25

      Real-world use cases

      • Internal search with heavy acronym use ("PTO", "WFH", "OOO")
      • Web-search RAG, where search engines prefer keyword queries (I4)
      • Multilingual front-ends that rewrite into the corpus language (I6)

      Python (sketch)

      rewrite_rag.py
      """B6 Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, plus Query2doc-style expansion for keyword search."""
from query_tools import rewrite                        # Chapter 10
from rag_common import FAST_MODEL, answer, llm, make_chunks
from retrievers import HybridIndex
from sample_docs import DOCS

index = HybridIndex(make_chunks(DOCS, size=300, overlap=0))
GLOSSARY = {"PTO": "paid annual leave", "rollover": "carry-over", "WFH": "remote work",
            "per diem": "daily meal allowance", "bot": "Rover robot"}


def query2doc(question: str) -> str:
    """Expand (not replace): repeat the query so its own words keep weight, add a pseudo-doc."""
    pseudo = llm(f"Write a short passage that answers: {question}", model=FAST_MODEL, max_tokens=200)
    return " ".join([question] * 5 + [pseudo])           # the paper repeats the query 5 times


for q in ["PTO rollover?", "per diem abroad?"]:
    variants = {"raw": q, "rewrite": rewrite(q, GLOSSARY), "query2doc": query2doc(q)}
    for name, text in variants.items():
        top = [index.chunks[i].id for i, _ in index.sparse(text, 3)]    # BM25 shows the effect best
        print(f"{q!r:20s} {name:10s} -> {top}")
    hits = index.search(variants["rewrite"], k=3)
    print("   answer:", answer(q, hits), "\n")

      Pros and cons

      Pros
      • Simple: one cheap call, no index changes
      • A glossary injects organisation knowledge the embedder lacks
      • The rewrite is a readable log line, which makes debugging easier
      • A trainable version can learn from your own feedback
      Cons
      • Can alter or drop exact terms (keep the original query too)
      • Adds latency in front of every search
      • The RL-trained rewriter needs a training pipeline; the official code is inactive

      Ratings

      Build complexity
      ●●○○○low
      Latency
      ●●○○○low
      Cost
      ●●○○○low
      Quality gain
      ●●●○○medium
      Maturity
      ●●●○○medium

      References

      • paper Ma et al., "Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models" EMNLP 2023 · arXiv:2305.14283
      • official repo xbmxb/RAG-query-rewriting inactive ~230★ · no commits since Feb 2024
      • paper Wang, Yang & Wei, "Query2doc: Query Expansion with Large Language Models" arXiv:2303.07678 · +3–15% for BM25

      Compared with

      • vs A6 Conversational: A6 resolves references to the chat history. B6 translates into document vocabulary. One combined prompt can do both.
      • vs B1 HyDE: HyDE targets dense search with a fake answer. Query2doc does the same for BM25 by appending the fake answer to the query.

      Family B side by side

      TypeTransforms the query into…Extra callsMain riskBest paired with
      B1 HyDEA fake answer passage (for dense search)1 LLMInvented domain factsBM25 on the original query
      B2 Multi-query / FusionSeveral paraphrases, fused with RRF1 LLM + N searchesGain vanishes behind a rerankerMeasure with your reranker on
      B3 DecompositionSimple sub-questions2–6 LLMMissing or wrong sub-questionA router that skips simple questions
      B4 Step-backA more general question as well1 LLM + 1 searchToo general, distractingRule- and policy-heavy corpora
      B5 RoutingA destination (index, tool, none)0 (semantic) or 1MisroutesA search-everything fallback
      B6 Rewrite-Retrieve-ReadA better search query (or an expanded one)1 LLMDropping exact termsA glossary + the original query

      Key takeaways

      • Query transformation is the cheapest family to experiment with, because the index never changes. It is also the easiest to fool yourself with, so measure every type inside your full pipeline.
      • Keep the user's original words somewhere in every pipeline: in BM25, in the reranker, or as one of the fused variants.
      • Routing and decomposition change what gets searched. HyDE, rewriting and multi-query change how the same thing is searched.
      • A strong reranker reduces the value of recall-boosting tricks like B2. Add them only where your evaluation shows a recall gap.

      Quick check

      HyDE made retrieval worse for "E42". Why, and what is the fix?

      The LLM does not know Northwind's private error codes, so its hypothetical passages describe made-up meanings (network timeouts, disk quotas). The averaged vector drifts towards those topics. The fix is to keep BM25 on the user's original words (the hyde_hybrid variant), or to route code-like queries away from HyDE.

      "Compare R2 and R3 battery life" gets a half answer from naive RAG. Which type fixes it, B2 or B3?

      B3. The question has two different targets (two product sheets). B2's paraphrases would all ask the same combined question, and one top-k might still miss one sheet. Decomposition retrieves for each product separately.

      When does a semantic router return "no route"?

      In semantic-router v1, only after calibration. You call fit() on labelled examples, including some labelled None, and set confidence_threshold. Without calibration the best-scoring route always wins, so always add a fallback.
